title: Citation
text:
If you use this software, please cite it as below.

Maj M (2026). pyplatypus: computer vision for medical imaging. Version 0.8.0a41. https://github.com/maju116/pyplatypus

@software{maj2026pyplatypus,
  author  = {Michal Maj},
  title   = {pyplatypus: computer vision for medical imaging},
  year    = {2026},
  version = {0.8.0a41},
  url     = {https://github.com/maju116/pyplatypus}
}
The machine-readable form is CITATION.cff, which is what GitHub’s “Cite this repository” reads.
The R package is cited separately, because it is a separate piece of software: citation("rplatypus") in R, or the Citation page on its site.

title: Change Log
text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.


hc18-unet, the fifth published name and the first whose headline figure is not an overlap score. maju116/rplatypus#205.



hc18-unet in the weights registry, pinned to Hub commit 9c6d8599: a U-Net at 544x800 for the fetal skull in 2D ultrasound, trained on HC18 and published for measuring head circumference in millimetres. CC BY 4.0 rather than MIT, because HC18 is - the same bracket as fives-unet and not a new one, read from the dataset’s own Zenodo record (10.5281/zenodo.1327317).
Median absolute error 2.44 mm against the sonographer’s measurement over 199 held-out images, mean 3.84 mm, worst 48.07 mm; 3.41 mm against the circumference of the truth mask, which is the model’s own contribution rather than the dataset’s drawing convention. The median and the mean are both published because they disagree: half the cases are inside 2.44 mm and a tenth outside 7.23 mm, so the mean describes the tail.
The entry warns the reader off the Dice, and that is the measurement rather than modesty. The Dice is 0.9494 and it orders the cases differently from the millimetres - Spearman 0.153 on this run - with 85 of the 144 cases scoring 0.95 or better still wrong by more than 2 mm. A ragged boundary barely moves an integral over a region and a systematically fat or thin mask moves it linearly, which are the two errors Dice is respectively most and least able to see, and they are the wrong way round for anybody measuring a length. So the description leads with millimetres and names the Dice only inside the sentence saying not to choose on it, and a test asserts that order.
examples/publish_hc18_weights.py, which trains the model measure_fetal_head_circumference.py documents and writes the file, the sidecar and the card. It imports specification(), prepare() and measure() from that example rather than copying them, and a test holds the two scripts’ defaults equal for every argument that shapes the model. It uploads nothing: the upload is the author’s.





The Spearman was quoted as a property of the task and it is one draw. The publishing script’s docstring said the two orderings disagree with “a Spearman of about 0.6”, “measured on the run this script publishes”, while the run it publishes measured 0.153. Three runs of the one recipe gave 0.620, 0.435 and 0.153: the direction holds in all three and the magnitude moves fourfold, and it moves the same way each time - the better the Dice, the less it orders anything, which is what a rank statistic does over a narrower spread. The card now carries all three in a table generated from a constant, and says three runs is a direction and not a law.
Two tests that could not have failed, both in this release’s own test for the registry description and both found by mutating the entry rather than by reading them. median, mean = 2.44, 3.84 followed by assert median < mean compares two literals and is true whatever the entry says, so swapping the two figures in the description left it green; and "85 of the 144 cases" in description survives the count becoming 185, because it is a substring of it. Both assertions now read the numbers out of the description by their role and compare what was read.
An interpolated block broke the card’s indentation. textwrap.dedent strips the common leading prefix, a block inserted at column 0 leaves none, and the whole section came out indented eight spaces - which the Hub renders as preformatted text. Found by reading the generated card, and now held by a test asserting it starts at column 0.





batch_size leaves the reported score. maju116/rplatypus#196.



An epoch’s numbers are weighted by the examples that produced them, not by the number of batches. _run_epoch divided each total by the batch count, which weights the examples of a short last batch by batch_size / last_size - so a split’s reported figure moved with a training setting that has no business in it. Measured on 199 validation cases: 2.3e-04 at batch_size 4 and 3.5e-03 at 32, and the gap is not monotone in the setting, because its size depends on which cases land in the short batch.
This was never a second definition of anything, which is why it is a fix and not a migration. The per-batch value is already the mean over the examples in that batch - overlaps sums the spatial dimensions only and SegmentationMetric.reduce ends in per_class.mean() over the batch - so a mean of means was reaching for the mean over examples and mis-weighting one batch of it.
evaluate() is the mean over cases, which its own docstring has claimed since at was added. It was not: the at="model" branch called trainer.evaluate(loader) without case names and got the batch mean, while the paragraph above it said “the pooling is the same in both, deliberately: the mean over cases” and the at="source" branch’s comment said it matched at="model" on purpose. Both rested on something the code did not do. evaluate() now passes the case names, so a tiled run’s tiles are pooled into cases rather than averaged as tiles - the reassembly score_cases argues for.
On a tiled run that second half is the larger change by an order of magnitude. Recomputed from the stored per-case rows of every FIVES arm on this disk: the figure moves +0.033 to +0.049 of Dice on the tiled arms and by 1e-9 on the untiled ones. The measured tables in both packages’ articles and vignettes do not move, because every one of them was built from the per-case route already - focal 0.8673, generalized_dice 0.8504, iou 0.8309, dice 0.8127, and the headline 0.8828 / 0.8014 are all the per-case means. This release brings evaluate() into agreement with prose that was already right.
evaluate()’s figure is now exactly the mean of evaluate_cases()’s own rows, which is the consequence the issue was filed for, and a test pins it at rel=1e-9 where it used to read abs=0.05. That tolerance was hiding nothing on its fixture - 12 samples at batch_size 2 is six full batches - which is why the test that replaces it scores one trained model through six batch sizes, five of which do not divide the split.
An epoch’s mean and its _worst are two readings of one set of per-case scores. They were computed from the accumulator separately; now the scores are taken once, so an epoch cannot report a worst case that is not among the cases its mean covers.





Trainer.evaluate takes cases. It was a one-line wrapper on the training path and is now the one place the difference is stated: a training pass is shuffled and has no case identity, so its line is the mean over examples; a caller scoring a split has the names.
best_model() needs no change and may answer differently. It ranks on evaluate(), so it gets this for free - and where two models sat within the pooling’s own shift of each other, the winner can change. Recomputed on the eleven-loss FIVES table: the winner is unchanged and its margin over the runner-up grows from +0.0006 to +0.0033, while the one pair that swaps rank differs by 1e-4, which that table already called a tie.





The detector’s epoch has a different defect and its own issue, maju116/rplatypus#218. DetectionTrainer._run_epoch divides by batches too, but every component of the YOLO loss is normalised by the number of objects in the batch, so averaging over batches weights a frame of thirty cells like a frame of two platelets. The repair there is a ratio of sums at the object level and needs LossParts to carry what it divided by - a different mechanism, and one release should not carry two poolings’ changes. No published detection number moves: the AP table is scored per image through its own path.
The published weights are retrained separately. restore_best selected on a quantity this release changes, and the histories do not store per-case scores per epoch, so which epoch a run would now keep cannot be recomputed from disk. Bounded from what is stored: on HC18’s run the mis-weighting can move an epoch by up to 5.8e-03 while the nearest rival sat 1.4e-03 behind, so the selection is not provably the one a correct weighting would have made.





Millilitres, square millimetres and millimetres, in the engine rather than in the R package. maju116/pyplatypus#270.



pyplatypus.measure, and five exported names: mask_volume, instance_sizes, largest_filled_object, ellipse_axes and ellipse_circumference. A voxel count is not a measurement - the same lesion is 4,000 voxels on one scanner and 12,000 on another - and until now this package had no way to turn one into the number a report is written in.
None of this arithmetic is new and none of it was reachable. mask_volume and instance_sizes were implemented in the R package, in R; voxel_ml was computed in inst/python/platypus_shim.py, which is Python shipped by the R package; and the head circumference was in examples/, which the wheel does not contain (include = ["pyplatypus*"]). So a pip install pyplatypus user asking how big a finding is got a voxel count. The third release in a row to move a mechanism off the wrong side of the bridge, after 0.8.0a29’s volume writer and 0.8.0a38’s device_report() - and the second to come out of that same file.
This package had also promised the first one twice and never had it: volume_spacing()’s docstring says it is needed by “anything reporting a volume in millilitres rather than in voxels - which is the number a clinician asked for”, and save_volumes() says “every volume in millilitres reads position and spacing out of it”. Both true, neither naming a function. The same shape as save_class_masks before 0.8.0a23.
MeasureError, so a refusal here is one kind rather than a ValueError. R turns it into platypus_measure_error by the rule it applies to every kind the engine has.





spacing multiplies the coordinates, not the answer - the one decision in this release that is not a name. For a volume or an area the two are the same thing, because a count scales by the product of the sides either way. For a length they are not: an ellipse’s perimeter is not separable in its axes, so there is no number to multiply a pixel-space circumference by unless the pixels happen to be square.
Measured on a circle of radius 100 px with spacing=(2, 1), which is an ellipse of semi-axes 200 and 100: scaling the coordinates gives 968.9 against 968.8 integrated, where the two scalings somebody would reach for answer 628.3 and 1256.7. HC18’s pixels are square, so examples/measure_fetal_head_circumference.py was correct and would have stopped being correct on the first anisotropic 2D dataset. Its own composition on square pixels is now that claim’s control, and the two have to agree to twelve digits.
examples/measure_fetal_head_circumference.py calls the engine instead of carrying 61 lines of its own geometry, which is what makes this a move rather than a second copy. fill() stays in the example: turning a sonographer’s open curve into the region it encloses is a convention of one dataset’s annotations rather than a measurement.
The configuration guide’s millilitre section calls mask_volume. The division it showed is correct and says why - at target_spacing: [1, 1, 1] a voxel is exactly one cubic millimetre - three sections before the same page says resampling is offered rather than imposed. Documentation to be copied, with a precondition the reader is invited to drop and a failure that is silent; a function taking spacing cannot fail that way.





What the work will run on, decided and reported in one place. maju116/pyplatypus#265, #266.



device_report(), exported: the torch version, the CUDA build, which accelerator will be used, what to call it, the architectures a CUDA build carries, and gpu_present_but_unusable - the one field worth acting on.
It is not new code. It has existed since the R package was written, in inst/python/platypus_shim.py - a file of Python shipped by the R package, where no user of this one could reach it. So a Python user whose card the build cannot use was told nothing, while an R user was told twice. The same move as 0.8.0a29’s volume writer: a mechanism that had been living on the wrong side of the bridge.
gpu_present_but_unusable reads device_count() rather than is_available(), and that is the whole subtlety: a CUDA 13 build on a Pascal card returns 1 from the first and False from the second - torch enumerates the card and cannot initialise it. Testing for zero detects nothing.





pick_device() asked about CUDA and nothing else, so every Apple Silicon Mac - and this project’s own macOS CI - trained on its processor with a working mps backend present in the same wheel. It asks cuda, mps and xpu in that order now, and the order is a decision: every published set of weights here was trained on CUDA, so a number from another backend is not obviously comparable.
A backend that raises while answering is_available() counts as unavailable. A build with no CUDA support has done exactly that, and a chooser that propagates it turns a usable processor into a failed run.





pick_device lives in pyplatypus.device and the trainer re-exports it. Two answers to what will this run on - one choosing, one reporting - cannot be allowed to disagree, and a test pairs them.





Five mutations, each caught - but two of them only after the tests learned to fake a machine this one is not. On hardware with CUDA, restricting the backends to CUDA alone changes no answer and a report that hardcodes "cuda" is right by accident: the defect this release fixes is invisible to any test that asks the real machine. Four tests now monkeypatch the backends and ask what an Apple Silicon or Intel machine would be told.
tests/test_public_api.py reported device_name() as a call a message tells somebody to make. It was a false positive of its own pattern - the scanner read the span between a dict key’s closing quote and the next literal’s opening one as a quoted sentence - and the call moved onto its own line rather than the test being loosened. Its docstring already records it catching its author once; this is the second shape.





A fourth callback hook, and the averager that needed it. maju116/rplatypus#203.



Callback.on_batch_end, fired after every optimiser step on the training pass, with state.step counting steps since training began. The protocol had three moments and none of them was a step.
It cannot stop the run, and returns nothing to say so. A run that stopped mid epoch would leave a record with training numbers and no validation ones, and every reader of the history - best(), the callbacks that watch it, R’s training_history() - would have to learn that a row may be half a row. stop_after’s budget is therefore still the budget plus one epoch, which its own description says.
ema, an exponential moving average of the weights updated every step. swa’s sibling and the reason the hook exists: a decay of 0.999 is 0.999 per step, which over 60 epochs of 200 batches is 12,000 updates and a half-life of about 700 steps. Announced per epoch the same number would do almost nothing, so offering it that way would have published a name whose documented values mean something else.
Buffers are averaged alongside the weights, which is the difference from swa: a uniform average of weights has batch-normalisation statistics belonging to no epoch, so swa recomputes them with a pass over the training data; an exponential average that also averages the buffers carries its own and needs no second pass.
One averager per run. ema and swa together are refused: both replace the model when training ends, so the second would average what the first had already written, in whichever order the list happened to have them.





Five mutations, each caught: firing the hook on validation batches fails 1 test, a step counter that never advances fails 1, an average that is counted but not folded fails 2, a run with no steps that still gets the average fails 1, and two averagers allowed fails 1.
One of those was not caught the first time, and the test was the problem again. AveragedModel is built from the model at on_train_begin, so with the weights untouched its snapshot and the model are the same numbers and writing one over the other is invisible. The test now moves the weights before asking whether they were left alone. The same shape as 0.8.0a35’s range assertion: a check that cannot tell the failure from the success.





The number this package tells everybody to read becomes one a callback can watch. maju116/rplatypus#205.



val_<metric>_worst in every epoch, for the metrics whose counts pool into one score: the lowest any single case scored. summarise_cases has said since it was written that “the minimum is the one nobody publishes and everybody should - a model averaging 0.86 that scores 0.11 on some patient has a failure mode, and the mean is where it hides”, and then every callback in this package watched a mean. A declaration beside a mechanism that did not describe it.
monitor: val_dice_worst works now, and so does a when condition on it.
Validation only. The training loader is shuffled, so a case has no identity in that pass and there is nothing honest to pool by.





score_cases and the epoch share one definition of a case’s score, _PerCase. The pooling is a ratio of sums - a case’s tiles, or a patient’s slices, are added up and the formula applied once - and that arithmetic now exists in one place rather than in the two that report it.





The worst case costs 5.6% of an epoch, on 40 cases at 128x128 on this machine’s processor: 620.9 ms of training plus 366.3 ms of validation becomes 1042.6 ms. It is computed in the pass that already happened - the counts are three reductions on a batch that has been forwarded anyway - rather than in a second pass, which would have doubled every epoch’s validation to report a number the first one had the parts for.
The share of the validation pass alone came out 23.3% and then 15.1% on two runs of the same measurement, so the epoch figure is the one worth quoting and the other is noise.
Five mutations, each caught: reporting the best instead of the worst fails 4 tests, replacing a case’s accumulation with its last piece fails 1, not noticing more examples than names fails 1, not reporting it at all fails 5, and a spec that does not admit the key fails 1.





The quiet failure of segmentation becomes a number, and then a refusal. maju116/rplatypus#206.



Every epoch reports foreground, for both passes: the share of the prediction that is not background. Beside the loss rather than among the metrics, and the distinction is the point - nothing is compared against the truth, so this is not a measure of quality. It answers is this still a segmentation rather than is it a good one.
Reported unconditionally rather than offered as a metric to opt into, because a collapse you have to opt into noticing is one you will not notice. A model predicting background everywhere is not visible in the numbers it already produced: with include_background the Dice is a mean over class channels and the background channel is nearly perfect, so a collapsed model reports around 0.5 while its loss falls.
terminate_on_collapse, terminate_on_nan’s quiet sibling: it ends the run when the foreground share stays at or below floor for patience epochs. A floor rather than a test for zero, because 0.01% foreground on a target that is 14% foreground has collapsed in every sense that matters; and a patience, because an early epoch legitimately predicts almost nothing. It can watch the training share instead, which answers a different question - a model collapsing on data it has seen has a different problem from one collapsing only on data it has not.





evaluate()’s rows carry foreground. It is the one column there that is not a quality measure, and it is there for the reason load_shape is: a collapsed model reports a plausible Dice, and a table that cannot show the foreground beside it is a table somebody misreads.





The test fixture collapses. Three 32x32 images trained for a few epochs predict no foreground at all - share exactly 0.0 - which is a fair demonstration of what this release is for and makes that fixture useless for comparing the reported number against a computed one. That test evaluates an untrained model instead, and says why.
One mutation was not caught the first time, and the test was the problem. Deleting the accumulation entirely left every test passing, because the assertion was 0.0 <= share <= 1.0 and a counter that was never added to is zero - which is in range. The test compares values now, with the fixture’s own share asserted non-zero first.





Three answers to one question - when may this callback act, and on what evidence - shipped together because they are one vocabulary rather than three features. maju116/rplatypus#199, #201, #207.



early_stopping takes a warm-up: start as a fraction of the run or start_epoch as an epoch, exactly one of the two. patience alone could not express it, because it is in force for the whole run: a model that needs fifteen epochs before its validation curve means anything forced patience > 15 permanently, paying the same slack at the end where the point was to cut quickly.
It delays the stopping and nothing else. An epoch inside the warm-up can still be the best one and restore_best can still return to it - those are the best weights the run has if it ends for another reason, and discarding them to tidy the bookkeeping would lose a real answer.
swa takes start_epoch as the exclusive alternative to its start fraction. The same concept and therefore the same two words, by §3A. Its refusal reads model_fields_set rather than the value, because start carries a default and 0.75 is both the default and a perfectly good thing to ask for.
model_checkpoint takes when: thresholds that must all hold before anything is written, {val_dice: 0.9, val_loss: 0.2}. The direction is derived, not configured - anything ending in loss has to be below its threshold and everything else above it, which is the rule monitor already uses, so there is no above/below to get backwards. The keys are checked against what the model actually reports when the specification is built, the same validator that refuses an impossible monitor.
when and save_best_only are both gates, not alternatives: with both, a file is written when the watched number improves and every threshold holds. And a run whose conditions never held says so when it ends, because silence there is indistinguishable from a callback nobody configured, and a run that kept no weights is worth knowing about before somebody goes looking for the file.
stop_after, a wall-clock budget in hours. An epoch cap is the wrong instrument: how long an epoch takes is a property of the data and the shape, and the cases where this matters are the ones where that was not what anybody expected. Checked at the end of an epoch, so the real limit is the budget plus one epoch - said in the field’s description rather than discovered. The run’s stop_reason names the clock, so a run that ran out of time does not read as a run that converged.





A fraction and an epoch are two fields in both places, never one that accepts either: 1 and 1.0 are the same value once YAML is parsed, so “epoch one” and “the whole run” would be one configuration and the mistake would be silent - both are in range for both meanings.
Eight mutations, each caught: ignoring the warm-up fails 2 tests, letting it gate the best fails 3, reading a fraction as an epoch fails 1, turning the conditions into an OR fails 4, reading every condition as above fails 1, staying silent about a run that wrote nothing fails 1, a clock that never runs out fails 1, and an unchecked condition key fails 1.





Two learning-rate schedules, and the discovery that the one we had could not be combined with the thing its own docstring said it combined with. maju116/rplatypus#200.



linear_annealing - the same shape as cosine_annealing with a straight line instead of a curve: min_lr, an optional epochs, each parameter group descending from its own initial rate.
step_decay - multiply by factor at fixed points, which is how published recipes are written: divide by ten at epochs 30 and 60. every for a period or milestones for the epochs a paper names, exactly one of the two, because every: 30 and milestones: [30] are different schedules and one field holding either would be read as whichever the author happened to type. The rate is computed as initial * factor ** drops rather than by multiplying what is there, so replaying an epoch cannot double a drop.





A schedule beside reduce_lr_on_plateau silently erased the plateau’s cuts, and cosine_annealing’s docstring had promised the opposite since it shipped. It said “a run may want both: a cosine floor with a plateau rescue on top is a legitimate recipe”. Measured instead of believed - the same six epochs, with a loss that never improves:
epoch   both configured   the plateau alone
  1          0.097553           0.100000
  2          0.090451           0.010000
  3          0.079389           0.001000
  4          0.065451           0.000100
  5          0.050000           0.000010
  6          0.034549           0.000001
The left column is the pure cosine from 0.1, digit for digit: a schedule recomputes the rate from the optimiser’s initial value at the end of every epoch, so whatever the plateau cut is gone before the next one begins. The spec refuses the pair now, by name, and the docstring says what the code does.
Two schedules in one model are refused for the same reason, where before the last one in the list won silently.





build_callbacks declares an order instead of inheriting one. swa pins a constant rate once averaging starts and a schedule recomputes it every epoch, so which one an epoch ended with depended on where they sat in the list and nothing said so. swa is moved last - a constant tail rate is the whole point of configuring it - and everything else keeps the order it was written in.
cosine_annealing, linear_annealing and step_decay share a base class, so the horizon, the per-group initial rates and the refusal to run without knowing the run’s length exist once rather than three times.





The honest comparison becomes a thing to ask for rather than a thing to write yourself. maju116/rplatypus#187.



evaluate(at="source") and evaluate_cases(at="source"): every prediction goes back onto the grid of the file it came from and is scored against the truth as stored. at="model" is the default and is unchanged, because changing it would silently restate every number anybody has written down.
What it is for: scored each through its own loader, a model at input_shape: [512, 512] is measured against a truth reduced to 512 while a model that tiles 2048 is measured against the truth as stored. Both are a real Dice of a real prediction against a real mask and they answer different questions. Measured on retinal vessels, that difference reported a resized model at +0.0187 where the honest figure was +0.0033 - 5.7 times

with the bias reversed on clDice, because upsampling smooths a prediction: better against a skeleton, worse against a boundary.

The grid is the files’ own and cannot be named by the caller. A named grid resamples the truth, so the thing every model is judged against would itself become an interpolation chosen by whoever typed the number - which is the defect this argument exists to remove. Here the truth is never touched; only predictions move.
Streamed. One case at a time through predict_stream, because the predictions are at full resolution and tiling exists for images too large to resize: 200 FIVES retinas at 2048 are 6.7 GB of probabilities, so this grid is exactly where holding the split would hurt most.
The spacing is each file’s own, which is what makes surface_dice mean millimetres here. On the model’s grid every case shares target_spacing by construction; on this one they do not, so the metrics are built per case.
Two prices, both named in the prose rather than discovered: interpolating probabilities softens a boundary, and where the forward crop cut anatomy away the inverse pads it with background - not examined rather than nothing there. For a comparison the second is correct rather than unfair, but a 0.000 arriving that way is a result and not a bug.
The load_shape column reads source when scored there, because what it has always meant is the grid the row’s numbers were computed on. The loss is not reported: a loss is defined by the objective a model trained with, on the grid it trained on.





The comparability warning now names evaluate(at='source') instead of describing what a reader would have to build. It had pointed at predict(space='source') since 0.8.0a30, which is the raw material rather than the answer - an instruction addressed to a human in the place where a mechanism now exists.
Dataset.to_target() is the three-way expansion __getitem__ used to end with, and Dataset.target_as_stored() reads a sample’s masks at the size its files hold. Reading size=None as as stored goes through the same reader as everything else: the three namings are the part that must not exist twice.





evaluate() means over batches and evaluate_cases() pools by counts, so a split’s figure depends on batch_size. at="source" deliberately matches evaluate()’s pooling so that the argument changes the grid and nothing else; the two poolings differ by 4e-5 on six similar cases and by more on unequal ones. Filed as maju116/rplatypus#196 rather than changed here, because changing it restates every number this project has published.
The warning cannot be narrowed to physical extent, and does not need to be. target_spacing lives on the data spec, so every model in one evaluate() shares it and the extent differs only by load_shape, which the warning already compares. The case that motivated the narrowing - three arms at one load_shape and three spacings - is three separate runs, which one engine never sees side by side. at="source" is what makes those comparable, because the files’ grid is shared by construction.





One defect, and it is the package disagreeing with its own naming convention. pyplatypus#256.



A checkpoint named .safetensors was written as a torch archive and then refused by the reader its own extension had selected. model_checkpoint called torch.save whatever the path said; load_into chose safetensors.load_file when the suffix was .safetensors. So the round trip failed with SafetensorError: Error while deserializing header: header too large - an error about a header, raised on a file that has none, and naming neither the cause nor the field that caused it.
The configuration that breaks is the one in this package’s own guide, on both sides: - {name: model_checkpoint, monitor: val_iou, path: runs/best.safetensors} appears in guide.qmd and in the R package’s configuration vignette. Every published set in the registry is .safetensors, so a person naming a checkpoint that way is following the convention this package teaches. Found while writing #202’s example, which had to work around it with a .pt and a comment.
Fixed in both directions, because they are not alternatives:

save_state() writes the format the extension names, and is now the one writer - export_weights() and the checkpoint callback had been two, which is the defect stated from the other end.
read_state() reads what the file is, from the first bytes: a zip is a torch archive, an 8-byte header length followed by { is safetensors. So a file written by an older version of this package loads under whatever name it was given, and renaming a file never changes whether it can be read.
A file that is neither now says what it begins with, instead of letting a library report a header that was never there.

Three mutations, each caught: a writer that ignores the extension fails 3 tests, a reader that trusts it fails 2, and a reader that returns {} rather than refusing fails 1.
And the same defect turned out to be inside torch, one layer down. torch.load reads the name as well: on torch 2.14.1 a path ending .safetensors is forwarded to safetensors.torch.load_file, while torch.save still writes a zip under that name - so the first fix failed every CI job on a suite that was green here, where torch is 2.7.1. read_state() hands torch.load an open file rather than a path, because a handle has no name to dispatch on. The fixtures were rebuilt the same way: an archive is written to a .pt and renamed, so the test does not depend on which side of torch’s own disagreement wins, and it asserts the file really is an archive before reading it.





model_checkpoint’s path description says the extension decides the format. The R package’s prose for it is unchanged until its pin moves, which is when the field-prose ledger asks.





Two things a table and a writer could not say, and the second one is 0.8.0a29’s own half finished. pyplatypus#251, maju116/rplatypus#187.



evaluate() says which grid each row was scored on, and warns when the rows do not share one. Each model is scored through its own loader, so a model at input_shape: [512, 512] is measured against a truth reduced to 512 while a model that tiles 2048 is measured against the truth as stored. Both numbers are a real Dice of a real prediction against a real mask, and they are not answers to the same question.
Measured on retinal vessels: that difference reported a resized model at +0.0187 where the honest figure was +0.0033 - the reported figure 5.7 times the real one - and the bias has the opposite sign on clDice, because upsampling a prediction smooths it and a smoothed vessel agrees better with a skeleton and worse with a boundary. So a comparison reporting one of the two metrics is wrong in a direction set by which one it picked.
The load_shape column is permanent and the warning fires only when the grids differ, which is the split that keeps a warning worth reading. It sits beside the metrics for the same reason loss_function sits beside loss - it is what decides whether two rows may be compared, and a table without it cannot be read correctly a month later. A string rather than the tuple, because this table crosses into R as a data frame and a list column is not plain data; the test that says so caught it on the first run.
Nothing here rescores. Putting two models on one grid is a thing to ask for rather than to do silently, and it is not offered yet - rplatypus#187 carries that decision.
save_volumes accepts a label map, not only channels-last probabilities. The R package’s predict() returns class indices where this one returns probabilities, so forwarding meant expanding a label map back into one-hot - a gigabyte of float32 for a 512-cubed volume - in order to collapse it again. #251, and it is what lets rplatypus::save_volumes() forward and the copy in that package’s shim be deleted.
A label map skips the overlap refusal, and that is not a hole: the refusal protects the collapse, because an argmax over channels silently picks one of the classes a voxel is in. An integer per voxel cannot express an overlap in the first place.
A bare rank-4 array is refused rather than guessed at: a stack of label maps (n, d, h, w) and one volume’s channels (d, h, w, c) have the same rank and nothing in the array says which. save_class_masks names the same ambiguity for pictures and the R package resolves it the same way, so a caller meets one rule rather than a third. save_class_volumes still takes channels only, because a binary file per class is a question about channels and a label map has none.





One writer, and it is the one this package’s own refusal has been telling people to use since 0.8.0a23. pyplatypus#249.



save_volumes and save_class_volumes: a predicted volume written as NIfTI onto the geometry of the scan it came from. Integer labels, int16, with reference required rather than optional because there is no sensible affine to invent.
The affine is the point. A mask array on its own cannot be laid over its scan: every viewer, every registration tool and every volume in millilitres reads position and spacing out of it, and a file carrying the wrong one is either silently misplaced or rejected. The reference is read through _load_canonical, the same function read_volume uses, because the reader reorients every volume to the closest canonical axes - so a prediction is in canonical space, and writing it with the file’s stored affine would produce a mask reflected or transposed with respect to its scan, opening in any viewer without complaint. The test that earns its keep writes a scan stored the other way round and demands the mask read back equal; mutated to use the stored affine, it fails along with the affine test beside it.
save_volumes refuses an overlapping prediction rather than taking the argmax, which is onehot_to_colours’s refusal one dimension along: a label map holds one integer per voxel, so a voxel in both the core and the whole tumour would be written as whichever channel read higher. Those are regions, and save_class_volumes is where they go - one binary volume per class, which is the writer BraTS actually needs, since regions was motivated by a dataset that stores its overlapping regions as volumes.
It also refuses case names that repeat, which is not a theoretical tidiness: volume datasets keep one directory per case with the same ct.nii.gz inside each, so names taken from the sources collide, every mask is written to one path, and the count of written paths is still right. Losing five masks of six while reporting success is the worst outcome available here.





save_class_masks’s refusal now names functions that exist. It has said “write each channel as NIfTI with the geometry of its source instead” since 0.8.0a23, and the only way to follow that instruction was to leave this package. The same shape as #230 and #231, one step worse: those were promises about this package’s own surface, and this was an instruction a reader could not carry out at all.




Not written from nothing. rplatypus/inst/python/platypus_shim.py has carried a correct write_volumes since the volume work landed - Python, shipped inside the R package, doing a thing this package’s own reader is half of. A pip install pyplatypus user never had it. The shim’s copy is the one to delete when R’s pin moves to this release; two implementations of an affine decision is the shape that keeps costing this project.




Two features and one lesson they share: a mechanism that existed twice, and a mechanism that existed once and was reached through a list somebody had to remember.
pyplatypus#236 - what a published file of instance weights may fill in for a reader, and the sentence that explained why it could not. pyplatypus#91 - one binary mask file per class, which is the half of multilabel segmentation that 2026-10-12’s decision deferred.



An instance model adopts architecture, blocks, filters and separation from the weights it names, where the specification stayed silent - the mechanism the semantic engine has had since 0.8.0a13 and the detection engine since 0.3.0a12, now with the one entry this task cannot be read without.
separation is that entry and it is the first adopted value that is not a shape: dsbowl-instances is a rim at width 2, which is a training decision rather than a geometry, and no reader can guess it. It is adopted as a block built from the sidecar’s separation_settings and then re-validated with the rest of the model, so an adopted value faces every check a written one does. The engine prints what it took - the argument for adopting a training decision at all is that the reader still sees it, and the run record carries it as if written.
What this cost a reader before, measured by writing R’s instance vignette: the shortest useful thing anybody could do with the published weights named four of this model’s fields, and the only place three of them are written down is a model card.
 u_net("objects", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
       separation = separation_rim(width = 2),
       weights = "dsbowl-instances", fit = FALSE)
is now
 u_net("objects", input_shape = c(256, 256),
       weights = "dsbowl-instances", fit = FALSE)
separation_settings is written by the engine into every instance weights file it exports. dsbowl-instances carries it because its publishing script added it by hand, so an adoption reading that key would have worked for exactly one file in the world. It stays out of the fingerprint’s comparison on purpose: a 2-pixel rim is both the right shape and the right meaning for a model asking for 3, which is the ordinary way to start one run from another.
classes_from: one binary mask file per class, the fourth way of saying what a mask’s classes are and the only one that can express classes which overlap independently - a vessel crossing an organ, or two annotators’ masks of the same structure. One pattern per class, in class order, matched against a sample’s mask files through the same matcher channels_from uses: exactly one file per pattern, no file matched twice, no file left out. pyplatypus#91, which has been open since 2022 and is this half of it; the author’s decision of 2026-10-12 was nested regions first, and deferred this rather than dropping it.
The whole feature is a reader. Everything from the target onwards arrived with regions in 0.8.0a14 and reads data.multilabel, which this naming now also answers: a sigmoid per channel, the binary forms of cce and focal, metrics thresholding each channel, a prediction that is a stack, save_masks refusing an overlapping prediction and save_class_masks writing one file per class. What was missing is the step before it. unite_masks takes the element-wise maximum of a sample’s mask files - the Data Science Bowl ships one per nucleus - and that maximum is exactly where per-class identity is destroyed: two overlapping annotations become one blob and nothing downstream can tell there were two. The test that carries this release is the control for it: the same two files, united, are one blob with two values; coded, they are two classes and their overlap.
One integer per voxel, still. The coded form sets a bit per class, so tiling and augmentation are untouched - both operate on a single-channel array - and the expansion to channels happens in the last step before the loss, where np.eye(n_class)[classes] and the regions’ table already live. This is the third expansion and the only one that is arithmetic rather than a table: a table of combinations would need two to the power of the classes, where the regions’ table needs one row per label value. Lossless to 62 classes in an int64 and refused above that rather than wrapping into a class nobody asked for.
The threshold for in this class is above zero rather than a midpoint, which is the decision in it worth not re-taking: these files arrive as both 0/255 pictures and 0/1 label maps, and >= 128 reads every voxel of the second kind as background - a whole dataset silently empty, scoring a Dice of 0 with nothing to say why.
_class_fingerprint records the patterns, the way detection records its class names: two independent classes read from two files and two exclusive ones read from a colormap are the same count and the same head, so weights from one read back as the other would label every channel wrongly and answer plausibly. n_class alone cannot tell the four namings apart, which is why the naming itself goes into every run record and every weights sidecar.





InstanceEngine._load_weights explained the absence of all this by a fact that had stopped being true. Its docstring said there are no published instance weights, so there is no registry entry to read blocks and filters out of - true when it was written, and ended by dsbowl-instances one release later without anybody noticing. A declaration beside a mechanism that no longer describes it, which is the same shape as #230 and #231, and found the same way: by writing the documentation a reader would follow.





separation is no longer required outright: it may be omitted when weights names a file that records it, and that permission is paid for in two places rather than assumed in one. The specification refuses the omission when there are no weights at all, which it can check without resolving anything; the engine refuses a file whose sidecar does not record the separation, which needs the registry and therefore cannot live in a layer that must be validatable without a download. In the window between the two, asking a model what its head predicts answers with a sentence naming the file rather than with an attribute error on a field nobody wrote.
decode is deliberately not adoptable. It is the reader’s question rather than the file’s property: one trained file answers it three ways - 0.5445, 0.5390 and 0.4822 on the published instance weights - and the sidecar lists every decoding it was measured with, so adopting from that list would silently pick whichever name came first.
One adoption mechanism instead of two copies of it. _adopt_from_weights existed twice, character for character apart from a type hint, in Engine and DetectionEngine; this release needed a third with one asymmetric entry. It lives on EngineBase now and each engine declares only ADOPTABLE, which became a mapping of field to the key the sidecar records it under - the two names differ exactly once, and that is the whole reason for the shape.
One matcher, two nouns. match_channels takes what= and says “class” where a class is what it matched. Every guard is the same for both fields and the only difference is whether a mismatch mislabels a measurement or a class; a second copy with the other noun is the shape §3F of the workbench’s notes is a list of.
Both multilabel namings are named by the refusals that mention one. lovasz and a written include_background: false are refused for classes_from exactly as for regions, and the message now names whichever field was written - a refusal that says regions to somebody who wrote classes_from sends them looking for a field they have not got. Same for the warning about unmatched voxels, which stays suppressed: neither naming has a background channel, so on a small target the fraction sits near 1 and is the correct answer.
One place reads a sample’s masks, instead of the copy _load and inspect_masks each had. The third naming would have made it three, and the read is not where either of them has anything of its own to say - which is also what gives inspect_masks its answer for free here: a pattern matching a file that is empty in every sample read is a channel of zeros, and missing_classes reports it by class with the pattern quoted.





The R half. segmentation_data() enumerates its parameters, so classes_from is an unused argument there today, and R’s exclusivity check has to become four-way - which is a code change rather than a pin bump, measured on regions and recorded on rplatypus#152. Engine first, published, then R: pyplatypus#91 stays open for it, and this release does not pretend otherwise.





One line, and it is a defect in 0.8.0a26 found by answering a question about it rather than by a test. A flag on the metric replaces a list of names, and the two layers that had the answer separately now read one.



A tiled run accepted a callback watching val_surface_dice, which its epochs cannot produce. The trainer decides what an epoch reports by asking the built metric (metric.accumulates); the specification decided what a callback may watch from _WHOLE_MASK_METRICS = frozenset({"cldice"}), a list of names in spec/models.py. So surface_dice arrived in 0.8.0a26 on one side of the question and not the other, and monitor: val_surface_dice beside splits was accepted, trained for an epoch and then raised KeyError out of state.logs - which EarlyStopping indexes directly - with the epoch already paid for.
The fix is not the missing name. whole_mask is now a class flag on the metric component, the shape continuous and supports_multilabel already have on a loss, and monitorable asks the component instead of a list. It stays in the specification layer and imports nothing, so tests/spec/test_spec_layer_is_light.py is unmoved: the reason the list existed was to keep torch out of the spec, and a flag on the spec’s own class does that without being a second place for the answer to live.
A test pairs the two answers, which is the part that outlives this release: for every metric the configuration offers, the component’s whole_mask must be the negation of the built metric’s accumulates, with a control asserting both values actually occur - a pairing is no evidence in a package where every metric answers the same way. The three tests that cover the tiled case were each written for cldice and are now parametrised over the metrics that say they are whole-mask, so the next one is covered by arriving rather than by somebody remembering three files. §4’s passing test whose fixture never contained the case, twice in two releases.
Nothing else changes: surface_dice and cldice were always measured per case by evaluate_cases on a tiled run and always absent from its epoch history, which is what both docstrings said while the specification disagreed.





Two of the four issues in the “Losses and metrics” milestone, and the other two are answered rather than built - both of them were filed with the measurement that says not to. maju116/rplatypus#113 and #114.



surface_dice, a metric: how much of each boundary lies within a tolerance of the other. rplatypus#113. The third question this package can ask of a mask, after volume (dice) and connectedness (cldice): how far wrong is the edge. The volume vignette ended on a model at Dice 0.88 whose volumes were 12% to 23% too large, and this is the number that says so directly rather than being inferred from two columns that disagree - and it is what boundary optimises while nothing here reported it, so that loss was being judged by the metric it exists to improve on.
Normalised surface Dice as published (Nikolov et al., 2018), symmetric: the truth’s surface near the prediction is the boundary’s recall, the prediction’s near the truth is its precision, and one ratio weights them by surface size.
tau is required and has no default, because a tolerance belongs to the structure and the dataset - conventionally the inter-observer variability for that structure. It is in millimetres when target_spacing puts the samples on a common grid and in voxels when it does not, which is the same pair of answers the signed distance map gives and for the same reason. The only metric here that reads the spacing, which is why it belongs in a package that carries one: a 0.5 mm and a 2.5 mm acquisition are not comparable in voxels at all. The spacing reaches it the way multilabel reaches the others - the builder joins the spec’s tolerance to the data’s voxel - and InstanceData has no target_spacing field, so an instance run measures in voxels and says so.
Written as a dilation rather than a distance transform, and measured. A voxel is within tau of a surface exactly when a ball of radius tau centred on it contains a surface voxel, so the question is a morphological dilation by that ball - which costs the ball’s volume per voxel where a transform costs the whole image whatever tau is:
 256x256, batch 8, two channels     2.7 ms on the GPU      41 ms on the processor
 128^3,            two channels    23.8 ms on the GPU     372 ms on the processor
 the same by scipy's transform                            948 ms on the processor
#113 worried that a distance transform at 128^3 costs 710 ms, which is the whole epoch budget; this is thirty times less and can therefore run every batch. Verified against scipy.ndimage.distance_transform_edt - a different algorithm, so agreement is evidence rather than a shared bug - exactly at four tolerances over isotropic and anisotropic spacings at both ranks, and the whole metric against a scipy-only implementation to 1e-6 over thirty pairs.
include_background defaults to False here, and for a measured reason rather than the usual one: the background’s boundary is the foreground’s boundary plus the edge of the picture, and that edge agrees between any two masks whatever the model did. Measured on four random pairs at tau 2, background 0.6110-0.7030 against foreground 0.5583-0.6266 - higher every time. That is agreement on the field of view. For the same reason a mask running off the edge has no surface there, which also makes two solid masks score 1.0 rather than 0/0.
generalized_dice, a loss: classes weighted by the inverse square of their volume. rplatypus#114, in both loss and boundary’s region.
The usual argument for it does not hold in this package and the help page says so. Generalized Dice is introduced as a fix for Dice being dominated by the background; dice here is a mean over the class channels, so a lesion in 1% of a frame already carries the same weight as the 99% around it. Measured on a 1% target with two predictions - one finding the lesion and leaking a false positive of equal size, one missing it entirely and getting the background perfect:
 dice               0.1658 finding   0.4731 missing   prefers finding by 0.3073
 cce                0.1600 finding   0.1600 missing   indifferent
 cce_dice           0.1629 finding   0.3166 missing   prefers finding by 0.1536
 generalized_dice   0.3278 finding   0.9511 missing   prefers finding by 0.6233
So what it adds is weight beyond an equal share - 1 to 9801 on that target rather than 1 to 1, and twice the margin between finding the lesion and missing it. And the objective that is genuinely dominated is the per-pixel half of cce_dice: to cce a false positive and a missed lesion of the same size are the same number of wrong pixels, which is the indifference in that table. The claim in the issue was inherited from the literature and is wrong about this implementation; it is corrected rather than copied, and the table is held by a test.
Two decisions, both in the docstring and both tested. An absent class has no volume and so an infinite weight; it is given the largest finite weight in its sample, as the published implementations do, so inventing a class that is not in the picture costs as much as missing the rarest class that is - weight zero would make it free. A sample with nothing present at all has no finite weight to borrow, so its weights are flat and it is scored exactly as dice scores it; without that fallback every empty-truth sample reads a perfect 1.0 and a model predicting a lesion on a clean frame is never told.
And the weights are rescaled to a mean of one, which the published quantity is invariant to and which is what makes smooth mean here what it means everywhere else: unscaled, the weights are of order 1/volume^2, so a smooth of 1.0 is not a small regulariser but the whole numerator. The control caught it - with three equal classes the coefficient read 0.855 where pooled Dice reads 0.355. With the rescaling, flat weights are exactly Dice pooled over the classes, which is a test rather than a hope.
Where each may be named, asked of the configuration rather than of the union. A loss in the union that every spec refuses is a name in a listing and nothing else, so this is tested through from_dict: generalized_dice is accepted as a semantic model’s loss, as an instance model’s loss for the mask, and as boundary’s region term - the combination worth having, since the case that motivates this loss and the case that motivates that one are the same picture. A flow block refuses it by name, because a flow field is a vector per pixel and this scores classes, and a detector refuses it for the reason it refuses every loss. surface_dice is a metric at both segmentation tasks and object_detection lists no metrics at all.





available_losses() is 11 and 14 where it was 10 and 13, and available_metrics() is 5. Nothing was edited to make that happen - both read the pydantic unions, which is what that design is for - but six pinned counts failed and each one is a place somebody had to look: the union’s member count beside the two loader flags (looked: a region loss on one-hot classes, so neither flag), the semantic set written out by hand, two task listings, the component count in the description test, and two doctests. The R package’s own listing test pins 13 and will fail when the pin moves, which is the ratchet working.





cbDice (rplatypus#115) stays a question. The issue blocks it on a measurement and says so in as many words: “if clDice is high while Dice is low - connected but the wrong calibre - that is this issue’s evidence, and without it this stays open.” The measurement exists now and points the other way: on FIVES, 200 held-out images, Dice 0.8789 against clDice 0.8330 - the skeletons agree less than the volumes, which is breaks in thin vessels rather than the wrong calibre. Building it would be building for a problem nobody here has demonstrated.
DIoU, CIoU and EIoU (rplatypus#116) stay unbuilt, which is what that issue was filed to record. giou already lost to offsets on this data - per-seed spread 0.000116 against 0.006863, sixty times tighter on the exact quantity GIoU targets - and anchor_mean_iou was 0.877 in all six runs, so the regime the whole family exists for is never entered. Three more names meaning roughly the same thing is the argument that kept the weights registry to one entry when four architectures scored within 0.0030.








dsbowl-instances, the fourth published weights, and the first whose score is not one number. A U-Net trained to tell touching nuclei apart on BBBC038v1 - interior, rim and background, separation: rim at width 2 - pinned in the registry at fd7bdc86. weights: dsbowl-instances fetches it, the sidecar refuses a model it does not belong to, and nothing about the numbers can change under the name.
Measured on the same 134 held-out images dsbowl-unet reports, seed 0, 120 epochs, 102 minutes on one GTX 1070. Instance average precision, one score per image, and the mask all three rows share:
 nearest_seed           0.5445   sd 0.2554   5378 objects found of 5999
 watershed              0.5390   sd 0.2532   5378 objects found of 5999
 connected_components   0.4822   sd 0.2440   4914 objects found of 5999

 foreground dice        0.9118
One file, three scores, and the registry description is written so that neither can be quoted without the other. The network predicts channels; turning them into objects is a separate step and decode is a list, so evaluate() returns a row per decoding on one forward pass - a second decoding of these 134 images costs 1.41 s against the 102 minutes. The spread between the best and the worst row is 0.0623, about seven times this configuration’s run-to-run spread of 0.009, so a headline number without its decoding would be a number about whichever decoding happened to run. A test holds the description to its own arithmetic: every score in it names its decoding, the signal’s claimed worth is the gap between the rows quoted, and the perfect-mask figure beside it is the larger of the two.
What the entry says about the signal is the milestone’s finding and not a sales line. connected_components ignores the separation signal entirely, so the signal is worth +0.0623 here, while substituting a perfect semantic mask into the same route is worth +0.2398 and a perfect mask through connected components caps any model at 0.7655. The mask is the limit on this data by nearly four to one. Published anyway, because the alternative is that the measurement exists only in a closed milestone and the weights it was taken on cannot be loaded by anyone who wants to argue with it.
examples/publish_dsbowl_instance_weights.py, which produced them. It reads its recipe out of examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml and the three recorded scores out of #215’s table rather than restating either, selects the one model through the same helper compare_instance_separations.py uses, and uploads nothing.
Its publication gate is a two-sided band, calibrated at both ends: every decoding has to land within +/-0.027 of the recorded value - three times the 0.009 spread - and a run far above the band is refused as well, because that is a changed recipe rather than a better model. The refusal is diagnosable: the measurements are written before the band is read, so a refused run says which decoding missed by how much. Its positive control is a real refusal - a three-epoch run of the same script named all three gaps and wrote nothing.
Four more controls, each one proven able to refuse:

The split is checked by the number a different 134 could not produce, 5999 ground-truth objects, not by its size. 134 directories is the weak half of that fingerprint and dsbowl-unet’s card is why: the 134 on this disk were once a different 134 and the discrepancy was 0.01 of Dice.
The data is fetched from the Broad rather than read off this disk, and the local Kaggle copy was proven byte-identical to it first - 670 cases, images and per-object masks, sha256 - so the licence chain runs to BBBC038v1’s CC0 rather than through a competition’s terms.
One model decoded three ways reports one mask, asserted rather than assumed, because a table whose three rows disagree about foreground_dice is a table of three models.
The sidecar cannot shadow what the weights say they are for. The extra carrying the separation’s settings is named separation_settings, and a check derives the reserved names from the spec’s own fingerprint and refuses a collision. Named separation it would have overwritten the fingerprint’s "rim" with a dict and made every later load of the file refuse it - caught before the training run rather than by a load failure afterwards.

The published name was loaded the way a user reaches it, before this entry was written. weights: dsbowl-instances with fit: false, resolved through the registry, downloaded from the pinned commit into an HF_HOME that had never seen it, sidecar checked against a model built from the specification, and scored on the same 134 images: all three decodings, the object counts and the foreground Dice came back identical to seven decimals, the largest disagreement 0.00e+00. The same file into a model with filters: 32 or blocks: 3 is refused by field name, which is the control that the acceptance means something.
The Hub card gains its section and two older lines are corrected. One card holds one section per model; this one is generated from the run’s own measurements and a check holds every figure in it to the sidecar beside the weights, with the same check aimed at dsbowl-unet’s section as its control. The corrections are the R example’s library(platypus), which has been the wrong name since the package was renamed on 2026-10-14 and was the one line a reader would have copied and had fail, and a tags: entry for what this file actually does.
What R needs from this is the pin and nothing else. available_weights() reads the registry from the engine, so a fourth published name appears on the R side as soon as the pin moves - the cheapest kind of R half there is, and the whole value of this release to an R user arrives through it.





A declaration beside a mechanism that does not describe it, in the one place this drawing exists for. _colour_index’s docstring said the wrap past the end of the palette “is said rather than hidden - overlay_instances reports it”, and overlay_instances reported nothing: grep -n warn pyplatypus/plots.py returned no hit at all. The sentence was right about what should happen, which is why this is a warning and not a deletion.



overlay_instances() now warns when the picture needs more colours than the palette has, naming how many it needs, how many there are and how many objects are drawn in a neighbour’s colour. maju116/pyplatypus#231.
The wrap is the one case this figure answers its own question wrongly in. Its subject is where does one object end, every other colour repeat is deliberate - a colour may repeat across the picture as long as it never repeats between neighbours - and a wrap is exactly the case where it does repeat between neighbours. Provably, rather than usually: a slot is only past the end of the palette once every colour before it was taken by a neighbour, so the fold lands on one a neighbour already holds and never on a free colour. The warning says that to the reader, so a test measures it rather than leaving the claim to the docstring that made this defect.
Not reachable on anything measured here - the hardest of 670 Data Science Bowl cases needs 3 of the 8 default colours, with 6 neighbours for the worst single object - which is exactly why nothing noticed the gap for as long as the function has existed. A guard for a picture nobody here has is still worth having when the alternative is a figure that draws two objects as one and says nothing.
Two things found while writing it, neither of them the warning:

The fold is inside the greedy and that is not cosmetic. Hoisting it out, so the colouring is computed in true slots and folded at the end, reads cleaner and changes the picture: measured on 440 overlays over 55 label maps, 234 of them differ. Folding in the loop means a later neighbour avoids the colour an object is actually drawn in, so one wrap does not cascade into the rest of the picture. The R package folds inside the loop too, so the clean-looking version would also have been a divergence between the two. Found by a control recorded before the change rather than by reading the diff - and the first attempt at this fix was that version.
A Warns: section cannot be published from here, which is why nothing in this package had one and why the warning is documented as prose. quartodoc has no renderer for it: uv run quartodoc build raises NotImplementedError: Unsupported type: DocstringSectionWarns, so the docs job fails and the site cannot be built. Measured both ways - the section fails and the prose builds - because the four gates here do not include the reference build, and the absence of any Warns: in the package read as “no convention” when it was “no renderer”.
_colour_index cannot report what it was said to report, and now does not claim to: it returns which objects wrapped, and overlay_instances - the function a person called, and the only one that knows the palette it was given - is what warns. The requirement in the message comes from the same function asked for a colouring with no palette at all, which is the number a short palette needs and cannot be read off a folded run.






overlay_instances, overlay_instance_agreement and flow_to_colours are now pairs rather than three functions with the same name on two sides. The R package drew neither until maju116/rplatypus#154; it draws both now, in its own code, because drawing there touches no Python on purpose. So tests/test_reference_groups.py pins where both are filed, which is this side’s half of §3F’s pair - the other half is in R’s test-reference-groups.R.
Nothing in the wheel changes for this one and it needed no release of its own; it rides with 0.8.0a24. Worth an entry anyway, because the subsequence test cannot catch what this one does: a name absent on one side is not a name filed differently, so until R had them there was nothing to disagree with and the pair could not have existed.
What holds the rule rather than the filing is on R’s side alone and has to be: it draws the same pictures with both packages and compares them pixel for pixel. The palette was already mirrored, so the two could have agreed about which eight colours exist while disagreeing about which object gets which. See maju116/rplatypus#154.





A writer the package had promised twice and never had, and the test that finds the next promise of that kind. onehot_to_colours has refused an overlapping prediction since regions shipped in 0.8.0a14, and its refusal ends “overlapping classes are written one file per class, not as a colour map” - nine releases in which nothing wrote that file.



save_class_masks() writes one binary picture per class, which is what that refusal points at and what Region.name’s own description= has been naming since 0.8.0a14. <case><suffix>_<region>.png, mode L, 0 or 255, in channel order - which is the order the regions were written in and the order every per-class score is reported in.
Four decisions in it, each one a failure this project has already made once in another shape:

A region’s name is not a filename. whole tumour becomes whole_tumour through class_filename, and two names that become the same filename are refused rather than written: one file would hold the second channel, the first would be silently gone, and the number of returned paths would still be right. That is the quiet shape, so it is the one that is refused by name.
The name is not lowercased. Core and core are one file on one platform and two on another, and the package already has one case-sensitivity story without a second.
A channel nothing reaches is an empty picture, not a missing file. A missing file reads as the run did not produce that class; an empty one reads as it did and the answer was nothing. Those are different findings and only one of them is true.
A volume stack is refused. A PNG carries neither voxel spacing nor orientation, so a volume written as pictures cannot be laid back over the scan it came from. Only rank 5 is refused, because a single volume (d, h, w, c) and a stack of images have the same rank and nothing in the array tells them apart - the same limit save_masks has on the R side, and it is stated rather than guessed at.

threshold defaults to 0.5, which is what every metric in the package thresholds a multilabel channel at. A different number writes a picture that disagrees with the score printed beside it, and the docstring says so.
The class names arrive as classes= rather than names=, decided by §3A before the function was released: R’s save_masks and save_volumes already use names for the files they write, and a sibling writer where the same word means the classes is the quiet kind - a call copied from one to the other would pass filenames as class names, the counts would match whenever they happened to, and nothing would refuse it.
Filed under Masks and volumes in the reference, which is the group R files save_masks and save_volumes under and which held nothing here until now. The shared order already carried the title; tests/test_reference_groups.py now pins the name’s placement in both suites, which is the fifth such pair.





The schema’s prose named two functions that do not exist here, and now a test says it cannot. tests/test_schema_prose_names.py reads every description out of spec_schema() - the strings tools/build_config_reference.py publishes as the configuration reference - and asserts every `name()` in them resolves to something this package has. It found the two it was written for and one it was not:

save_class_masks, named in Region.name and built above. The name was decided on maju116/platypus#91 and written into the schema before anything existed; nothing read the sentence again for nine releases.
training_history(), in CsvLogger.path and its class docstring, which is the R package’s function. True for the R reader it was written with in mind and a dead end for the Python reader the generated page is for. Both now say fit(), which is what this package answers the same question with.

§4’s “an instruction addressed to a human is code nothing runs”, in the one place this project generates documentation out of code. The test is the engine’s because the schema and the page are the engine’s, and it carries the usual guard against passing by looking at nothing - it asserts it found more than 150 descriptions and more than five names before asserting anything about them.





The guide has a section on overlapping classes, which 0.8.0a14 shipped the field for and deliberately did not document in narrative form: Overlapping classes instead of one per voxel, between the augmentation section and the instance one, because regions is still semantic_segmentation and what changes is what a channel means. The page’s section list is pinned by a test here and the same list in R’s suite, so this lands in both repositories or neither; maju116/rplatypus#152 is the other half.
The numbers in it are measured rather than asserted: the same masks are four classes written as labels: [0, 1, 2, 4] and three channels written as the three BraTS regions, and a voxel whose value is 4 belongs to all three at once. The YAML block is validated by test_every_configuration_in_the_guide_is_accepted like every other block on the page - checked by breaking it, which fails that test at its line rather than passing quietly.
The section says one voxel gets one colour and a voxel here may be in three classes, and it now names what writes such a prediction out: save_class_masks(), added in this same release. _brand.yml now names the test that holds its two copies together, because as of maju116/rplatypus#160 there is one. It is on the R side alone - it fetches this file from this repository’s default branch and compares it line by line - for the reason the field-prose ledger is one-directional: the engine owns the look, so R’s copy is the copy. Nothing here changes but the comment, and nothing is in the wheel either way.
The R package is rplatypus. It was platypus until 2026-10-14; the name collided with Platypus, archived from CRAN on 2026-02-02, which archiving does not release, so it was renamed rather than waiting on a reserved name. One name per language, beside this package on PyPI. Nothing in the wheel changes: this is the engine’s own links, its _brand.yml, and the citation("rplatypus") the generated Citation page prints - §3E’s shape, a change R needs nothing from, said here rather than only in a commit message.

maju116/platypus-weights is a different repository - the published weights on the Hub - and is untouched. Worth saying because a rename done by pattern would have taken it, and resolve_weights would then look for weights nobody published.

The second entry under this heading and the same reason as the first: it records an outcome, and neither examples/ nor the guide page is in the wheel. What is in the wheel is one docstring, so nothing here changes what a run does. What is new is that the outcome includes two corrections to things this project had written down - a column it printed, and a claim about a table it builds.




Both separation signals, five decodings, one command (#215, the instance milestone’s deliverable). examples/compare_instance_separations.py against examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml, 185 minutes on one machine, scored on the 134 validation cases --expect-cases pins by name:
 model  separation  decode                class dice  AP      objects  truth
 rim    rim         nearest_seed          0.8550      0.5442  5414     5999
 rim    rim         watershed             0.8550      0.5396  5414     5999
 rim    rim         connected_components  0.8550      0.4767  4875     5999
 flows  flows       follow_flows          0.9464      0.5174  5400     5999
 flows  flows       connected_components  0.9464      0.4512  4849     5999
The signal is worth +0.0676 to the rim route and +0.0661 to the flow route, over each route’s own connected-components row. Both reproduce what was measured separately - +0.0640 in 0.8.0a15’s sweep and +0.0680 in #212 - so §4bq’s reading stands: a perfect mask is worth +0.2398 and the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6.
The noise floor is measured here rather than borrowed. The flow model was configured identically in both runs of this file and its average precision moved 0.0112 between them, which is larger than the 0.0074 two runs of one configuration differed by in 0.8.0a15’s sweep - so a gap smaller than 0.0112 says nothing on this table, and the rim route’s 0.0268 lead over the flow route is 2.4x it on a sample of two runs.
The rim model was undertrained at 60 epochs and is not undertrained at 120, which is why the two models’ epoch counts differ in the configuration and why that asymmetry is a comment rather than a typo. Doubling it bought +0.0451 of average precision; the last twenty epochs of the hundred and twenty bought +0.0018, and the best epoch was 118 of 120.





The configuration guide has a section on the third task, in both packages: Instances instead of one mask, between the model’s own fields and detection. It is the §3C rule that a change to how a run is written belongs in the guide on both sides with the same sections, and task: instance_segmentation shipped in 0.8.0a20 without it - the guide had zero occurrences of the word.
What a reader needs that no reference page tells them: the data block gets shorter (there is no colormap and no labels, because the classes are always background and object and the per-object files are what name the objects), separation is one block per model with no default while decode is a list, no value appears in both because one is a noun and the other a verb, and a model’s own loss scores the mask while a flows block carries its own for the vector channels. The section also carries what the task is worth - +0.068 against a perfect mask’s +0.2398 - for the same reason the reference does.
Both guides’ YAML is validated by each suite, and the new block is: it was mutated to name follow_flows under separation: rim and the Python test failed on that line.





evaluate()’s own docstring claimed the yardstick is in every model’s rows “whether it was asked for or not”, and it is not. connected_components is in the pair decode derives to when a model stayed silent; a model that writes a decode list gets the list it wrote and nothing added. The code is right - the engine does not add a row to somebody’s table that they did not ask for - and three pieces of prose were wrong, including 0.8.0a20’s own entry, which is corrected in place below with the correction left visible.
It went unnoticed because only the kind half had a test. test_the_yardstick_is_in_the_table_without_being_asked_for covers the derived pair and says so in its docstring; nothing covered a written list, so the claim about the branch with no test is the one that drifted. test_a_written_decode_list_is_what_you_get is the missing half, and it fails when the code is mutated to make the old sentence true.
examples/compare_instance_separations.py already kept the yardstick in its own --decode handling, which in hindsight is the evidence: an example compensating for behaviour the engine was documented as having.
The table’s fg dice column was neither a foreground Dice nor one quantity, and is now called class dice. It is the engine’s dice metric, a mean over the class channels the model’s head actually has: three for rim - background, interior and the rim band - and two for flows, whose metrics are shown the class block alone. So the rim model’s number is averaged against a thin band scoring 0.6857 where its own background and interior score 0.9852 and 0.8721, and reading it across the two models compares two different things.
