 cce                0.1600 finding   0.1600 missing   indifferent
 cce_dice           0.1629 finding   0.3166 missing   prefers finding by 0.1536
 generalized_dice   0.3278 finding   0.9511 missing   prefers finding by 0.6233
So what it adds is weight beyond an equal share - 1 to 9801 on that target rather than 1 to 1, and twice the margin between finding the lesion and missing it. And the objective that is genuinely dominated is the per-pixel half of cce_dice: to cce a false positive and a missed lesion of the same size are the same number of wrong pixels, which is the indifference in that table. The claim in the issue was inherited from the literature and is wrong about this implementation; it is corrected rather than copied, and the table is held by a test.
Two decisions, both in the docstring and both tested. An absent class has no volume and so an infinite weight; it is given the largest finite weight in its sample, as the published implementations do, so inventing a class that is not in the picture costs as much as missing the rarest class that is - weight zero would make it free. A sample with nothing present at all has no finite weight to borrow, so its weights are flat and it is scored exactly as dice scores it; without that fallback every empty-truth sample reads a perfect 1.0 and a model predicting a lesion on a clean frame is never told.
And the weights are rescaled to a mean of one, which the published quantity is invariant to and which is what makes smooth mean here what it means everywhere else: unscaled, the weights are of order 1/volume^2, so a smooth of 1.0 is not a small regulariser but the whole numerator. The control caught it - with three equal classes the coefficient read 0.855 where pooled Dice reads 0.355. With the rescaling, flat weights are exactly Dice pooled over the classes, which is a test rather than a hope.
Where each may be named, asked of the configuration rather than of the union. A loss in the union that every spec refuses is a name in a listing and nothing else, so this is tested through from_dict: generalized_dice is accepted as a semantic model’s loss, as an instance model’s loss for the mask, and as boundary’s region term - the combination worth having, since the case that motivates this loss and the case that motivates that one are the same picture. A flow block refuses it by name, because a flow field is a vector per pixel and this scores classes, and a detector refuses it for the reason it refuses every loss. surface_dice is a metric at both segmentation tasks and object_detection lists no metrics at all.





available_losses() is 11 and 14 where it was 10 and 13, and available_metrics() is 5. Nothing was edited to make that happen - both read the pydantic unions, which is what that design is for - but six pinned counts failed and each one is a place somebody had to look: the union’s member count beside the two loader flags (looked: a region loss on one-hot classes, so neither flag), the semantic set written out by hand, two task listings, the component count in the description test, and two doctests. The R package’s own listing test pins 13 and will fail when the pin moves, which is the ratchet working.





cbDice (rplatypus#115) stays a question. The issue blocks it on a measurement and says so in as many words: “if clDice is high while Dice is low - connected but the wrong calibre - that is this issue’s evidence, and without it this stays open.” The measurement exists now and points the other way: on FIVES, 200 held-out images, Dice 0.8789 against clDice 0.8330 - the skeletons agree less than the volumes, which is breaks in thin vessels rather than the wrong calibre. Building it would be building for a problem nobody here has demonstrated.
DIoU, CIoU and EIoU (rplatypus#116) stay unbuilt, which is what that issue was filed to record. giou already lost to offsets on this data - per-seed spread 0.000116 against 0.006863, sixty times tighter on the exact quantity GIoU targets - and anchor_mean_iou was 0.877 in all six runs, so the regime the whole family exists for is never entered. Three more names meaning roughly the same thing is the argument that kept the weights registry to one entry when four architectures scored within 0.0030.

title: Change Log
text:
dsbowl-instances, the fourth published weights, and the first whose score is not one number. A U-Net trained to tell touching nuclei apart on BBBC038v1 - interior, rim and background, separation: rim at width 2 - pinned in the registry at fd7bdc86. weights: dsbowl-instances fetches it, the sidecar refuses a model it does not belong to, and nothing about the numbers can change under the name.
Measured on the same 134 held-out images dsbowl-unet reports, seed 0, 120 epochs, 102 minutes on one GTX 1070. Instance average precision, one score per image, and the mask all three rows share:
 nearest_seed           0.5445   sd 0.2554   5378 objects found of 5999
 watershed              0.5390   sd 0.2532   5378 objects found of 5999
 connected_components   0.4822   sd 0.2440   4914 objects found of 5999

 foreground dice        0.9118
One file, three scores, and the registry description is written so that neither can be quoted without the other. The network predicts channels; turning them into objects is a separate step and decode is a list, so evaluate() returns a row per decoding on one forward pass - a second decoding of these 134 images costs 1.41 s against the 102 minutes. The spread between the best and the worst row is 0.0623, about seven times this configuration’s run-to-run spread of 0.009, so a headline number without its decoding would be a number about whichever decoding happened to run. A test holds the description to its own arithmetic: every score in it names its decoding, the signal’s claimed worth is the gap between the rows quoted, and the perfect-mask figure beside it is the larger of the two.
What the entry says about the signal is the milestone’s finding and not a sales line. connected_components ignores the separation signal entirely, so the signal is worth +0.0623 here, while substituting a perfect semantic mask into the same route is worth +0.2398 and a perfect mask through connected components caps any model at 0.7655. The mask is the limit on this data by nearly four to one. Published anyway, because the alternative is that the measurement exists only in a closed milestone and the weights it was taken on cannot be loaded by anyone who wants to argue with it.
examples/publish_dsbowl_instance_weights.py, which produced them. It reads its recipe out of examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml and the three recorded scores out of #215’s table rather than restating either, selects the one model through the same helper compare_instance_separations.py uses, and uploads nothing.
Its publication gate is a two-sided band, calibrated at both ends: every decoding has to land within +/-0.027 of the recorded value - three times the 0.009 spread - and a run far above the band is refused as well, because that is a changed recipe rather than a better model. The refusal is diagnosable: the measurements are written before the band is read, so a refused run says which decoding missed by how much. Its positive control is a real refusal - a three-epoch run of the same script named all three gaps and wrote nothing.
Four more controls, each one proven able to refuse:

The split is checked by the number a different 134 could not produce, 5999 ground-truth objects, not by its size. 134 directories is the weak half of that fingerprint and dsbowl-unet’s card is why: the 134 on this disk were once a different 134 and the discrepancy was 0.01 of Dice.
The data is fetched from the Broad rather than read off this disk, and the local Kaggle copy was proven byte-identical to it first - 670 cases, images and per-object masks, sha256 - so the licence chain runs to BBBC038v1’s CC0 rather than through a competition’s terms.
One model decoded three ways reports one mask, asserted rather than assumed, because a table whose three rows disagree about foreground_dice is a table of three models.
The sidecar cannot shadow what the weights say they are for. The extra carrying the separation’s settings is named separation_settings, and a check derives the reserved names from the spec’s own fingerprint and refuses a collision. Named separation it would have overwritten the fingerprint’s "rim" with a dict and made every later load of the file refuse it - caught before the training run rather than by a load failure afterwards.

The published name was loaded the way a user reaches it, before this entry was written. weights: dsbowl-instances with fit: false, resolved through the registry, downloaded from the pinned commit into an HF_HOME that had never seen it, sidecar checked against a model built from the specification, and scored on the same 134 images: all three decodings, the object counts and the foreground Dice came back identical to seven decimals, the largest disagreement 0.00e+00. The same file into a model with filters: 32 or blocks: 3 is refused by field name, which is the control that the acceptance means something.
The Hub card gains its section and two older lines are corrected. One card holds one section per model; this one is generated from the run’s own measurements and a check holds every figure in it to the sidecar beside the weights, with the same check aimed at dsbowl-unet’s section as its control. The corrections are the R example’s library(platypus), which has been the wrong name since the package was renamed on 2026-10-14 and was the one line a reader would have copied and had fail, and a tags: entry for what this file actually does.
What R needs from this is the pin and nothing else. available_weights() reads the registry from the engine, so a fourth published name appears on the R side as soon as the pin moves - the cheapest kind of R half there is, and the whole value of this release to an R user arrives through it.

title: Change Log
text:
A declaration beside a mechanism that does not describe it, in the one place this drawing exists for. _colour_index’s docstring said the wrap past the end of the palette “is said rather than hidden - overlay_instances reports it”, and overlay_instances reported nothing: grep -n warn pyplatypus/plots.py returned no hit at all. The sentence was right about what should happen, which is why this is a warning and not a deletion.



overlay_instances() now warns when the picture needs more colours than the palette has, naming how many it needs, how many there are and how many objects are drawn in a neighbour’s colour. maju116/pyplatypus#231.
The wrap is the one case this figure answers its own question wrongly in. Its subject is where does one object end, every other colour repeat is deliberate - a colour may repeat across the picture as long as it never repeats between neighbours - and a wrap is exactly the case where it does repeat between neighbours. Provably, rather than usually: a slot is only past the end of the palette once every colour before it was taken by a neighbour, so the fold lands on one a neighbour already holds and never on a free colour. The warning says that to the reader, so a test measures it rather than leaving the claim to the docstring that made this defect.
Not reachable on anything measured here - the hardest of 670 Data Science Bowl cases needs 3 of the 8 default colours, with 6 neighbours for the worst single object - which is exactly why nothing noticed the gap for as long as the function has existed. A guard for a picture nobody here has is still worth having when the alternative is a figure that draws two objects as one and says nothing.
Two things found while writing it, neither of them the warning:

The fold is inside the greedy and that is not cosmetic. Hoisting it out, so the colouring is computed in true slots and folded at the end, reads cleaner and changes the picture: measured on 440 overlays over 55 label maps, 234 of them differ. Folding in the loop means a later neighbour avoids the colour an object is actually drawn in, so one wrap does not cascade into the rest of the picture. The R package folds inside the loop too, so the clean-looking version would also have been a divergence between the two. Found by a control recorded before the change rather than by reading the diff - and the first attempt at this fix was that version.
A Warns: section cannot be published from here, which is why nothing in this package had one and why the warning is documented as prose. quartodoc has no renderer for it: uv run quartodoc build raises NotImplementedError: Unsupported type: DocstringSectionWarns, so the docs job fails and the site cannot be built. Measured both ways - the section fails and the prose builds - because the four gates here do not include the reference build, and the absence of any Warns: in the package read as “no convention” when it was “no renderer”.
_colour_index cannot report what it was said to report, and now does not claim to: it returns which objects wrapped, and overlay_instances - the function a person called, and the only one that knows the palette it was given - is what warns. The requirement in the message comes from the same function asked for a colouring with no palette at all, which is the number a short palette needs and cannot be read off a folded run.






overlay_instances, overlay_instance_agreement and flow_to_colours are now pairs rather than three functions with the same name on two sides. The R package drew neither until maju116/rplatypus#154; it draws both now, in its own code, because drawing there touches no Python on purpose. So tests/test_reference_groups.py pins where both are filed, which is this side’s half of §3F’s pair - the other half is in R’s test-reference-groups.R.
Nothing in the wheel changes for this one and it needed no release of its own; it rides with 0.8.0a24. Worth an entry anyway, because the subsequence test cannot catch what this one does: a name absent on one side is not a name filed differently, so until R had them there was nothing to disagree with and the pair could not have existed.
What holds the rule rather than the filing is on R’s side alone and has to be: it draws the same pictures with both packages and compares them pixel for pixel. The palette was already mirrored, so the two could have agreed about which eight colours exist while disagreeing about which object gets which. See maju116/rplatypus#154.

title: Change Log
text:
A writer the package had promised twice and never had, and the test that finds the next promise of that kind. onehot_to_colours has refused an overlapping prediction since regions shipped in 0.8.0a14, and its refusal ends “overlapping classes are written one file per class, not as a colour map” - nine releases in which nothing wrote that file.



save_class_masks() writes one binary picture per class, which is what that refusal points at and what Region.name’s own description= has been naming since 0.8.0a14. <case><suffix>_<region>.png, mode L, 0 or 255, in channel order - which is the order the regions were written in and the order every per-class score is reported in.
Four decisions in it, each one a failure this project has already made once in another shape:

A region’s name is not a filename. whole tumour becomes whole_tumour through class_filename, and two names that become the same filename are refused rather than written: one file would hold the second channel, the first would be silently gone, and the number of returned paths would still be right. That is the quiet shape, so it is the one that is refused by name.
The name is not lowercased. Core and core are one file on one platform and two on another, and the package already has one case-sensitivity story without a second.
A channel nothing reaches is an empty picture, not a missing file. A missing file reads as the run did not produce that class; an empty one reads as it did and the answer was nothing. Those are different findings and only one of them is true.
A volume stack is refused. A PNG carries neither voxel spacing nor orientation, so a volume written as pictures cannot be laid back over the scan it came from. Only rank 5 is refused, because a single volume (d, h, w, c) and a stack of images have the same rank and nothing in the array tells them apart - the same limit save_masks has on the R side, and it is stated rather than guessed at.

threshold defaults to 0.5, which is what every metric in the package thresholds a multilabel channel at. A different number writes a picture that disagrees with the score printed beside it, and the docstring says so.
The class names arrive as classes= rather than names=, decided by §3A before the function was released: R’s save_masks and save_volumes already use names for the files they write, and a sibling writer where the same word means the classes is the quiet kind - a call copied from one to the other would pass filenames as class names, the counts would match whenever they happened to, and nothing would refuse it.
Filed under Masks and volumes in the reference, which is the group R files save_masks and save_volumes under and which held nothing here until now. The shared order already carried the title; tests/test_reference_groups.py now pins the name’s placement in both suites, which is the fifth such pair.





The schema’s prose named two functions that do not exist here, and now a test says it cannot. tests/test_schema_prose_names.py reads every description out of spec_schema() - the strings tools/build_config_reference.py publishes as the configuration reference - and asserts every `name()` in them resolves to something this package has. It found the two it was written for and one it was not:

save_class_masks, named in Region.name and built above. The name was decided on maju116/platypus#91 and written into the schema before anything existed; nothing read the sentence again for nine releases.
training_history(), in CsvLogger.path and its class docstring, which is the R package’s function. True for the R reader it was written with in mind and a dead end for the Python reader the generated page is for. Both now say fit(), which is what this package answers the same question with.

§4’s “an instruction addressed to a human is code nothing runs”, in the one place this project generates documentation out of code. The test is the engine’s because the schema and the page are the engine’s, and it carries the usual guard against passing by looking at nothing - it asserts it found more than 150 descriptions and more than five names before asserting anything about them.





The guide has a section on overlapping classes, which 0.8.0a14 shipped the field for and deliberately did not document in narrative form: Overlapping classes instead of one per voxel, between the augmentation section and the instance one, because regions is still semantic_segmentation and what changes is what a channel means. The page’s section list is pinned by a test here and the same list in R’s suite, so this lands in both repositories or neither; maju116/rplatypus#152 is the other half.
The numbers in it are measured rather than asserted: the same masks are four classes written as labels: [0, 1, 2, 4] and three channels written as the three BraTS regions, and a voxel whose value is 4 belongs to all three at once. The YAML block is validated by test_every_configuration_in_the_guide_is_accepted like every other block on the page - checked by breaking it, which fails that test at its line rather than passing quietly.
The section says one voxel gets one colour and a voxel here may be in three classes, and it now names what writes such a prediction out: save_class_masks(), added in this same release. It was written without that sentence, because the function existed in neither package at the time and the honest thing was to say nothing rather than to name it; maju116/rplatypus#152 is where the decision to build it was taken.





_brand.yml now names the test that holds its two copies together, because as of maju116/rplatypus#160 there is one. It is on the R side alone - it fetches this file from this repository’s default branch and compares it line by line - for the reason the field-prose ledger is one-directional: the engine owns the look, so R’s copy is the copy. Nothing here changes but the comment, and nothing is in the wheel either way.
The R package is rplatypus. It was platypus until 2026-10-14; the name collided with Platypus, archived from CRAN on 2026-02-02, which archiving does not release, so it was renamed rather than waiting on a reserved name. One name per language, beside this package on PyPI. Nothing in the wheel changes: this is the engine’s own links, its _brand.yml, and the citation("rplatypus") the generated Citation page prints - §3E’s shape, a change R needs nothing from, said here rather than only in a commit message.
The GitHub repository was renamed with it and the former addresses redirect, so the issue cross-references in the entries below are left exactly as they were written. They name maju116/platypus because that is what it was called when they were written, and they still resolve.
maju116/platypus-weights is a different repository - the published weights on the Hub - and is untouched. Worth saying because a rename done by pattern would have taken it, and resolve_weights would then look for weights nobody published.

The second entry under this heading and the same reason as the first: it records an outcome, and neither examples/ nor the guide page is in the wheel. What is in the wheel is one docstring, so nothing here changes what a run does. What is new is that the outcome includes two corrections to things this project had written down - a column it printed, and a claim about a table it builds.




Both separation signals, five decodings, one command (#215, the instance milestone’s deliverable). examples/compare_instance_separations.py against examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml, 185 minutes on one machine, scored on the 134 validation cases --expect-cases pins by name:
 model  separation  decode                class dice  AP      objects  truth
 rim    rim         nearest_seed          0.8550      0.5442  5414     5999
 rim    rim         watershed             0.8550      0.5396  5414     5999
 rim    rim         connected_components  0.8550      0.4767  4875     5999
 flows  flows       follow_flows          0.9464      0.5174  5400     5999
 flows  flows       connected_components  0.9464      0.4512  4849     5999
The signal is worth +0.0676 to the rim route and +0.0661 to the flow route, over each route’s own connected-components row. Both reproduce what was measured separately - +0.0640 in 0.8.0a15’s sweep and +0.0680 in #212 - so §4bq’s reading stands: a perfect mask is worth +0.2398 and the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6.
The noise floor is measured here rather than borrowed. The flow model was configured identically in both runs of this file and its average precision moved 0.0112 between them, which is larger than the 0.0074 two runs of one configuration differed by in 0.8.0a15’s sweep - so a gap smaller than 0.0112 says nothing on this table, and the rim route’s 0.0268 lead over the flow route is 2.4x it on a sample of two runs.
The rim model was undertrained at 60 epochs and is not undertrained at 120, which is why the two models’ epoch counts differ in the configuration and why that asymmetry is a comment rather than a typo. Doubling it bought +0.0451 of average precision; the last twenty epochs of the hundred and twenty bought +0.0018, and the best epoch was 118 of 120.





The configuration guide has a section on the third task, in both packages: Instances instead of one mask, between the model’s own fields and detection. It is the §3C rule that a change to how a run is written belongs in the guide on both sides with the same sections, and task: instance_segmentation shipped in 0.8.0a20 without it - the guide had zero occurrences of the word.
What a reader needs that no reference page tells them: the data block gets shorter (there is no colormap and no labels, because the classes are always background and object and the per-object files are what name the objects), separation is one block per model with no default while decode is a list, no value appears in both because one is a noun and the other a verb, and a model’s own loss scores the mask while a flows block carries its own for the vector channels. The section also carries what the task is worth - +0.068 against a perfect mask’s +0.2398 - for the same reason the reference does.
Both guides’ YAML is validated by each suite, and the new block is: it was mutated to name follow_flows under separation: rim and the Python test failed on that line.





evaluate()’s own docstring claimed the yardstick is in every model’s rows “whether it was asked for or not”, and it is not. connected_components is in the pair decode derives to when a model stayed silent; a model that writes a decode list gets the list it wrote and nothing added. The code is right - the engine does not add a row to somebody’s table that they did not ask for - and three pieces of prose were wrong, including 0.8.0a20’s own entry, which is corrected in place below with the correction left visible.
It went unnoticed because only the kind half had a test. test_the_yardstick_is_in_the_table_without_being_asked_for covers the derived pair and says so in its docstring; nothing covered a written list, so the claim about the branch with no test is the one that drifted. test_a_written_decode_list_is_what_you_get is the missing half, and it fails when the code is mutated to make the old sentence true.
examples/compare_instance_separations.py already kept the yardstick in its own --decode handling, which in hindsight is the evidence: an example compensating for behaviour the engine was documented as having.
The table’s fg dice column was neither a foreground Dice nor one quantity, and is now called class dice. It is the engine’s dice metric, a mean over the class channels the model’s head actually has: three for rim - background, interior and the rim band - and two for flows, whose metrics are shown the class block alone. So the rim model’s number is averaged against a thin band scoring 0.6857 where its own background and interior score 0.9852 and 0.8721, and reading it across the two models compares two different things.
Measured by identical code on both, on the same 134 cases: the binary foreground Dice is 0.9159 for the rim model and 0.9097 for the flow model. Where the column read them 0.09 apart it is 0.0062, and the sign is the other way round - the rim model has the better mask. The control is the Unreleased entry above this one: foreground Dice held at 0.917-0.920 across four rim runs there, which is the family 0.9159 belongs to and 0.8565 does not.
examples/train_instance_separation.py:261 had already written the rule down - “against three is not the comparison; foreground against foreground is” - and computes the quantity by hand at line 263. So this is a lesson lost rather than one learnt, which is §4’s “documentation rots in the direction of the work having been done” wearing a column heading. What #215 asked for, a foreground Dice the table can be read across, needs the engine to return one. This entry said evaluate() has no such column; 0.8.0a22 below gives it one (#222), and the example prints that rather than a third hand-rolled copy. The two training scripts keep theirs, which is a decision rather than an oversight: they score an empty case as 1.0 where the engine’s column reports it as unscorable, so substituting silently would move a published number’s definition.
examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml named its checkpoints weights.safetensors while model_checkpoint is torch.save - a pickle in a zip, whatever the path says. They are weights.pt now. export_weights() remains the safetensors path, and naming a pickle after the format this package chose because it is not a pickle is the kind of label that gets believed.

title: Change Log
text:
One column, and it is the one an instance table is read across. #222 came out of #215 and was deliberately left out of the instance milestone: the methods were delivered and the measurement taken, and this is a defect in how a result is reported.



evaluate() carries foreground_dice on every instance row - the binary overlap of anything the model called an object against anything that is one, computed identically whatever the separation signal is. The table already had a mask column and it was not one quantity: dice reduces over the class channels a head has, three for rim (background, interior, rim band) against two for flows, so on the Data Science Bowl’s 134 validation cases it showed the two masks 0.09 apart where they are 0.0062 apart, and with the sign reversed. class dice is the honest name for that one and it stays, beside the new column rather than instead of it, because a rim model’s three class numbers are where a thin band that never learned shows up at all.
Three decisions, each written into the function’s docstring because each is worth more than some of the effects this table is read for:

Both sides binarised, through read_prediction. That is the one place the channel layout is read - the vectors sit in front of the classes for flows and nowhere for rim - so the column cannot acquire a second opinion about where the classes start.
Unsmoothed, and an unscorable case says so. The +1 the training metrics carry scores an empty prediction on empty truth 1.0; foreground_dice returns None there, which is this module’s existing convention - score_cases leaves such a case’s average_precision at None and summarise_instances filters on exactly that.
Averaged over images, which is how the average_precision beside it is pooled. The training metrics pool over batches with each batch weighed equally, worth 0.0088 on that split, so a row carrying both poolings would hide a difference larger than several it exists to show.

It costs no second forward pass. The number is taken inside _decoded’s existing loop, once per case rather than once per decoding, which is also what makes “the same for every row of one model” structural: _Decoded carries the mask number beside the decodings instead of inside each of them.
examples/compare_instance_separations.py prints it as fg dice, from the engine’s row. The issue asked for this rather than a third copy of the arithmetic, and test_the_instance_table_does_not_call_its_dice_a_foreground_dice still holds the other column’s title, which is the label that was wrong in the published table.





tests/test_instance_engine.py’s module docstring said the yardstick is in every row “whether it was asked for or not” - the fourth copy of the claim 0.8.0a21’s entry corrected in three places. Found by working in the file rather than by a sweep, which is the argument for the sweep.





The guide says which mask column to read across models, in the section the third task got in 0.8.0a21’s cycle. The engine’s copy ships here because it describes what this release returns; R’s copy is written at the same time and ships with the pin move, because a vignette cannot describe a column its pinned engine does not return.




Almost nothing, and structurally rather than by decision: R’s score table is the engine’s rows, so the column appears on the R side the moment the pin moves - §3E’s shape, the same one 0.8.0a12 had, where a release R needs nothing from is still a release whose whole value to an R user arrives through the pin. What R owes beyond the pin is one assertion, because a column that arrives untested is the next thing to drift: test-instances.R now names foreground_dice and holds it to one value per model.

title: Change Log
text:
One refusal, moved to the class it belongs to. A semantic model’s own loss accepted mse, l1 and smooth_l1, trained with them, and reported a small number for a mask that was half missing (#223).



loss: mse on a semantic model is refused, by name and before anything is built. The validator existed and sat on InstanceModel, which is a subclass of SegmentationModel, while the thing it protects - loss scoring a target of classes - belongs to the parent. So the semantic task had no guard, and nothing downstream supplied one: Engine builds the loader with with_foreground=loss_needs_mask(model.loss) and the trainer hands a third tensor to any loss that asks for one, so a run completed.
The number it reported was the good one, which is why this is refused rather than documented. where defaults to foreground, and for a semantic target the foreground is not the background channel - so the objective was evaluated only inside the labelled objects and the background was unconstrained. Measured on eight 32x32 samples whose single object is where the picture is bright, 80 epochs, u_net, a task cce solves exactly:
 the model's own loss                 val_dice   val_loss
 cce (control)                        1.0000     0.086507
 mse, silent - so where: foreground   0.5367     0.001430
 mse, where: everywhere               0.9838     0.055150
The middle row is the finding: a validation loss sixty times smaller than the control’s, and the only place the missing half of the mask shows is val_dice.
The last row is why the refusal is a decision rather than a correction of nonsense, and it is recorded rather than buried: an unactivated squared error is a crude surrogate, not gibberish. It is refused anyway, because loss is the objective on the class channels and an activated regression would be a new loss with its own name and its own measurement - not this family, whose entire content is where and whose documentation is about flow fields. The decision is on #223 with the two alternatives it was taken against.
Admissibility is still read off the continuous flag on the loss itself, so a fourth regression loss is refused with nothing edited. InstanceModel now contributes only the extra clause that names where a continuous loss does belong - the flow block’s own loss - so that refusal still names both halves.
Nothing in this repository used it: no example, configuration, test or fixture builds a semantic model with a regression loss, so the behaviour change costs nothing here. An R caller reaches the same hole through loss_mse(), which R gains when its pin moves.





available_losses() answers per task: ten at semantic_segmentation, thirteen at instance_segmentation. The three in the difference are the regression family, and at the semantic task they can be named nowhere - a listing that offers what the next validator refuses is a list maintained against a validator, which is what continuous exists to avoid. The instance task keeps all thirteen because a separation: flows block’s own loss is that same union; which loss goes where is the tree, and available_separations() is where the tree lives.
The listing-against-schema test now asks the losses of the instance task, because that is the only task whose answer can equal the schema’s discriminator.mapping: the mapping is per field and cannot express a validator. The semantic task’s shorter list has its own test which names the three excluded losses literally rather than deriving them the way the code does - so a fourth regression loss fails it, and failing is right.
R reads this listing through the bridge, so available_losses() there changes with the pin and the R suite’s count moves with it. Said here rather than discovered: §3E.

title: Change Log
text:
task: instance_segmentation: the third task, and the last engine piece of the instance work (#160). Two axes on a model - separation, one per model, and decode, a list - a head whose width is derived rather than stated, and a score computed after a post-process rather than from (logits, target).
What the tag is honestly worth is in its own documentation and it is not flattering. On the Data Science Bowl the separation signal is worth +0.068 of instance average precision at best while a perfect mask is worth +0.2398, so the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6. connected_components - which ignores the signal entirely - is in the pair decode derives to when a model stayed silent, because it is the row the signal’s row has to be read against, and a perfect semantic mask scores 0.7655 through it. (This sentence read “in every model’s decodings whether it was asked for or not” until the Unreleased entry above corrected it: that was never true of a model which wrote its own decode list.) The capability is real, the ceiling is measured, and both are in the configuration reference rather than in a footnote.



task: instance_segmentation, with InstanceData, InstanceModel and InstanceSpec. Two new fields and everything else inherited: input_shape, channels, blocks, filters, batch_size, epochs, splits, the pretrained encoders, the callbacks and the augmentation all mean what they mean for a semantic model.
separation:, a block named rim or flows carrying that mechanism’s own settings, which sets the head’s width and which losses are admissible. hv is deliberately not a name: its markers lose to a one-pixel erosion on perfect inputs (0.9382 against 0.9807), so naming it would promise a mechanism #213 measured as absent.
decode:, a list of blocks keyed on name - connected_components, nearest_seed, watershed, follow_flows - with each block declaring which separation it can read, so follow_flows with separation: {name: rim} is refused at load time with both halves named. Left unset it derives to the signal’s own decoding plus the yardstick.
The mechanisms’ own settings, inside the block they belong to: width under rim, and mode, loss and weight under flows. So a setting crossed with the wrong mechanism is not a refusal somebody had to write, it is an unknown key - the first shape of this field was separation: rim beside rim_width, flow_mode, flow_loss and flow_weight, which parses on every model and therefore needed a table of which field belongs to which mechanism and a validator reading it. extra="forbid" was already doing that job for every other key in a specification. mode defaults to diffusion on a measurement (0.9924 decoded against centroid’s 0.9478); width defaults to 2 on an argument rather than a measurement, and the field says so - the published sweep peaked at 3 pixels of source resolution, which on a 520-pixel case read at 256 is about 1.5 pixels of model input, and a sweep in model pixels has not been run.
InstanceEngine, on EngineBase: fit, evaluate, evaluate_cases, predict, predict_instances, export_weights, best_model, dataset, loader. evaluate() returns one row per (model, decoding); evaluate_cases() is one row per case for one decoding, so summarise_cases keeps meaning what it means.
InstanceDataset, which reads the per-object files as a label map instead of uniting them, and builds the target after the resize, the tiling and the augmentation - pyplatypus#210’s rule, pinned here by a recording augmenter.
pyplatypus.instances.targets and pyplatypus.instances.decode: the channel contract going in and coming back, with a test that a perfect prediction decodes into the objects it was built from. That is the only check that catches a channel swapped between the two, because both arrays keep the right shape and range.
available_decodings(), with a needs column read off each decoding rather than written down; available_separations(), with the head width each signal needs derived rather than stated; and a third row in available_tasks().
examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml and examples/compare_instance_separations.py: both signals and five decodings from one configuration file. This is the test of whether the tag earned its place - the script says where the data is and the engine does the rest.
A refusal specific to this task: a split whose objects have all vanished in the resize. The objects are on disk, the resize removes them, and without the check the loss falls, every metric stays finite and the run learns to answer “nothing here”. Some cases losing theirs is a warning with the count; all of them is an error naming input_shape.





Trainer.activate is a method rather than one inlined call, which is what InstanceTrainer overrides: a flows head is two raw vector channels in front of a block of classes, and a softmax across all of them would return a number, a gradient and no error anywhere.
A dataset answers foreground_of for its own channels. The loader used to call onehot_to_foreground, which reads channel 0 as background - for a flows target that is the row component of a vector field, and the loss would have been handed a mask of everything.
labels_in_test_split is one function the two mask-reading engines share, rather than the same method written twice. EngineBase diverged twice before, and the second time the fix was written twice on the same night.
tests/test_engine_base.py has a third column rather than a second file: the thing worth asserting is that the three engines give the same answer, which a file per engine cannot say.
The two hand-assembled instance scripts say what they now are - the record of the measurements they produced, not the way to run one - and the sentence claiming the engine could not derive a flow head’s width is corrected rather than quietly deleted.





The configuration reference published the third task’s data: and models: under the heading “for detection”. short = "segmentation" if tag == "semantic_segmentation" else "detection" was a binary over a set that grew, and the heading-collision test is what caught it rather than anybody reading the page.

title: Change Log
text:
Looking at instance results instead of reading their arrays (#214), the trained half of flows (#212), and #213’s cheap test answered before anything was trained for it. All three end in the same place, which is the entry’s finding rather than three coincidences: the separation signal is not what limits instance segmentation on this data. The mask is.



overlay_instances(), overlay_instance_agreement() and flow_to_colours() in pyplatypus.plots. An instance result has no figure today - overlay_mask paints every object one colour, which is the one thing an instance map must not do - and #159’s four training runs were read entirely off tables.
overlay_instances colours an exact graph colouring and that was an open question on #214, settled by measurement rather than by preference. What a reader needs from an instance map is where one object ends and the next begins, which is adjacency, not identity, so a colour may repeat as long as it never repeats between neighbours. Measured over all 670 Data Science Bowl cases, 524 of which hold touching objects and 5436 adjacent pairs between them: an exact colouring (Welsh-Powell) needs at most 3 of the 8 colours CLASS_COLOURS already has - 146 cases need one, 412 two, 112 three - against at most 6 neighbours for any one object. The cheap alternative the issue offered, cycling the palette by object value, paints 550 of those 5436 pairs in one colour: 10.12%. One touching pair in ten drawn as one object, in a figure whose whole subject is whether two objects are two.
overlay_instance_agreement matches objects with iou_matrix, the function the metric uses, and at the same strictness - which is a correction rather than a design note. It matched at iou >= threshold for an hour; average_precision compares strictly greater, and a merged pair sitting over two equal truth objects lands at exactly 0.5, so the figure would have drawn one hit where the metric counts two misses. Caught by a test written against what the figure means rather than what it draws, and pinned by one. The threshold below 0.5 that the metric refuses is refused here too, in the metric’s own words.
Nothing was added to pyplatypus.style, which is why the R pin does not move for this (§3E): hue-for-direction is the convention optical flow has used for twenty years and not a decision this project gets to make differently, and the drawing style R reads from the engine is unchanged. platypus#154 carries the R half.
examples/train_instance_flows.py, the second half of #212: the flow target trained and scored, with the pair of oracles that says which half of the pipeline the result is limited by. Sixty epochs on dsbowl-unet’s architecture and the 536/134 directory split, the target rebuilt from the augmented label map on every sample (#210), and the model assembled outside Engine because a flow head is 2 + n_class wide and the engine takes its width from spec.data.n_class - the derivation #160 has yet to name. The script says so in its own docstring rather than leaving it to be inferred.
 134 cases, 5999 objects, 256x256     score   objects back
 foreground Dice                     0.9029
 flow angle, median of case medians    6.6 degrees
 AP flows                            0.5278           5424
 AP connected components             0.4598           4686   same mask, no signal
 TRUE identity, this mask            0.5941           6138   perfect vectors
 this field, TRUE mask               0.7676           5421   perfect mask
The flow signal is worth +0.0680 over connected components on the same predicted mask, which is the only honest comparison here - same model, same mask, same pictures, with and without the signal. The rim route was worth +0.0640 on its own set (#159, JOURNAL.md §4bo), and the difference between the two, 0.0040, is below the 0.0074 run-to-run spread of one configuration at a fixed seed that §4bo measured. So the structural argument for flows - that it spends no pixel on being a boundary, where a rim wide enough to learn hollows the object out - does not show up in the score. Two runs of this configuration here came back 0.5278 and 0.5315, a difference of 0.0037, which is consistent with that spread and is still two runs rather than a spread of its own.
And the oracle pair says why, which is the part worth keeping. A perfect mask is worth +0.2398 and perfect vectors +0.0663: the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6, and 0.7676 with a perfect mask is already about what connected components reaches on the truth (0.7505). A third separation target would be measured against the same wall, which is what #213 now has to answer for rather than assume.
Each row prints the number of objects it handed back, and that is not decoration. The first version of the TRUE-field oracle scored 0.2220 with 18758 objects back against 5999 in the truth, because it handed flows_from_instances(labels) - zero everywhere off the truth’s own objects - to the model’s mask, and a zero field moves nothing, so every voxel the mask got wrong stood still and became a basin of its own. It is truth_field_on now, substituting identity and not the field: every voxel of the mask joins the nearest truth object and the field is built from that. An average precision alone cannot tell a route that mislabels from one that shatters; an object count can. One blind spot is left and it is counted rather than argued about: 259 of the 6138 objects the TRUE-identity row returns are pieces of predicted foreground holding no truth voxel at all, which join the nearest object by identity but, under diffusion, receive no heat and keep a zero vector. Under centroid they would cost nothing - a straight line to a sink needs no path - and the run prints the count beside the row with the mode it belongs to.
separation_ceiling.py --separation hv, which is #213’s own cheap test and answers it before a model is trained. The issue, after #211 narrowed it: “if the markers from hv do not beat eroded interiors on the ground truth, they will not beat them predicted either, and this issue closes before a model is trained”. They do not. Both recipes for getting markers out of HoVer-Net’s two distance maps are swept, over the 134 held-out cases and 6000 objects:
 marker source                 AP    over the bar   markers   objects with none
 eroded interiors, 1 px    0.9807        +0.2224      6030                   0
 hv centres, |h|,|v|<=0.6  0.9382        +0.1799      5900                   5
 hv gradient, >=0.6        0.7995        +0.0412      5404                   0
 connected components      0.7583          the bar
The maps’ own zeros - #213’s own narrowing, the extrema as seeds rather than the gradient as a surface - are the better of the two and still 0.0425 below a one-pixel erosion. HoVer-Net’s published gradient route recovers a fifth of what that erosion does over the bar. Both curves turn over at 0.6 rather than at an edge of the range (--hv-sweep prints them), so neither number is a tuning artefact, and the erosion’s thin-object fallback cannot account for the difference: it rescues 4 objects of 6000.
Two rows of that table are controls. The connected-components bar and the eroded-interior ceiling reproduce 0.8.0a18’s recorded 0.7583 and 0.9807 to four decimals, which is how a reader knows this measurement is on the same pictures as those

and the direct answer to the provenance failure that left #159’s ceiling without a set it could be reproduced on.

The two marker functions live in the example rather than in the package, because #160 has not named separation: hv and this measurement is the reason it may never need to. Seven mutations, six caught; the seventh is named in the code as uncatchable with the reason, rather than left as a gap.
--separation both is now --separation all, because there are three signals.





labels without 0 is refused when any voxel matches none of them (platypus#153). Index 0 means two things in this package and always has: the first entry of a naming, and matched nothing. labels: [0, ...] makes them agree, and labels is the one naming where the 0 can be left out - after which every unmatched voxel, which is usually most of the image, is trained as the first declared class. Measured on the issue: labels: [1, 2] over a mask of 0s, 1s and 2s put the background into class 1 with an unmatched fraction of 0.5, and nothing in the shape of the target gives it away - it is in range, one-hot and plausible.
Refused in fit’s existing mask check, which already reads a sample of the training masks, and only when the data actually has unmatched voxels: labels: [1, 2] over masks that really do fill every voxel is correct and keeps working. That was the author’s reading on the issue, between four options, because the failure is in the data rather than in the configuration.
The threshold is any unmatched voxel at all, not the 5% the unmatched warning uses, and that is a calibration rather than strictness: a label map holds integers, is read nearest-neighbour and compared with half a unit of tolerance, so a naming that describes it matches exactly everything. The compression and antialiasing the 5% exists for belong to colormaps, and a colormap cannot omit a background entry. Five mutations, five caught - including the one where the refusal is hung on the warning threshold, which the fixture is deliberately sized to catch at 1.6%.

title: Change Log
text:
The first half of flows (#212): the target, its decoding, and their ceiling measured on the ground truth before anything is trained - the order #159 was done in, now the pattern rather than a one-off. #212 stays open; what is here is everything that can be settled without a training run, and it settled more than expected.



flows_from_instances() and instances_by_flows(), with FLOW_MODES as the question they exist to answer. A unit vector per foreground pixel pointing at its own object’s sink, decoded by following the field until the pixels that arrive together are one object. No interior, no rim, nothing eroded - which is the premise of #212, because #159 closed measured-and-no for a structural reason: an interior and a rim are two classes competing for the same pixels, so a rim wide enough to learn hollows the object out. A flow field spends no pixel on being a boundary, and an object one pixel wide is an ordinary object with a sink in it rather than a case for parts_from_instances’s fallback.
The ceilings, one run over 134 held-out Data Science Bowl cases and 6000 objects:
 flows:diffusion + follow     0.9924      6043 objects back
 flows:centroid  + follow     0.9478      6268
 rim + nearest_seed           0.9807      6074
 rim + watershed              0.9703
 connected_components         0.7583      the bar any model using it is capped by
So the flow route’s ceiling is 0.0117 above the rim route’s on the same pictures, and the route is not what caps a model either way. separation_ceiling.py --separation both prints all five rows and the set they belong to.
follow_flows() exposed on its own, because the decoding’s parameters are not equally dangerous and only a measurement says which is which. The step count does not matter: AP 0.9914 at one step against 0.9923 converged over fifteen cases, a span of 0.0009, below the 0.0013 run-to-run spread of a training run. The reason is structural - the field is continuous, so one object’s endpoints stay a connected set however far along they get, and it diverges at a seam, so the gap between two objects opens on the first step. The step size is a cliff: 0.9923 at 1.0 or below, 0.4715 at 2.0 with 868 objects back where the truth has 633, and 0.0303 at 10.0 with 4337. A step longer than a pixel jumps past the sink and keeps jumping. Both are in the suite with both ends written down.





The two flow targets differ by 0.0446 of AP, and the obvious explanation was measured at 0.32%. The cheap mode aims a straight line at the sink, and the reading everybody reaches for is that it fails on concave objects whose centroid falls outside them - of 6000 objects 19 do. The cause is one level down: a straight line between two pixels of a discrete set can step outside the set even when the set looks convex, because the boundary is ragged. Measured on 274 of those objects: 0.27% of foreground pixels have such a path, 6 objects come back split, and every one of the 6 has pixels whose path leaves it while 10 objects have such pixels and survive. Necessary, not sufficient.
The build cost is the number that decides the training half, and it is 23x apart between the modes: 4.9 ms per case for centroid against 113.6 ms for diffusion, with decoding at ~335 ms for both. #210 says the target is rebuilt from the augmented label map on every sample, so the build is paid once per image per epoch: 429 training cases at 113.6 ms is 48.7 s against a 15.5 s training epoch, 3.1x it serially and absorbed by the loader’s four workers rather than eliminated. The decode is paid once per evaluation and the step-count measurement above makes it twenty times cheaper than its default.





The diffusion target carried a full unit vector at every object’s sink, found by the mutation gate rather than by a test: (0.707, 0.707), because normalising the residue a central difference leaves across a maximum produces a unit vector from nothing. A model trained on that learns noise at exactly the pixel the method is about. The decoding survived it unchanged - 0.9925 before the fix against 0.9924 after - which is why nothing noticed, and is the shape of the whole category: the defect was in the target and the only instrument pointed at the decode. The sink is now zeroed by construction, and the test that should have caught it is parametrised over both modes; with the default mode alone it was asserting a property of the straight-line field.
instances_from_parts’s docstring said scikit-image is not a dependency. It became a hard one in 0.8.0a16 and nothing re-read the sentence.





The ceiling of 0.9846 and the bar of 0.7655 on the record for “the 134 held-out cases” are not reproducible from anything on this disk, and separation_ceiling.py now prints the case and object count beside every number so this cannot recur. Four candidate sets were measured: the 134 directories of stage1_validation give 0.9807 and 0.7583 over 6000 objects, the seed-1 fifth of stage1_train gives 0.9905 and 0.7876 over 107 cases and 4044 objects, all 536 of stage1_train give 0.9818 and 0.7618 over 23461, and the same 134 at the training resolution give 0.9627 and 0.7504. The recorded object count of 5774 appears in none of them.
No conclusion drawn against that bar changes - #159’s 0.5587 and #211’s 0.5561 are below every one of these - but a new number cannot be put beside an old one, which is why the table above is one run over one set of pictures and quotes nothing from before it.

title: Change Log
text:
The two gates in front of flows and hv (#212, #213), and neither is about either of them: a continuous target has nothing in the ten overlap-and-cross-entropy losses to be trained against (#209), and augmented as a mask it comes back geometrically consistent and physically wrong (#210). Both were to be settled before any number produced with them could be believed.



mse, l1 and smooth_l1, and the question they exist to force: where is the target defined? (#209) A continuous instance target - a flow field, or horizontal and vertical distances - is defined on the objects and undefined off them, so a builder writes zero on the background. Measured on the 536 Data Science Bowl cases: the foreground is 13.97% of the pixels at 256x256 (13.48% at native size, 0.03% to 59.2% per case, 167 cases under 5%), so an unmasked mean spends 86% of the objective on a value a single output bias satisfies exactly.
So where: is a field rather than a convention. foreground divides by the mask’s own total, which makes the number mean average error per object voxel; everywhere is the other defensible answer and is what CellPose and HoVer-Net’s plain regression terms do - their background zero is a real value rather than a missing one. foreground is the default because it is the reading whose number means something, and because the trap is otherwise on by default.
The mask is asked of the loader, never read off the target. needs_mask and loss_needs_mask(spec) are the same mechanism boundary uses for its distance map, for the same reason - the loader is built before the loss. Reading it off the target is the one shape this family refuses: a flow field is exactly zero at the centre of every object and the hv maps are each zero along a line through it, so “the voxels where the target is non-zero” excludes precisely the seeds - and #211’s oracle measured that the seeds, not the seams, are what limits this approach. A mask inferred that way would be wrong in the one place the method depends on and right everywhere a test would look.
Nothing activates the prediction, which is the other sigmoid-shaped way to be wrong here: squashing an unbounded flow into (0, 1) would still return a number and a gradient.
onehot_to_foreground(), one home for a convention the package already depends on everywhere: channel 0 is background in the two exclusive namings, because labels_to_classes and colours_to_classes both send an unmatched voxel to index 0, and regions has no background channel at all. Its own docstring states the limit, which is filed as maju116/platypus#153: labels: [1, 2] makes the first entry a real class and there is then nothing that means background.





A vector target is rebuilt from the augmented label map, never corrected (#210). Two measurements, both in tests/data/test_vector_targets.py where a library bump re-runs them:

albumentations 2.0.8 never invents a label value. Sixteen transforms, twenty seeded draws each, a label map of forty distinct ids: not one output value was absent from the input, and the control is that the same transform with the map sent down the image path invents hundreds. So an instance label map travels through the augmenter unharmed and the target can be built from what comes back.
A crop moves an object’s centre, and no correction can answer that. Negating x after a horizontal flip is exact - 0.0% of foreground voxels disagree with a field rebuilt from the flipped labels, at 0.0 degrees, against a median of 90 and a maximum of 167.3 if the negation is left out. After a 32-pixel crop 49.5% disagree, by a median of 8.9 degrees and up to 180, and there is no component to negate: the surviving part of an object has a new centre, so the arrows carried in point at a place that is no longer in the picture.

Rebuilding is therefore correct by construction for every transform rather than for an admissible list of them, which also retires the idea of refusing transforms by name. It covers tiling for free - a tile is a crop, it happens before augmentation, and a 2048-pixel retina cut into sixteen would otherwise carry sixteen fields built for the whole picture.
The data path already had the right shape and the wrong array in it: masks are augmented as class indices and one-hotted afterwards, which is exactly the route, but _to_classes throws instance identity away first. So #212 carries the instance label map into the dataset rather than deriving a target offline, and a test pins that ordering instead of a docstring claiming it.
AlbumentationsAugmenter refuses a floating-point mask, which is what keeps that decision from being quietly undone. A flow field sent through as a mask comes back the right shape, the right dtype and the right range with its arrows pointing the wrong way; the loss falls, the model trains, and nothing downstream can tell. Every path in this package sends an integer - labels_to_classes, colours_to_classes and labels_to_regions all return int64 - so the guard costs nothing it should not.

title: Change Log
text:
instances_by_watershed(): a second decoding of the rim target, and scikit-image as a hard dependency. One trained model serves both decodings, because they share a target and differ only in how its channels become objects - which is why decode will be a list on an instance model and separation will not (#160). A decoding costs 11 ms per image against 15.5 s per training epoch, so it is a row in a table rather than a run.
scipy.ndimage.watershed_ift is not a substitute: it wants integer markers and implements the image-foresting-transform watershed, a different algorithm from the one this literature means. scikit-image is hard rather than an extra for the reason scipy is, plus one more: every published comparison on this problem uses skimage.segmentation.watershed, so writing our own would make a difference from the literature indistinguishable from a defect in ours.
What to pass as the surface is the part the name gets wrong. Not the image - a nucleus is bright and so is the next one, and the seam between two touching nuclei is not reliably darker than either. The model’s own predicted rim probability is the surface, which is the information nearest_seed throws away: it thresholds the rim and never looks at it again, so a confident boundary and a marginal one move the seam by the same amount.





The watershed does not help, and an oracle says why (#211). Four decodings of one trained rim model at width 3, its optimum:
 nearest_seed, distance only                 0.5561
 watershed, predicted rim probability        0.5458     -0.0103,  7.8x sd
 watershed, the TRUE rim as surface          0.5590     +0.0029,  2.2x sd
 connected_components, signal discarded      0.4988
sd 0.0013, from three runs of the identical configuration - 0.5587, 0.5574, 0.5561. (The 0.0074 quoted in the entries below is the range of two runs at width 1; at width 3 the spread is a quarter of that, and §4’s warning about a sample of two applies to the looser figure.)
The hypothesis was that the watershed is held back by its surface, rim Dice being 0.7292. Half right, and the half that is wrong is the one that matters. Surface quality is the largest effect in the table - the oracle beats the predicted surface by 0.0132, ten times the sd. And a perfect surface still only draws level with ignoring the surface entirely.
So the limit is not where the seam falls: both decodings share the same seeds, and the seeds decide which objects exist at all. Perfect seam placement buys 0.003 of the 0.21 still missing to the 0.7655 bar.





A ceiling run cannot test the watershed, and separation_ceiling.py now says so beside the number. With perfect parts the rim is binary, the surface is flat and the flood has nothing to climb, so rim + watershed reads 0.9756 there against nearest-seed’s 0.9846 - an artefact of flooding order rather than a comparison. A test asserts the caveat is printed, because the figure without it is misleading in the most-read place.
train_instance_separation.py reports four decodings of one forward pass, including the oracle row - predicted seeds, true surface - labelled a diagnostic and not a route. That pattern is how the above was settled at the cost of one row and no extra training, and it is the pattern #212 and #213 should both inherit.





A boundary separation signal is not worth it on this data (#159, closed measured-and-no). 0.8.0a15 below measured the ceiling of interior-plus-rim separation at 0.9846 and set the bar for “separation did something” at 0.7655, which is where a perfect semantic mask with no separation at all already lands. Four runs then measured what a model actually reaches:
 rim   fg Dice  interior  rim Dice  objects  matched@0.5   AP sep   AP cc   effect
 1 px   0.9188    0.9012    0.4808     4923         4020   0.5169  0.4893  +0.0276
 2 px   0.9199    0.8908    0.6419     5086         4248   0.5486  0.4907  +0.0579
 3 px   0.9186    0.8554    0.7292     5481         4513   0.5587  0.4947  +0.0640
 4 px   0.9171    0.8068    0.7622     5525         4438   0.5306  0.4791  +0.0515
The best is 0.5587 and the curve turns over, so the optimum is bracketed rather than guessed at. The mechanism is in the two middle columns: a rim wide enough to learn is wide enough to hollow the object out, so rim Dice climbs 0.48 to 0.76 while interior Dice falls 0.90 to 0.81. Two runs of one configuration differ by 0.0074, so the best effect is 8.6x the noise and the turnover 3.8x - real, and small.
The mask never moved across the four (foreground Dice 0.917-0.920 against the two-class model’s 0.9205), which is what makes the comparison one variable rather than two.
This entry is here because the 0.8.0a15 notes below would otherwise read as an open recommendation. They end with the bar and the ceiling and no outcome, and a changelog entry about work in flight goes stale the moment the flight lands.





examples/train_instance_separation.py - the script every row above came from, kept because a negative result nobody can reproduce is an opinion. Not packaged in the wheel, like the rest of examples/, which is why this is not a release.

title: Change Log
text:
Instance separation, and the measurement that says it is worth training (#159). The proposal was a semantic mask plus a separation signal; of the two signals on the table this takes the boundary, because it turns the problem into three mutually exclusive classes - background, object interior, object rim - which is ordinary semantic segmentation on the softmax path this package already has. Nothing new in the model, the loss or the metrics.
parts_from_instances() decomposes an instance label map into those parts and instances_from_parts() grows them back: the interiors become seeds and every other foreground pixel joins the nearest seed, which distance_transform_edt(return_indices= True) answers in one call. No new dependency - scikit-image is not here and is not worth adding for one function.
No model is trained, and that is the point of this release. The post-process is what caps the approach, and a cap can be measured without the thing it caps: feed the ground truth through it and score the result against the same ground truth. On the exact 134 cases dsbowl-unet’s card reports:
 interior and rim, grown back        0.9846    median 1.0000
 connected components                0.7655
 the published weights, as measured   0.4888    (0.8.0a13)
Three readings, and the middle one is new. Connected components caps any model at 0.7655 on this data - a perfect semantic mask still scores that, because touching nuclei are one region. So the published weights’ 0.4888 is not one failure but two: 0.4888 to 0.7655 is the mask’s own error, and 0.7655 to 0.9846 is what separation can buy and no better mask ever will. examples/separation_ceiling.py is the script, it trains nothing, and it prints both ceilings from one run over one set of pictures.
What the decomposition costs, counted rather than assumed, over those 134 cases: the plain erosion would have erased 6 objects in 4 cases - a nucleus one or two pixels wide has no interior - and an interior falling into two pieces gained 52 objects in 20 cases, which is most of the 0.0154 the ceiling sits below 1.0.
The erased objects are handled rather than ignored, because an object absent from the target is an object the model is told not to find: a false negative in every epoch and in the score, with nothing to say the target was at fault. An object whose interior comes back empty falls back to an erosion that only removes pixels touching a different object, and one still empty after that keeps itself whole.





The weak erosion could not see the objects it was protecting against. It was handed a label map with every other object masked out, so a pixel touching a neighbour read background there - and background counts as agreement in that pass by design. The thin object was kept whole and handed a seed it shared with its neighbour, which is the one outcome that fallback exists to prevent. Found by a test, not by reading, and the ceiling above was re-measured afterwards: it had been 0.9853 with the defect, which is wrong in the third decimal and was nearly published.





Nothing in pyplatypus.instances is in pyplatypus.__all__, deliberately: the top-level namespace is paired with R’s reference groups and the shared order is held by tests on both sides. These names live on pyplatypus.instances until R has something to say about them.





Nothing, and the pin should not move for this. No R surface reaches the instance post-process yet; platypus#103 is the R half of the whole milestone and it waits on #160, the spec tag, which is what will make any of this reachable from a configuration.

title: Change Log
text:
regions: overlapping classes, named as unions of a label map’s values. The first half of multilabel segmentation (#91), and the decision in front of it was the author’s: nested regions first, one binary file per class deferred.
The case is BraTS and the lesion-inside-an-organ family - liver and tumour, kidney and cyst, lung and nodule. The ground truth gives every voxel one of {0, 1, 2, 4} and the three scored classes are unions of those values:
 regions:
   - name: enhancing
     of: [4]
   - name: core
     of: [1, 4]
   - name: whole
     of: [1, 2, 4]
So the overlap is a convention applied to exclusive data, not a different file format, and nothing new is read off disk. regions is a third way of naming classes rather than an addition to labels: a region is a membership test, so the complete vocabulary of values never has to be declared. Exactly one of colormap, labels and regions is given, and - as with detection’s classes, for the same reason - regions have no background entry, because each channel is an independent binary question.
Why nested first was the cheaper half as well as the one the data wanted. One integer per voxel survives tiling and augmentation, both of which operate on a single-channel array today, so neither had to learn anything. The expansion to channels stays in the last step before the loss, where classes_to_onehot already was:
 exclusive    onehot = np.eye(n_class)[classes]
 overlapping  onehot = table[classes]      table[v] = the regions value v belongs to
Same indexing; np.eye is the special case where the table is the identity. The one difference that matters is row 0, which is zeros rather than a class. labels_to_classes sends an unmatched voxel to index 0 because index 0 is a class there - the background a colormap puts first - so reusing it unchanged would have made background a member of whichever region holds the lowest value. On BraTS that is 1, which is in both core and whole, so every background voxel would have been in two of the three regions and the model would have trained on it without complaint.
Per-channel objectives, and the four places mutual exclusivity was hiding. probabilities gained a multilabel argument and is the single home of the softmax-or-sigmoid decision; every overlap-based loss reads it through SegmentationLoss.probabilities rather than calling the functional form, so Dice, IoU, Tversky, focal Tversky, combo and the surface term all moved with one line. cce and focal gained binary forms, metrics threshold each channel instead of taking an argmax, and predict returns a stack whose channels do not sum to one.
binary_focal agrees with torchvision.ops.sigmoid_focal_loss to within float32’s resolution over five (gamma, alpha) settings, and reduces exactly to binary_cross_entropy at gamma=0 - a control the implementation could not satisfy by accident. Both are in the suite, and the torchvision numbers are baked in rather than imported because torchvision arrives only with the encoders extra.
No tighter number than that is pinned, because there is not one to pin: these are float32 reductions over 384 elements, so the last digit belongs to the order the hardware adds them in. macOS on ARM and Linux on x86 disagree by 8.6e-08 relative, under float32’s eps of 1.19e-07, and a first version of the test asserting 2e-08 absolute turned one macOS job red while being right about the arithmetic. The bound that replaced it is rel=1e-6, chosen against both ends: twelve times the platform noise, and five orders of magnitude under the 55% to 67% that the mutation this test exists to catch actually moves the numbers by.
The reduction differs from the categorical form and that is deliberate. Categorical cross-entropy sums over channels, which picks out the one true class of a one-hot target. Here every channel contributes, so a sum would make the loss grow with the number of regions: three regions would read three times the scale of one, and cce_weight in a blended loss would mean something different on every dataset. The mean keeps one voxel worth the same whatever it was asked. label_smoothing divides by two rather than by n_class for the same reason - each channel is a two-outcome question.
A metric now reports what the model was asked. With an argmax, a voxel correctly predicted in both the core and the whole tumour was credited to whichever channel read higher and scored as a miss in the other. On the smallest case that can show it - one voxel, in two regions, both predicted - Dice went from 0.833 to 1.000.





inspect_masks reports regions by name, and unmatched means something different there. missing_classes keeps its meaning exactly and gains the failure regions invites: of: [3] against data holding 4 is a channel of zeros, which trains to predict nothing and scores a Dice of 0 while every other number looks ordinary. It is refused before training with the region named. unmatched, on the other hand, counts background - which is deliberately not a region - so it sits near 1 on any dataset where the thing being found is small. On BraTS that is the correct answer and it looks like the catastrophic one, so the warning that reads it is suppressed for regions rather than left to cry wolf on every correct run.
The class fingerprint written into every run record and weights sidecar now names the regions. n_class alone cannot tell three exclusive classes from three overlapping ones, and weights from one must not be read back as the other.





lovasz with regions. Lovasz-Softmax sorts the errors of a softmax over mutually exclusive classes; the independent form is the Lovasz-Hinge, a different construction rather than a setting on this one. Run as it stands on sigmoid channels it would return a number and a gradient, which is the worst available outcome. The property lives on the loss specification (supports_multilabel), so the refusal arrives at load time and pyplatypus.objectives.losses reads it rather than keeping a second list.
include_background: false with regions, but only when it was written down. There is no background entry, so channel 0 is the first region somebody asked for and dropping it would drop a class. cldice defaults the flag to False and a default is not a request, so with regions the setting is ignored rather than honoured - model_fields_set tells those apart, the same way channels_match_the_data already does for channels.
A colour map holding an overlap. onehot_to_colours refuses an array where some voxel is confidently in two classes instead of taking the argmax and writing one of them, which would have produced a plausible picture of something else. Detected from the array rather than from a flag, so a caller holding only a prediction can answer it; a softmax output never trips it, because its channels sum to one.





classes_from - one binary file per class - is the only shape that can express genuinely independent overlap, a vessel crossing an organ or two annotators’ masks. Deferred, not dropped: #91 stays open for it and unite_masks’s element-wise maximum is still where per-file identity is destroyed.
Drawing a multilabel prediction. What one picture of three overlapping regions should look like is a real question with no answer yet, and half of one would be worse than none. onehot_to_colours refuses rather than guessing, which is the honest state until it is designed.
A guide section. The guide’s section list is pinned and paired with the R package’s (“change both or neither”), so a narrative section on regions lands with the R half rather than documenting in R something R cannot do. The field’s own description is on the generated configuration reference now, which is where a reader meets it.





Nothing moves yet, and the pin should not. regions is reachable from R the moment the pin moves, because R forwards the data block it is given - but available_weights()-style free inheritance is not what this is: the R surface documents its fields by hand, so regions needs roxygen prose of its own, and save_masks() needs the refusal the author chose for an overlapping prediction. Both are the R half’s work, filed as its own issue.
The field-prose ledger will fire, and that is the mechanism working: regions and Region.of are new descriptions R has never been written against.

title: Change Log
text:
pyplatypus.instances: the Data Science Bowl’s own metric, and the number the published weights score under it. First piece of instance segmentation, and it deliberately builds no model. Detection worked here because it was built metrics-first - every piece checked against something outside itself - and a model chosen before there is a way to score it is a model chosen on nothing.
The baseline, measured on the exact 134 cases dsbowl-unet’s card reports:
 Dice, on the model's grid                   0.9205
 instance average precision, source grid     0.4888
The card for those weights says semantic, not instance, and that caveat has been true and unmeasured since they were published. Touching nuclei come back as one region; connected components found 4658 objects where the data holds 5774, and every nucleus a merged region swallows costs twice - a false negative, and a false positive through the region that swallowed it.
The split is reproduced rather than assumed, and the Dice is the control that proves it.
