title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
HC18 is 999 two-dimensional ultrasound images of the fetal skull, each with an ellipse drawn round it by a sonographer, and a CSV giving every image’s pixel size in millimetres and the head circumference that was recorded. It is CC BY 4.0.
Every other article here ends on an overlap score. This one ends on a length in millimetres, because that is what a clinician writes down and charts against gestational age. Nobody charts a Dice.
The run below is examples/measure_fetal_head_circumference.py, and the weights it produced are published as hc18-unet. Where a number belongs to those published weights rather than to this run, it says so - the two are different draws of one recipe, and how different is itself one of the findings.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: Why a circumference is not a score
text:
Why a circumference is not a score
A Dice asks how many pixels two masks share. A circumference asks how long the boundary of one of them is. The two fail in different directions, and the directions are the wrong way round for anybody measuring a length.
A ragged boundary barely moves an integral over a region. Add and remove pixels along an edge in roughly equal measure and the area, and the ellipse fitted to it, hardly move - while the Dice falls with every one of them.
A mask that is systematically fat or thin moves it linearly. Grow the whole outline by a pixel and the circumference grows with it, every time, in one direction - while the Dice barely notices, because a one-pixel rim is a small share of a large blob.
So the error a Dice sees best is the one that does not matter here, and the error it sees worst is the one that does. That is an argument until it is measured, and the last three sections measure it.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
The data
The archive unpacks to training_set/ with an image and an _Annotation.png beside it, and training_set_pixel_size_and_HC.csv giving the pixel size and the recorded circumference.
The annotation is a drawn curve rather than a filled region - an ellipse two or three pixels wide with nothing inside it - so the region has to be filled before anything can be trained. The example does that with a hole fill before it builds the configuration, and the criterion for a usable case falls out of the fill rather than being chosen: a curve that runs off the edge of the frame encloses nothing, so the fill returns it unchanged.
186_HC, 346_HC, 628_2HC, 787_HC
Four of the 999, left out. The sonographer’s ellipse continues outside the picture, so the recorded millimetres describe a shape the file does not contain - a limitation of this instrument rather than a defect in the data, and the reason fitting a conic to the visible arc is how the literature handles it.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: Splitting by examination, not by image
text:
Splitting by examination, not by image
HC18 names its files 000_HC, 628_2HC: the leading number is the examination, and several images can come from one. Dividing at random by file puts an image of an examination in training and another image of the same examination in the test set, and the score becomes partly a memory test.
split.group_by is where that belongs. It is a regular expression over the sample key, and the key here is the file name without its extension:
split:
  fractions: [0.6, 0.2, 0.2]
  group_by: '^(\d+)_'
  seed: 1
995 usable images from 803 examinations. Three fractions rather than two, because the millimetres are reported on the third: no number on this page comes off the data early_stopping watched.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
The specification
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: measurements/hc18/cases.csv
  mode: config_file
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
  split:
    fractions: [0.6, 0.2, 0.2]
    group_by: '^(\d+)_'
    seed: 1
models:
  - name: skull
    architecture: u_net
    # 800 x 540 arrives as 800 x 544, which divides by 2^4 and resamples the data almost
    # not at all. A measurement that ends in millimetres should argue with the ellipse,
    # not with the interpolation.
    input_shape: [544, 800]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    batch_size: 4
    epochs: 40
    loss:
      name: cce_dice
    metrics:
      - name: dice
        include_background: false
      - name: iou
        include_background: false
    optimizer:
      name: adam
      learning_rate: 0.001
    callbacks:
      - name: early_stopping
        monitor: val_dice
        patience: 8
        restore_best: true
    augmentation:
      # No vertical flip: an ultrasound fan has a top and a bottom, and a mirrored one is a
      # picture of nothing. The ellipse is symmetric under the horizontal one.
      - name: HorizontalFlip
        params:
          p: 0.5
      - name: RandomBrightnessContrast
        params:
          p: 0.3

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
Training
from pyplatypus import Engine, from_yaml

engine = Engine(from_yaml("examples/hc18.yaml"))
engine.fit()
Forty epochs at 544 x 800, about half an hour on a GTX 1070. The run this page describes reached a mean Dice of 0.9347 on its held-out third; the published hc18-unet weights are a different draw of the same recipe and reached 0.9494.
Neither number is the point of the page, which is the next three sections.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: From a mask to a millimetre
text:
From a mask to a millimetre
A prediction is a mask on a grid. A circumference is a length in the world, and what connects them is the pixel size, which is a property of the file rather than of the model.
from pyplatypus import ellipse_circumference

for case, prediction in engine.predict_stream("skull", split="test", space="source"):
    mask = prediction.argmax(axis=-1) == 1
    mm = ellipse_circumference(mask, spacing=(pixel_mm, pixel_mm))
Two things in those four lines decide whether the number means anything.
space="source", not the model’s grid. The pixel size in the CSV describes the image as it is on disk. A prediction resized to the model’s input shape has pixels of a size nobody recorded, and multiplying by the file’s number would be wrong by the ratio of the two shapes.
spacing scales the coordinates, not the answer. For an area the two are the same thing, since a count scales by the product of the sides either way. For a length they are not: a perimeter is not separable in its axes, so there is no number to multiply a pixel-space circumference by unless the pixels happen to be square. Measured on a circle of radius 100 px at spacing=(2, 1), which is an ellipse of semi-axes 200 and 100: scaling the coordinates gives 968.9 against 968.8 integrated, where the two scalings somebody reaches for answer 628.3 and 1256.7. HC18’s pixels are square, so this example would have been right either way and would have stopped being right on the first anisotropic dataset.
ellipse_axes() returns the two axes if the shape rather than the perimeter is what is wanted, and mask_volume() and instance_sizes() are the same idea for areas and volumes.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: What the annotation costs before the model does
text:
What the annotation costs before the model does
Before blaming a model for a millimetre, measure what the pipeline costs with no model at all: put the truth masks through the same ellipse fit and compare with the sonographer’s figures.
truth masks against the chart, 200 cases      +0.692 mm
the annotation's drawn line                    2.523 px
pi * w * pixel predicts                       +0.685 mm
correlation of prediction with error            0.9994
left unexplained                               0.008 mm
The floor is biased rather than noisy - every case too large by about the same amount - and the cause is the annotation’s own line. The curve a sonographer drew is two and a half pixels wide, not one; filling it puts the region’s boundary half a width outside the curve, and a radius larger by w/2 makes a circumference larger by pi * w.
That is the difference between an explanation and a guess, and it is why the prediction is reported beside the bias rather than subtracted from it: a correction folded into the measurement would hide the one number here that is about the dataset rather than about us.
A model reproducing the truth masks perfectly would still read +0.69 mm high. So the model’s own contribution is the comparison against the truth masks rather than against the chart, and both belong on a page that reports millimetres - the first blames the model for a drawing convention, the second hides the convention from whoever reads the number.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: The Dice cannot see this error
text:
The Dice cannot see this error

mean Dice                                       0.9347
median absolute error                           2.00 mm
mean absolute error                             5.66 mm
75th and 90th percentile                  4.43, 12.36 mm
worst case                                     96.35 mm
Spearman between the two orderings               0.620
Of the 136 test images scoring 0.95 or better - a figure anybody would publish - 49 are still wrong by more than 2 mm, which is 36% of them. On the published weights the same count is 85 of 144, or 59%.
Read the vertical spread of the right-hand panel at any fixed Dice. A column of points two orders of magnitude tall is the finding: the score does not tell you what the measurement will be.
The median and the mean are both here because they disagree. The error distribution has a long tail - half the cases inside 2.00 mm and a tenth outside 12.36 - so the mean describes the tail rather than a typical case, and the median alone would hide that some images are out by the width of a head.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
What this does not settle
One run. The same recipe trained again gives a different correlation. Four draws of it have been measured:
the run on this page                             0.620
a second                                         0.435
the published hc18-unet weights                  0.153
the R vignette's own                             0.458
All four are far from a shared ordering and they span a factor of four. The direction is the finding; the magnitude is one draw, and a single number quoted from this page would overstate the case at one end.
from pyplatypus import available_weights

available_weights()["hc18-unet"]
A measurement is not a measuring instrument. The worst case here is out by 96 mm. These weights are not a biometric tool with a person looking at them, let alone without.
The ellipse is the shape assumed. ellipse_circumference() fits one, which is right for a fetal skull and wrong for anything that is not an ellipse - and it measures one object per image, which is HC18’s shape rather than the general one. Every object in an image, measured separately, is #272 and is not built.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
Notes on the machine
A GTX 1070, which wants the CUDA 12 line of PyTorch; device_report() says what the card can do and pick_device() chooses without assuming CUDA. Training is about half an hour at these settings, and filling the 999 annotations into masks takes a couple of minutes before it. Nothing on this page depends on which card it was, except how long it took.

title: Counting cells in blood smears
text:
BCCD is 364 photographs of blood smears with 4,888 boxes in three classes - red cells, white cells, platelets - and its own train/validation/test split. It is small, it is MIT-licensed, and its classes are wildly unbalanced, which turns out to be the most instructive thing about it.
Where the numbers come from. The anchor figures and the box counts below were produced on this machine from the published weights, with nothing trained; the five-seed table is examples/detect_blood_cells.py’s, measured with the engine on its own at four loader workers. Which number came from where matters here more than usual, and the section on scoring says why.

title: Counting cells in blood smears
section: Before any of that: boxes in a few lines
text:
Before any of that: boxes in a few lines
A detector trained on this data is published, so the shortest way to see whether this works is to borrow it. No training, no GPU, no waiting.
A detection dataset arrives in Pascal VOC’s layout - one flat directory of images beside one flat directory of XML - which is neither of the two layouts the package reads. Turning it into one is the only data wrangling here:
import pyplatypus as pp

# `annotations`, not `masks`: a detection specification looks for that column, because what
# labels an image here is an annotation file and not a picture. Absolute paths, because a
# path in a CSV is resolved against the CSV's own directory.
Path("bccd-test.csv").write_text(
    "images,annotations\n"
    + "\n".join(
        f"{(root / 'JPEGImages' / f'{name}.jpg').resolve()},"
        f"{(root / 'Annotations' / f'{name}.xml').resolve()}"
        for name in names
    )
)
BCCD’s own split - 205 train, 87 validation, 72 test - and not one invented here, which is the only reason the numbers below can be compared with anybody else’s on this dataset.
published = pp.from_dict(
    {
        "task": "object_detection",
        "data": {
            "train_path": "bccd-test.csv",
            "validation_path": "bccd-test.csv",
            "classes": ["RBC", "WBC", "Platelets"],
            "mode": "config_file",
        },
        "models": [
            {
                "name": "cells",
                "architecture": "yolo3",
                "input_shape": [416, 416],
                "weights": "bccd-yolo3",
                "fit": False,
            }
        ],
    }
)
engine = pp.build_engine(published)
engine.fit()
found = engine.predict("cells", "validation")
fit() loads rather than trains when fit: false is set; predict before it answers no model has been trained or loaded yet.
Predictions come back as one table per image in the photograph’s own pixels - xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax, score, label, name - so the boxes land on the picture without anything being undone first.

And here, unlike the nuclei article, a score means something
Those weights were trained on BCCD’s 205 training images. Its 72 test images the model has never seen, so measuring on them is honest - which is the opposite of the nuclei article, where the convenient directory overlapped the training data and no number was reported at all.
The model card’s own figures are mAP@0.5 of 0.857, mAP@[.50:.95] of 0.500 and a mean matched IoU of 0.806, and available_weights() carries them. The description is the part to read before trusting them: published is the median of five seeds rather than the best, and platelets are the unreliable class - which the scoring section shows rather than asserts.


One refusal worth meeting now
A detector’s weights decode boxes relative to the anchors they were trained with. Read with any others, the same numbers produce boxes scaled by a fixed factor: plausible boxes, plausible scores, wrong places, and nothing in any output to say so. So a specification that names both is two claims about one model with one of them untrue:
ConfigError: The configuration has 1 problem:
  - models[0]: model 'cells' names both `weights` and `anchors`. A detector's weights decode
    boxes relative to the anchors they were trained with, so loading uses the ones recorded
    beside the file - which would leave the anchors in this specification describing nothing.
    Remove `anchors` to use theirs, or remove `weights` to fit new ones to your own boxes.
Refused by the file, before any path was read - and that is a different stage from the nuclei article’s refusal, which waits for the weights because only then is there a shape to compare. Two claims in one file need nothing but the file; a claim about a file on disk needs the file.

title: Counting cells in blood smears
section: Anchors, which a detector has and a U-Net does not
text:
Anchors, which a detector has and a U-Net does not
YOLOv3 does not predict a box from nothing. It predicts a correction to one of nine anchors - fixed shapes, three per grid - and which anchors you use decides how much correcting is left to learn. Unset, they are fitted to your own boxes with k-means; the published weights carry theirs in the sidecar beside the file.
Measured here on the published anchors against BCCD’s training boxes: mean IoU 0.8769. COCO’s own nine, borrowed, manage 0.65 on the same boxes - which is the difference between a correction and a rewrite, and it costs nothing to avoid.
A mean hides which class it is made of. A coverage of 0.65 is either every class covered adequately or two covered well and the third not at all, and those want different fixes. The picture tells them apart:
figure = pp.plot_anchors(engine, log=True, model="cells", split="train")

Each point is one annotated box - its width against its height, both as fractions of the 416x416 input - and the diamonds are the anchors. Log axes, because the anchors alone run from about 24 to 147 pixels a side, and on linear ones the smallest class collapses into the corner.
Three clouds, because the three cell types are three sizes, and a diamond near each. The diamonds are not spread evenly: most sit in the crowded middle where the red cells are, which is k-means doing exactly what it was asked - put the anchors where the boxes are, not where the classes are.
And one point sits far below everything else, at about two thirds of a pixel a side. That is not a drawing error and not an outlier in the statistical sense - it is a bad row. Counted here, straight out of the XML:



split
boxes
of zero extent




train
2,805
1


validation
1,138
1


test
945
0



A zero-width box read under Pascal VOC’s inclusive convention comes out one pixel across. k-means drops it, because an overlap with a box that has no area is undefined - which is why the anchors were fitted to 2,804 boxes while the plot draws 2,805. The plot keeps it deliberately: a dataset’s bad rows are worth seeing once, and this is the only place in the whole run where that one is visible at all.
It is also the clearest way to see why COCO’s nine manage only 0.65 here. Those span 10 to 373 pixels a side, because COCO holds objects of every size; these three cell types span about six-fold. Most of that range is spent on boxes this dataset does not contain.
Worth drawing for the split they were not fitted on. Anchors covering the training boxes well and the validation boxes badly would say the two halves hold different objects, and no training curve shows that:
figure = pp.plot_anchors(engine, log=True, model="cells", split="validation")

tools/readme_figures.py article-bccd draws both, from the published weights and without training. The issue that asked for them priced them at a 37-minute run, which is the cost of fitting anchors rather than of drawing the ones a published file already carries.

title: Counting cells in blood smears
text:
What the loss is doing
The run reports four parts rather than one, and the total is the least useful of them.
The total does not reach zero and that is not a stall. Cross-entropy against a soft target bottoms out at the target’s own entropy, so the coordinate term has a floor above zero that depends on the data. Which is exactly why the parts are separate: a total of 5.95 means nothing alone, while coordinates 5.94 beside objectness 6.7e-04 says the model has learned what is where and is still refining the boxes.

title: Counting cells in blood smears
section: Scoring, and the number that is missing on purpose
text:
Scoring, and the number that is missing on purpose
engine.evaluate("test") returns mAP@0.5, mAP@[.50:.95] and mean_matched_iou, with the truth and prediction counts beside them. There is no overall precision and no overall recall, and the absence is deliberate: averaging them over classes needs a weighting, and every choice of weighting is a different claim. Over BCCD’s 4,155 red cells, 372 white and 361 platelets, a single precision is a statement about red cells wearing the costume of a statement about the model.
engine.evaluate_classes("test") is the form in which they mean something. White cells are nearly perfect - one per image and large. Platelets come back at a precision near 0.56, meaning about 44% of the platelets reported are not there, and their boxes fit worst of the three at an overlap near 0.73.

mAP@0.5, mAP@[.50:.95], and which to believe
Two averages answering different questions. The first asks whether an object was found; the second averages over ten overlap thresholds and so also asks how well the box fits. The gap between them is localisation, and mean_matched_iou says that in one number instead of through a difference.
On this dataset the overlap is far steadier than the average precision. Five runs of one recipe differing only in the seed:




mean
sd




mAP@0.5
0.8660
0.0159


mAP@[.50:.95]
0.5159
0.0199


mean IoU of matched boxes
0.8041
0.0026



Six times steadier. Which rank the model gives a borderline platelet moves average precision and leaves the overlap alone - so on a dataset this size, a point of mAP is not a result, and mean_matched_iou is the number to read first. That is not a general law about detection; it is what these 364 images do, and it was found by running five seeds rather than one.
And a seed does not pin the number. It pins which random numbers are drawn, not the order they are consumed in, and the loader’s worker count changes that order. So the same seed means the same recipe on one machine with one worker count. The R vignette this page mirrors records the cost of learning that: a paragraph there quoted a single run’s mAP, and the next knit of the same document disagreed with it by more than a point.

title: Counting cells in blood smears
text:
Looking at it
The comparison is the point. Truth in one colour, predictions in another, on the same image, with plot_boxes(images, predictions, truth=truth, min_score=0.5).
One detail in reading the truth matters more than it looks. Pascal VOC is 1-based and inclusive of both ends, so a box written xmin=1 xmax=10 is 0 to 10 as a continuous interval. Reading it as 0-based shifts every box by a pixel and shrinks it by one - invisible by eye, and real IoU on a platelet 41 pixels across.
A detector that found the right number of objects in the wrong places and one that found the wrong number in the right places score similarly and look nothing alike, which is why this picture is worth more than either average.

title: Counting cells in blood smears
text:
What this does not do
It is not a cell count. A precision near 0.56 on platelets means a count taken from these boxes is too high by about 79%. Counting needs either a better model for the small class or a threshold chosen for counting rather than for a figure, and either way it needs measuring against truth on your own data.
It is one small collection. 205 training images at one magnification, stained one way. BCCD is a demonstration dataset.
It is not a diagnostic tool, and a result from it is not a laboratory result.

title: Counting cells in blood smears
text:
Notes on the machine
YOLOv3 is 61.5 million parameters, thirty times a U-Net at the settings in the nuclei article, so this is the one place in the package where the hardware matters: 150 epochs is about 37 minutes on a GTX 1070.
A card of that generation needs the CUDA 12 build of PyTorch. This package does not install torch and will not choose a build for you - you install your own, so the equivalent of the R package’s platypus_use_torch("pascal") is asking your index for the CUDA 12 wheels. If torch.cuda.is_available() is False on a machine that has a GPU, check that first: a run that quietly went to the processor looks exactly like a run that is simply slow.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
data_science_bowl.yaml finds the nuclei in these pictures and stops there. The mask it produces says nucleus or not nucleus for every pixel, so two nuclei touching each other come back as one region, and a count taken from it would be wrong.
This is the same dataset, read a different way. Nothing new was collected: the 2018 Data Science Bowl ships one mask per nucleus, and data_science_bowl.yaml unites them. Here they keep their identity, which turns the question from where are the nuclei into how many are there, and which pixels belong to which one.
Where the numbers come from. The two object counts below were produced by running the code shown, on this machine, against the published weights - no training. Everything else is cited where it is used: the weights’ three scores are the registry’s own description, the ceilings are pyplatypus#159 and #212, and the trained rows are examples/publish_dsbowl_instance_weights.py’s. That division is deliberate - an article that re-trains a published recipe with fewer epochs adds a number nobody will compare.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: Before any of that: objects in four lines
text:
Before any of that: objects in four lines
Weights for this are published, so the difference is visible before anything is trained. The borrowed model predicts three channels - background, the interior of a nucleus and a rim around it - and decode says how those channels become objects:
import pyplatypus as pp

borrowed = pp.from_dict(
    {
        "task": "instance_segmentation",
        "data": {
            "train_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "validation_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "mode": "nested_dirs",
        },
        "models": [
            {
                "name": "published",
                "architecture": "u_net",
                "input_shape": [256, 256],
                "blocks": 4,
                "filters": 16,
                "separation": {"name": "rim", "width": 2},
                "decode": [{"name": "nearest_seed"}, {"name": "connected_components"}],
                "weights": "dsbowl-instances",
                "fit": False,
            }
        ],
    }
)
engine = pp.build_engine(borrowed)
engine.fit()
objects = engine.predict_instances(split="validation", decode="nearest_seed")
len(objects)
fit() is still the call, and fit: false only changes what it does. With the flag set it loads rather than trains, and nothing before it has touched the weights: build_engine reads the data and builds the model, so a predict straight after it is refused with no model has been trained or loaded yet. That is one line a reader would otherwise find out by being refused, and this page had it wrong in its first version.
Loading does check the weights against the model they are going into, and before torch is reached: a wrong shape is a refusal naming the field rather than a tensor-size error from inside a loss.
predict_instances returns one integer label map per image, in the split’s own order - objects numbered from 1, with 0 for background. A list rather than a stacked array, because what a caller does with these is read one case at a time.
predict is the other call and it is not the same thing: it returns the model’s own channels, class probabilities and raw vector components, which is what predict_instances decodes. A softmax across a flow component and a class would return a number and mean nothing, so that one is left raw.
Now the same loaded file, decoded the other way. connected_components ignores the rim channel entirely - it labels connected foreground, which is what a semantic mask gives you:
merged = engine.predict_instances(split="validation", decode="connected_components")

counts = [(a.max(), b.max()) for a, b in zip(objects, merged)]
worst = max(range(len(counts)), key=lambda i: counts[i][0] - counts[i][1])
counts[worst]
On the picture where the two disagree most, that is 245 objects against 180: one file of weights, one forward pass, two answers to how many nuclei are in this picture, and sixty-five touching nuclei run together by the second. Over all 134 images it is 5,378 against 4,914, which is the same gap counted once rather than per picture. Drawn with overlay_instances, neither colour map is decoration - adjacent objects are guaranteed different colours, so a colour shared across a boundary is two nuclei the decoding ran together.
No score is reported here, on purpose. These weights were trained on stage1_train and this directory is stage1_validation, which is the split they were measured on - the numbers that mean something travel with them, and available_weights() carries them:
U-Net, 256x256, nuclei in light microscopy, trained to separate touching objects:
interior, rim and background. BBBC038v1 (the 2018 Data Science Bowl, CC0), the same 134
held-out images as `dsbowl-unet`. **One file, three scores** - instance average
precision 0.5445 by nearest_seed, 0.5390 by watershed and 0.4822 by
connected_components - so a number from these weights means nothing without the
decoding it came from. Foreground Dice 0.9118. The separation signal is worth +0.0623
here while a perfect mask is worth +0.2398: the mask is the limit on this data, not the
signal.
That description is the thing to read before quoting anything. One file, three scores: the decoding is part of the number, and 0.0623 separates the best from the worst.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: The semantic sibling, side by side
text:
The semantic sibling, side by side
dsbowl-unet is the published model data_science_bowl.yaml trains: same data, same held-out images, one foreground class. It is the comparison this whole document is about, so it is worth running rather than describing - the same from_dict with task: semantic_segmentation, a colormap of black and white, and weights: dsbowl-unet. Its predict returns a stacked array of masks, not a list of label maps, and that difference is the whole point.
A mask is not worse. It answers a different question, and if the answer you need is what fraction of this slide is nuclei it is the one to use. The label map is what you need to count them, or to measure one of them.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
The data
The directory layout is data_science_bowl.yaml’s, because it is the same directory:
stage1_train/
  00ae65c1c.../
    images/00ae65c1c....png
    masks/8a0ac8e3c....png      # one file per nucleus, 70 of them in this case
    masks/9a1e2f4b7....png
    ...
536 cases in stage1_train, and mode: nested_dirs is what reads that shape. The one difference from the semantic file is the task: instance_segmentation reads those per-object files as identities, where semantic_segmentation takes their element-wise maximum and destroys them.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: The specification, with the borrowed model beside a new one
text:
The specification, with the borrowed model beside a new one
Two models in one file, and evaluate() returns a row per model and decoding, so one table holds the comparison the rest of this document rests on. The shipped version of this is examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml, which trains rim beside flows rather than a borrowed file beside a new one - two separation signals, which is the question that file was written to answer.
separation is one block per model and decode is a list, and the asymmetry is not cosmetic: the separation sets what the network predicts, so changing it means another training run, while a second decoding is another pass over the same predictions. Measured on these 134 images, a second decoding costs 1.41 seconds against sixteen minutes for a second training run - so the right analogy is metrics: and not callbacks:.
connected_components is in both models’ decode lists on purpose. It ignores the separation signal, so it is the row the other rows have to be read against: not a weaker model, the same model asked a question that throws half its output away.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
Train
spec = pp.from_yaml("examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml")
engine = pp.build_engine(spec, num_workers=4)
history = engine.fit(verbose=True)
num_workers=4 is worth copying: the GPU spends most of a run waiting for PNGs to be decoded, and nothing about the model changes.
The epoch counts in that file are asymmetric and deliberately so - 120 for rim against 60 for flows. Measured at 60 each on 2026-10-13, rim was still climbing while flows had flattened, and a table ranking two models needs both converged or a column reports the budget rather than the signal.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
Compare
engine.evaluate("validation") returns one row per (model, decoding). Three things in it, in the order they matter.
Within either model, the mask is identical across its rows. There is one forward pass; the rows differ only in how its channels were turned into objects. So the spread between a model’s own rows is the decoding’s contribution and nothing else.
connected_components is the row the others are read against, for the reason above.
The two separation signals are a tie. rim is worth +0.0676 of instance average precision over its own connected_components row and flows +0.0661 - a difference of 0.0015 against a run-to-run spread of 0.0112 measured on that same file. On foreground Dice they are 0.9159 and 0.9097, which is 0.0062 apart.
That last number is worth a warning, because the table had it wrong once. dice is a mean over whichever class channels a head has - three for rim, two for flows - so the column named dice compares two different quantities and showed the two masks 0.09 apart with the sign reversed. foreground_dice is the one to read across models; class dice is the honest name for the other.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: What this does not settle, measured rather than guessed
text:
What this does not settle, measured rather than guessed
The instance milestone closed on numbers that say the interesting part is somewhere else:







route
instance AP on these 134 images




the published semantic weights through connected components
0.4888


a perfect semantic mask through connected components
0.7655


the published separation weights, nearest_seed
0.5445


a perfect mask through the same separation route
0.9846



So connected components caps any model here at 0.7655 - a flawless mask still scores that - and the separation signal is worth about +0.06 on top of the mask it is computed from, where fixing the mask is worth +0.24. Three trained signals were compared and they agree.
Read that as a closed direction rather than as a run to tune: on this data the headroom is in the mask, and a document that ended on a score would be claiming the opposite of what was measured.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: Which objects, not how many pixels
text:
Which objects, not how many pixels
A score cannot tell you whether you found the wrong nuclei or drew the right ones badly. overlay_instance_agreement matches predicted objects to true ones the way the metric does and colours the three outcomes, so the failure is visible by kind: a true object a prediction matched, one that nothing matched, and a prediction matching nothing.
The truth has to be assembled from the per-object files, and read_image(nearest=True) matters - interpolating a label map invents numbers belonging to no object:
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

def truth_map(case: Path, size=(256, 256)) -> np.ndarray:
    labels = np.zeros(size, dtype=np.int32)
    for index, file in enumerate(sorted((case / "masks").glob("*.png")), start=1):
        mask = pp.read_image(file, channels=1, size=size, nearest=True)
        labels[mask[..., 0] > 0.5] = index
    return labels
The threshold the matching uses is an IoU of 0.5 and it cannot be lowered below that: under 0.5 one prediction can satisfy two true objects at once, the match stops being one to one, and the average precision refuses the same thing for the same reason.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
A decoding changed without retraining
This is what decode being a list is for. No model is loaded again and nothing is trained:
for how in ("nearest_seed", "watershed", "connected_components"):
    maps = engine.predict_instances("rim", split="validation", decode=how)
    print(how, sum(int(m.max()) for m in maps))
Against 5,999 objects in the truth over 134 images. The counts, not the scores, are where the decoding shows itself most plainly: the gap between the first row and the last is nuclei that were found and then run together with a neighbour.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: What it was for: a count and a size distribution
text:
What it was for: a count and a size distribution
One label map in, one row per object out - and this is the one place where the R package has a function and this one deliberately does not:
labels = engine.predict_instances("rim", split="validation", decode="nearest_seed")[0]
objects, voxels = np.unique(labels[labels > 0], return_counts=True)
numpy.unique with return_counts is the operation, so a wrapper here would be a name to learn in place of one a reader already has. The R package carries an instance_sizes for this, because R’s idiom for the same two lines is clumsier; it is pure R and calls nothing in this package, which is why there is nothing here to point at instead.
Written without parentheses on purpose, and the test is the reason: tests/test_articles.py reads a backticked name followed by parentheses as something offered to a reader to call, and resolves it against this package. A name belonging to the other package is not that, so it is named rather than offered - which is the same distinction test_schema_prose_names.py was written for after the schema’s prose sent a Python reader to R’s training_history.
In pixels, because this dataset has no physical scale. A CT scan carries its spacing in its header and target_spacing is where that enters a run; these are microscopy images with no calibration recorded, so a number in micrometres here would be invented. A count is still a count.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: The same thing from a file
text:
The same thing from a file
Everything above is one file in this repository:
spec = pp.from_yaml("examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml")
That file is also the longest commented configuration here, because two of its decisions needed their reasons written down: the asymmetric epoch counts, and a correction kept in place rather than deleted after dice was read across two models with different numbers of class channels. The configuration guide’s Instances instead of one mask section has the same fields with a reader’s explanation beside each.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: A note on older graphics cards
text:
A note on older graphics cards
PyTorch 2.8 and later ship CUDA 13 builds, and CUDA 13 dropped the Maxwell, Pascal and Volta generations - a GTX 10-series card cannot run them, and no driver update changes that.
This package does not install torch and will not choose a build for you, which is the difference from the R package: there, platypus_use_torch("pascal") exists because reticulate provisions the environment and something has to decide. Here you install your own, so the equivalent is asking your index for the CUDA 12 wheels before anything else. If torch.cuda.is_available() is False on a machine that has a GPU, that is the first thing to check - otherwise everything above runs on the processor instead, perhaps ten times slower, and says nothing about it.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
One YAML file describes a whole run. This page is the walk through it; every field it accepts is the reference beside it, generated from the same models that read the file.
The same file works in both packages. Python reads it with from_yaml(), R with platypus_spec(yaml = ...), and both hand it to the same validator. Nothing on this page is Python-specific except the two lines that run it.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
One file, one run
The shortest thing that trains:
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: first_try
    input_shape: [256, 256]
from pyplatypus import build_engine, from_yaml

engine = build_engine(from_yaml("run.yaml"))
engine.fit()
print(engine.evaluate())
Four things are required and the rest have defaults: task, data.train_path, and a name and input_shape for each model. Everything else - the architecture, the loss, the optimiser, how many epochs - has a default that lives in the engine, so a short configuration is a complete one rather than an incomplete one.
colormap says which colour in a mask means which class, darkest first. Masks stored as label maps rather than pictures use labels: [0, 1] instead, and giving both is an error: exactly one says how a mask is encoded.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Several models at once
models: is a list, and that is the reason this file format exists rather than only the code path. Each entry trains on the same data and lands in the same table, so the comparison is one run rather than a loop somebody has to write.
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: shallow
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    blocks: 3
    filters: 16
  - name: deep
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    blocks: 5
    filters: 32
    architecture: u_net_plus_plus
name has to be unique, because it is how a model is identified in every score table, in every record and in engine.predict(model_name=...). Two models called the same thing is refused rather than resolved.
Two entries differing only in blocks is a legitimate configuration and a common one: this is for comparing variants, not only architectures.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Dividing one folder
With no validation_path, say how to divide train_path:
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/all
  split:
    fractions: [0.7, 0.15, 0.15]
    group_by: "^(patient\\d+)_"
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: by_patient
    input_shape: [256, 256]
Two fractions give train and validation, three add a test set. Nothing is written to disk - the samples are divided after they are discovered, so there are no new folders and no CSV.
group_by is required and may be null. It is a regular expression whose first group is the thing that must not appear on both sides - a patient, a scan, a slide. The mistake it prevents leaves no trace: slices of one patient in both sets make validation measure memory rather than generalisation, and every number in the output still looks reasonable. An omitted key would be that choice made silently; null is the same choice made on purpose, for data where every sample is independent.
Exactly one of split and validation_path. If a run genuinely has no validation set - a final fit on everything - say validation: false, which is the third answer rather than an absence, because “I have no validation set” and “I forgot” look identical otherwise.

title: Writing a configuration
section: Augmentation, callbacks, and the rest of a model
text:
Augmentation, callbacks, and the rest of a model
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: augmented
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    epochs: 40
    loss: {name: dice}
    metrics: [{name: iou}, {name: dice}]
    optimizer: {name: adam, learning_rate: 0.001}
    callbacks:
      - {name: early_stopping, monitor: val_loss, patience: 10}
      - {name: model_checkpoint, monitor: val_iou, path: runs/best.safetensors}
    augmentation:
      - {name: HorizontalFlip, params: {p: 0.5}}
      - {name: RandomBrightnessContrast, params: {p: 0.3}}
loss, optimizer, each metric and each callback are blocks chosen by name:, and the name decides which other keys that block accepts. A key the chosen one does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
There is no mode on a callback that watches a number. The direction is taken from the name: anything ending in loss is better lower, anything else better higher. So monitor: val_iou maximises and monitor: val_loss minimises, and there is nothing to set inconsistently.
Augmentation applies to the training data only - never to validation, where the point is to measure the same thing every epoch. The names are albumentations’ own, and available_transforms() lists what the installed version offers; at rank=3 the list is shorter, because support for volumes is uneven. Each step is probed at the model’s own input size while the pipeline is built, so a transform that cannot do the job says so before the first epoch rather than during it.

title: Writing a configuration
section: Overlapping classes instead of one per voxel
text:
Overlapping classes instead of one per voxel
colormap and labels both say the same thing about a voxel: it is in exactly one class. regions is the third way of naming classes and the only one that drops that assumption - classes named as unions of a label map’s values, which is how BraTS and the lesion-inside-an-organ family actually store their ground truth.
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  regions:
    - {name: whole tumour, of: [1, 2, 4]}
    - {name: tumour core, of: [1, 4]}
    - {name: enhancing, of: [4]}
models:
  - name: brats
    input_shape: [240, 240]
    loss: {name: focal}
The task is still semantic_segmentation. What changes is what a channel means.
There is no background entry, so the class count is not the one you would write as labels. Those same masks as labels: [0, 1, 2, 4] are four classes; as the three regions above they are three channels. And a voxel whose value is 4 is in all three of them at once, which is the point rather than a tolerated side effect.
Each channel is an independent binary question - a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them - so the channels do not compete and do not sum to one. That is what makes the overlap expressible, and it is also why a prediction cannot be written back as a single picture: one voxel gets one colour, and a voxel here may belong to three classes. A colour map refuses such a prediction rather than taking the strongest channel, and save_class_masks() is what it points at - one binary picture per region, named after the region, which is the only form a picture can hold without losing the overlap.
Two regions are the minimum, because one region is ordinary binary segmentation and labels: [0, 1] already says that - with a background channel, which regions has none of. Disjoint regions are allowed and are not a mistake: they group several values into one class and drop the background channel, which is a useful thing to ask for and is refused nowhere.
The failure this invites is quiet, so it is refused loudly. A region whose of matches nothing in the data - of: [3] against a label map holding 1, 2 and 4 - is a channel of zeros. It trains to predict nothing and scores a Dice of 0 for that region while every other number in the run looks ordinary, which is the kind of result that gets read as “that class is hard”. The mask check refuses it before training and names the region rather than its position, and inspect_masks answers the same question over as much of the data as you want, naming it the same way.

When the overlap was drawn separately: classes_from
regions needs the overlap to be a union of one label map’s values, which is how BraTS stores it - one integer per voxel, and the scored classes are conventions over those integers. Some overlaps are not like that. A vessel crossing an organ, or two annotators’ masks of the same structure, were drawn independently and no single integer can hold both. Those arrive as one binary file per class, and classes_from names them: one regular expression per class, in class order, matched against a sample’s mask files.
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  classes_from:
    - _vessel\.png$
    - _organ\.png$
models:
  - name: crossing
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    loss: {name: cce_dice}
Everything the section above says about a channel still holds: independent binary questions, no background entry, a prediction that cannot be written back as one picture, save_class_masks() where a colour map refuses. The difference between the two namings is the file on disk and nothing else.
Every pattern must match exactly one of a sample’s mask files, and every mask file must match a pattern. Both halves are refused, because each is invisible from the other side: a pattern matching nothing is a class the model is never shown, and a file matching no pattern is a class the data has and nobody asked for. The order is written rather than inferred for the reason channels_from gives, with worse consequences here - sorting the names is reproducible and anatomically meaningless, and a model trained with the vessel in channel 0 and used where channel 0 is the organ answers plausibly, in range, with nothing downstream able to tell.
#91 asked which of the two shapes this package needed; the answer, in 2026-10-12’s decision, was nested regions first. This is the other half.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Instances instead of one mask
task: instance_segmentation keeps the objects apart rather than uniting them. The data block gets shorter rather than longer: no colormap and no labels, because there are always exactly two classes - background and object - and what names the objects is the directory of per-object mask files itself.
task: instance_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  mode: nested_dirs
models:
  - name: rim
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    separation: {name: rim, width: 2}
    loss: {name: cce_dice}
    decode: [{name: nearest_seed}, {name: connected_components}]
  - name: flows
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    separation:
      name: flows
      loss: {name: mse, where: foreground}
Two axes, and they are deliberately different shapes. separation is one block per model and has no default: it is what the network is trained to predict, so it sets the width of the head - three channels for rim, four for flows at two classes - and that width is derived rather than written anywhere. decode is a list, because several decodings share one forward pass: a second decoding of 134 images costs 1.41 s against an hour and a half for a second training run, so it belongs beside metrics: rather than beside callbacks:. evaluate() then returns a row per (model, decoding).
Which mask column to read is a decision the table makes for you and it used to make it wrongly. Every row carries foreground_dice - the binary overlap of anything the model called an object against anything that is one, the same arithmetic whatever the separation is - and that is the one to read across models. The dice beside it is the training metric, a mean over the class channels the head has, so three for rim against two for flows: read down one model’s rows, never across two. On the Data Science Bowl’s validation cases the class column showed two masks 0.09 apart that are 0.0062 apart, and in the other direction.
No value appears in both lists, which is what settles which field a new idea belongs in: separation is a noun and decode is a verb. rim can be decoded by nearest_seed or watershed, flows by follow_flows, and connected_components reads no signal at all and works with every target. Leave decode out and it derives to the signal’s own decoding plus connected_components; write a list and you get the list you wrote.
A model’s own loss and metrics score the mask at either separation, so they are an overlap or a cross-entropy loss here as everywhere else. A flows block carries its own loss for the two vector channels, which is where mse, l1 and smooth_l1 belong: where: foreground averages the error over the voxels the target is defined on, and on these images that is 13.97% of them.
What this task is worth is measured, and it is not flattering. On the Data Science Bowl the separation signal is worth +0.068 of instance average precision at best while a perfect mask is worth +0.2398, so the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6 - and a perfect semantic mask decoded by connected_components still scores only 0.7655. That is what the yardstick row is for: a run that improved the mask and did nothing for the separation improves every row at once, and without the row that ignores the signal there is nothing to notice it against.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Detection instead of segmentation
task: object_detection changes which fields the file accepts. Boxes rather than masks, so classes and an annotation format rather than a colormap:
task: object_detection
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  annotation_format: pascal_voc
  classes: [rbc, wbc, platelets]
models:
  - name: cells
    input_shape: [416, 416]
Leave anchors out and they are fitted to your own boxes by k-means on an IoU distance, anchors_per_grid of them per grid. That is worth about 0.23 of mean overlap against COCO’s nine on blood cells - measured, 0.65 against 0.88 - so the default is the useful one and naming anchors by hand is for reproducing a published model.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Not training at all
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/images
  validation_path: data/images
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: published
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    weights: dsbowl-unet
    fit: false
weights takes a registry name, a local path, or hf://owner/repo/file@commit - and the hf:// form requires the commit, because weights that change under a stable name are the worst kind of irreproducibility. A registry name carries one already.
With fit: false nothing trains and engine.predict() works immediately. The weights are checked against the model they are being loaded into before torch is touched: a shape, a channel count or a class count that does not match is a refusal naming the field, not a tensor-size error from inside a loss.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
What is checked, and when
Validation happens in this order, and the first two cost no epochs:

The file, against the schema. Unknown fields, missing required ones, a name: that no block has, a callback watching a number nothing will produce. Before any path is read.
The data on disk, when the engine is built: that the folders exist, that images and masks correspond, and that every class in colormap or labels actually appears in the masks - because a declared class appearing in none has a target channel of zeros, so the model is never shown what it is being asked to find.
Everything else, during the run.

A refusal names the field and says what to do. models[0].callbacks[1].model_checkpoint.path: Field required is the whole message - the path through the file, then the problem.

title: Writing a configuration
pyplatypus
text: The engine behind rplatypus: semantic segmentation and object detection in PyTorch, described by one specification and run from it.

title: pyplatypus
text:
A run, in five lines
import pyplatypus

spec = pyplatypus.from_yaml("run.yaml")
engine = pyplatypus.build_engine(spec)
engine.fit()
engine.evaluate("validation")
from_yaml and from_dict build the same object, so a specification written by hand and one read from a file are the same thing. build_engine returns the engine the specification’s task asks for.

title: pyplatypus
section: The same run as a configuration file
text:
The same run as a configuration file
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: train/

  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: unet
    architecture: u_net
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    loss: {name: dice}
    metrics: [{name: iou}]
Everything not written down has a default, and the defaults live here rather than in the caller - so a short configuration is a complete one.

title: pyplatypus
section: What the reference is generated from
text:
What the reference is generated from
The pages under Reference come from the docstrings through quartodoc, so they cannot describe a function this package does not have. The >>> examples in them are run by pytest --doctest-modules, which means the site cannot publish an example that does not work - five claims written into Args: and Returns: were false when they were first written, and the doctests caught every one.
The configuration fields are documented on the models themselves, so the YAML reference and the validation messages say the same thing because they are the same text.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
text:
The 2018 Data Science Bowl asked for the nuclei in microscopy images: several hundred pictures, taken down different microscopes under different stains, each with its nuclei outlined. It is a good first problem because it is genuinely varied and genuinely small.
This walks through it end to end.
Where the numbers come from. The figure and the foreground shares below were produced on this machine by the code shown; the trained rows are examples/data_science_bowl.yaml‘s, and the published weights’ scores are the registry’s own. Nothing was trained to write this page.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
section: Before any of that: a mask in four lines
text:
Before any of that: a mask in four lines
A model trained on this data is published, so the shortest way to see whether the package does anything useful is to borrow it. No training, no waiting:
import pyplatypus as pp

published = pp.from_dict(
    {
        "task": "semantic_segmentation",
        "data": {
            "train_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "validation_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "mode": "nested_dirs",
            "colormap": [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]],
        },
        "models": [
            {
                "name": "nuclei",
                "input_shape": [256, 256],
                "weights": "dsbowl-unet",
                "fit": False,
            }
        ],
    }
)
engine = pp.build_engine(published)
engine.fit()
masks = engine.predict("nuclei", "validation")
masks.shape
fit() is still the call and fit: false only changes what it does - with the flag set it loads rather than trains. build_engine reads the data and builds the model; a predict straight after it answers no model has been trained or loaded yet.
Notice what the specification does not say: no architecture, no blocks, no filters. A published file records its own geometry and the engine adopts it, so naming them would risk a specification that disagrees with the file - and the file would win.
figure = pp.plot_masks(images, prediction=masks[:3])

The weights came down from the Hub on first use and are cached afterwards, so running this again costs nothing. tools/readme_figures.py article-dsbowl is the script that drew it.
No score is reported here, on purpose. This directory and the one the weights were trained on come from the same collection and overlap, so anything measured here would flatter the model. The numbers that mean something were measured on a held-out split when the weights were published, and travel with them - available_weights() carries the description, and it says these are semantic, so touching nuclei come back as one region and a count taken from them would be wrong. Telling touching nuclei apart is the article about that.
One thing worth meeting here rather than later. Weights belong to an exact model, not to a task, and the rest of this page trains at 160x160 while these were trained at 256:
mismatched = pp.from_dict(
    {
        "task": "semantic_segmentation",
        "data": {
            "train_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "validation_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "mode": "nested_dirs",
            "colormap": [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]],
        },
        "models": [
            {
                "name": "nuclei",
                "architecture": "u_net",
                "input_shape": [160, 160],
                "blocks": 4,
                "filters": 16,
                "weights": "dsbowl-unet",
                "fit": False,
            }
        ],
    }
)
pp.build_engine(mismatched).fit()
WeightsError: 'dsbowl-unet' was trained for a different model:
  - input_shape: weights say (256, 256), the model says (160, 160)
Loading anyway would either fail inside torch or, where the shapes happen to agree, produce
a model that predicts confidently and means nothing.
The file itself is fine and that is the point of the two stages. from_dict accepts this: every field is spelled correctly and 160 is a legal input_shape. The refusal comes when the weights are loaded, because only then is there something to compare them against - which is why the message names the field rather than a tensor size.
Refused with the field that differs, and before torch was reached. That check exists because the failure it prevents is silent: weights trained on a different colormap with the same number of classes load perfectly and predict nonsense.
Everything below trains a model from scratch instead, which is what you will actually do on your own data - the published weights are a demonstration and a baseline, not an answer to your problem.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
text:
The data
One directory per image, each holding an images and a masks subdirectory. The masks subdirectory holds one file per nucleus:
stage1_train/
  00ae65c1c.../
    images/00ae65c1c....png
    masks/8a0ac8e3c....png      # one file per nucleus, 27 of them in this case
    masks/9a1e2f4b7....png
    ...
536 cases in stage1_train and 134 in stage1_validation, and mode: nested_dirs is what reads that shape. For a semantic task the per-nucleus files are united - their element-wise maximum - which is the step that turns which nucleus into nucleus or not. That is the right thing here and the wrong thing for counting, which is the other article’s subject.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
section: Look at it before training on it
text:
Look at it before training on it
The most useful thing to know before choosing anything else is how much of each picture is actually the thing you are looking for.
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

def foreground(case: Path, size=(160, 160)) -> float:
    united = np.zeros(size, dtype=bool)
    for file in (case / "masks").glob("*.png"):
        united |= pp.read_image(file, channels=1, size=size, nearest=True)[..., 0] > 0.5
    return float(united.mean())
Over forty cases drawn from stage1_validation, measured on this machine:




min
Q1
median
mean
Q3
max




foreground share
0.013
0.033
0.109
0.133
0.214
0.455



Nuclei are a minority of the pixels in every image, and how small a minority varies by a factor of 35 between images. Both facts are worth acting on now rather than discovering later. The R vignette this page mirrors reports 0.011 to 0.334 over its own forty - a different sample of the same data, and the same conclusion.
Because the foreground is a minority, a model that predicts background everywhere and finds nothing at all still scores well on accuracy, and well on a Dice averaged over both classes. So the metrics in the configuration below are asked for with include_background: false: the number reported is then the one about the nuclei, and a model that finds none of them scores zero, as it should.
Because the share varies so much, the loss has to hold up at both ends. Plain cross-entropy will happily settle into predicting background on the sparse images; blending it with Dice, or using Focal-Tversky with alpha above a half, keeps the rare class worth getting right.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
text:
The specification
Two models, so there is something to compare. They share the data and differ in architecture and objective - u_net with cce_dice, and linknet with focal_tversky at alpha: 0.7:
models:
  - name: unet
    architecture: u_net
    input_shape: [160, 160]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    loss:
      name: cce_dice
    metrics:
      - name: dice
        include_background: false
      - name: iou
        include_background: false
    epochs: 6

  - name: linknet
    architecture: linknet
    input_shape: [160, 160]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    loss:
      name: focal_tversky
      alpha: 0.7            # weight missed nuclei more than false alarms
    epochs: 6
The alpha: 0.7 weights false negatives above false positives: it would rather flag something that is not a nucleus than miss one. Whether that is the right trade depends entirely on what the count is for.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
text:
Train
spec = pp.from_yaml("examples/data_science_bowl.yaml")
engine = pp.build_engine(spec, num_workers=4)
history = engine.fit(verbose=True)
num_workers=4 is worth copying: the GPU spends most of a run waiting for PNGs to be decoded, and nothing about the model changes.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
text:
Compare
engine.evaluate("validation") returns one row per model, and the columns to read are the metrics rather than the loss.
Read the loss column with care, and note that loss_function sits beside it. These two models were trained on different objectives, so their losses are not on a common scale - a Focal-Tversky of 0.31 is not better or worse than a CCE-Dice of 0.22, it is not the same question. The metrics are comparable, because they measure the mask rather than the objective.
That is the column this table exists to make unquotable, and it is the same shape of mistake as dice in the instance table, where a mean over a different number of class channels made two models look 0.09 apart when their masks were 0.006 apart.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
text:
Look at what it did
predictions = engine.predict("unet", "validation")
figure = pp.plot_masks(images, prediction=predictions[shown], truth=truth)
The last column is the one that repays attention. Green is what was found, red what was missed, yellow what was invented - and a single overlap score cannot tell you which of the three you have.
On this data almost all of the red is a thin rim around nuclei that were otherwise found. The model is locating nuclei well and drawing them slightly too small. If the question is how many nuclei are there, that hardly matters. If it is how large are they, it is exactly what matters - and the fix is a longer run or a loss that weights boundaries, not a different architecture.
Neither the Dice nor any other single number distinguishes those two situations from a model that found three quarters of the nuclei and missed the rest. That is the reason to draw the picture.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
section: The same thing from a file
text:
The same thing from a file
Everything above is one file in this repository:
spec = pp.from_yaml("examples/data_science_bowl.yaml")
The configuration guide walks the fields; Every configuration field is the reference beside it, generated from the models that read the file.

title: Finding nuclei in microscopy images
section: A note on older graphics cards
text:
A note on older graphics cards
PyTorch 2.8 and later ship CUDA 13 builds, and CUDA 13 dropped the Maxwell, Pascal and Volta generations - a GTX 10-series card cannot run them, and no driver update changes that.
This package does not install torch and will not choose a build for you. You install your own, so the equivalent of the R package’s platypus_use_torch("pascal") is asking your index for the CUDA 12 wheels. If torch.cuda.is_available() is False on a machine that has a GPU, that is the first thing to check - otherwise everything above runs on the processor instead, perhaps ten times slower, and says nothing about it.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
FIVES is 800 colour fundus photographs at 2048 x 2048 - 200 each of normal, AMD, diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma - with a vessel tree drawn over every one. It is CC BY 4.0, it ships its own balanced train/test split, and it is the only dataset in this documentation that cannot be handed to a network whole.
Three things here appear in no other article, and each is the reason this dataset was chosen.
It tiles. splits reads each image at full resolution and cuts it into a grid of inputs.
It is scored on a metric Dice cannot stand in for. clDice asks whether a structure is connected rather than whether its pixels coincide, and a skeleton is a property of a whole mask, so it is measured on the reassembled image rather than on the tiles.
It reports per disease rather than as one mean, which is how the interesting thing about this dataset was found - and the interesting thing turns out not to be about the disease.
Where the numbers come from. Everything below is one run of examples/segment_retinal_vessels.py at its own defaults - 40 epochs, 6.7 hours on a GTX 1070 - whose record is measurements/fives/fives.json in the project’s workbench, with the quality join printed by measurements/fives/quality.py and the figure drawn by that same script’s --figures. Unlike the other articles’ figures, this one cannot be redrawn from published weights alone: it is this run’s prediction, and the script draws it at the end of the run rather than from a file. The published fives-unet weights are a second run of exactly this configuration and score 0.8789 where this one scores 0.8828; where a number below belongs to those weights rather than to this run, it says so. The last section is different again and says so in its own first paragraph.
This page mirrors vignette("retinal-vessels") in the R package, which is the source for the prose: the walk is the same, the route is not. R reaches these destinations through constructors; here they are reached through a configuration file.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
section: Why a vessel cannot be resized
text:
Why a vessel cannot be resized
FIVES images are 2048 x 2048, and the obvious move is to resize them to something a U-Net is comfortable with. It is the wrong move here, and the reason is a measurement rather than a preference.
A FIVES vessel is about nine pixels wide - measured as mask area over skeleton length, over six random masks. Resized to 256 the same vessels are about 1.2 pixels. That matters because of what happens at one pixel: shift a one-pixel structure by a single pixel and it overlaps the truth nowhere at all, so Dice, IoU and clDice alike read zero and none of them can tell a near miss from a total failure. Tiling keeps the data out of that regime, which is what splits is for.
(The nine-pixel figure corrects the one-to-five this dataset is usually described with. One to five is what remains after a resize - a property of the preprocessing, not of the retina.)
The last section of this page measures what that claim is actually worth, and it is narrower than this paragraph makes it sound.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
The data
One 1.7 GB download, CC BY 4.0. The authors’ own split is already balanced across the four groups - 150 train and 50 test of each - so it is used rather than replaced.
The archive is laid out as Original/ and Ground truth/ with matching file names, which is not a layout the package discovers on its own, so the pairs are written into a CSV and the specification reads that:
from pathlib import Path

FOLDER = "FIVES A Fundus Image Dataset for AI-based Vessel Segmentation"

def write_split(root: Path, split: str, out: Path) -> int:
    # `glob("*.png")` rather than everything in the directory: the archive ships a
    # `Thumbs.db` beside the 600 training images, and a Windows thumbnail cache is not a
    # fundus photograph. Filtering by extension is also what keeps the pairing below honest.
    images = sorted((root / FOLDER / split / "Original").glob("*.png"))
    rows = ["key,images,masks"]
    for image in images:
        mask = root / FOLDER / split / "Ground truth" / image.name
        if not mask.exists():
            raise SystemExit(f"{image.name} has no mask beside it")
        # The key is the file's own name. Without it a `config_file` sample is called
        # `row 55`, which names nothing on disk and cannot be grouped by - and grouping is
        # most of what this page has to say.
        rows.append(f"{image.stem},{image.resolve()},{mask.resolve()}")
    out.write_text("\n".join(rows) + "\n")
    return len(images)
The disease is in the file name - _N, _A, _D, _G for normal, AMD, diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma - which is what the grouping below reads.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
The configuration
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: measurements/fives/splits/train.csv
  validation_path: measurements/fives/splits/test.csv
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
  mode: config_file
models:
  - name: vessels
    architecture: u_net
    input_shape: [512, 512]
    # 2048 read whole and cut 4 x 4. This is the field the page exists for.
    splits: [4, 4]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    batch_size: 4
    epochs: 40
    loss:
      name: cce_dice
    metrics:
      - name: dice
        include_background: false
      - name: iou
        include_background: false
      # Measured on the reassembled image by `evaluate_cases()`, not per tile.
      - name: cldice
        iterations: 12
        include_background: false
    optimizer:
      name: adam
      learning_rate: 0.001
    callbacks:
      - name: early_stopping
        monitor: val_dice
        patience: 8
        restore_best: true
    augmentation:
      - name: HorizontalFlip
        params:
          p: 0.5
      - name: VerticalFlip
        params:
          p: 0.5
seed: 1
Two things about that worth saying out loud.
cldice sits among the metrics even though the run is tiled, and the engine reassembles each case before measuring it. It will not appear in the epoch log, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: an epoch averages its metrics over batches, which is exact for Dice - a ratio of sums - and meaningless for a skeleton, because a tile severs every vessel crossing its edge. So there is no val_cldice to watch, early_stopping watches val_dice, and a callback that asked for the other is refused when the specification is read.
iterations: 12 is the skeleton’s peel count, and it is chosen against the nine pixels measured above: a structure nine pixels across needs about half that many erosions to reach its centreline, and twelve leaves room for the widest vessels in the set rather than the average one.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
Training
import pyplatypus as pp

spec = pp.from_yaml("fives.yaml")
engine = pp.build_engine(spec, num_workers=4)
history = engine.fit(verbose=True)["vessels"]
num_workers=4 is worth a line of its own here rather than in a footnote. Training shuffles in windows so that one decoded image serves all sixteen of its tiles; four workers decoding 2048-pixel PNGs ahead of the GPU is the difference between an epoch that waits on the disk and one that does not. This run took 403 minutes over 40 epochs, with its best validation Dice at epoch 34 - it did not stop early, which is worth remembering when the last section compares budgets.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
clDice beside Dice
Over the same 200 cases:



correlation of dice and cldice
0.9779


mean of clDice minus Dice
+0.0041


sd of that difference
0.0219



Read the first two together, because they say different things. The correlation is high: the two metrics rank the cases much the same way, so clDice is not finding a different set of bad images. The mean difference is small and positive, which says the vessels this model draws are about as connected as their pixel overlap suggests.
That is a property of the model rather than of the metric, and the R vignette’s own run is the evidence. At fifteen epochs instead of forty, clDice sits about five points below Dice there: the model is getting the right pixels and breaking the lines. The better-trained model closes the gap, so a large negative gap is not clDice being pessimistic - it is clDice measuring what fifteen epochs had not finished learning, and Dice not noticing.
The last section finds the same column doing the same work across eleven objectives, which is the strongest version of this point available.

section: Two of those choices, measured afterwards
text:
Two of those choices, measured afterwards
loss: cce_dice and splits: [4, 4] are the two decisions in the configuration above that read as taste. Both have since been measured on this dataset - after this page’s walk was written, and with every arm kept rather than described - and one of the answers contradicts the section this page opens with.
The tables below are transcriptions. The runs live in the project’s workbench under measurements/fives/, and each table is printed by a script that reads the stored records back: losses-read.py, boundary-read.py and tiling-read.py. Nothing on this page runs them.
The setting is not this page’s, which is the first thing to know before comparing anything to the numbers above. Every arm trained on 148 of the 600 training retinas - every second one within each disease group, so the four stay balanced - for up to 40 epochs with early stopping on val_dice at patience 8, and every arm was scored case by case on the same 200 test images. So no absolute Dice below is comparable to the 0.8828 above; what the tables are for is the differences, each paired case against case.
A difference is read against a measured floor rather than against zero. The baseline ran twice with different seeds, and the floor is the larger of that pair’s mean difference and that mean’s own standard error: 0.0009 over all 200 cases and 0.0022 over the 67 that FIVES’s quality assessment flags. The x columns are multiples of that floor, and a row at 2x says nothing.
