The menu spans 0.0760 of Dice, 87 times the floor and 25 times the 0.0030 that separated the four architectures measured on nuclei. So the loss is a decision where the architecture was a menu - which is worth knowing before spending an afternoon choosing between u_net and linknet.
And nothing in the menu beats the default. focal at +0.0001 and cce at +0.0000 tie cce_dice, both below every floor measured anywhere here, and nine rows are worse. The family designed for thin structures under class imbalance - Tversky, Focal-Tversky, Lovasz - holds four of the five worst rows. cce_dice has been this example’s objective since it was written and nobody had measured whether that was right.
Two cautions the table carries about itself:
Nine of eleven rows have one seed. The four at the top move by less than the seed floors measured on any non-baseline loss here - 0.0120 for boundary at surface 0.3, 0.0465 for lovasz - so one seed cannot distinguish them from the baseline. Everything from boundary at surface 0.1 downwards is 10x to 87x the floor, and a second seed will not move it. lovasz is the warning worth reading twice: one of its seeds scores 0.8706, the highest single number in this table, and the other scores 0.8418.
The stopping rule is a confound, and it was priced rather than argued. Four arms stopped early enough that part of their deficit is convergence - focal_tversky at 20 epochs, lovasz’s second seed at 21, dice at 25, iou at 26 - while all three boundary arms ran into the 40-epoch cap. Re-read at 20 epochs, the budget every arm was granted, the ordering does not change.
The clDice - dice column also goes somewhere, and it was nobody’s question: it grows as the loss gets worse, from +0.0052 at the baseline through +0.0098 for iou and +0.0154 for dice to +0.0188 for focal_tversky. A worse objective loses more Dice than clDice, so what degrades first is the vessel’s bulk and its connectedness survives longer. There is exactly one exception, and it is the next table’s subject.


A surface loss is the one that breaks the lines, and it gets worse with the dose
boundary is the obvious thing to reach for on a nine-pixel structure: the boundary is the object, so an objective weighing the surface should be the one that helps. It does the opposite here, and it does so by a dose. alpha weights the region term, so the surface term’s share is 1 - alpha:

So the argument for this loss was backwards - connectedness is what it costs first, and on the flagged photographs it costs 15 to 27 times the noise.
Two things keep that honest. The dose has its own noise and it is ten times the baseline’s, which is the last column: the two arms at surface 0.3 sit 0.0120 apart on the flagged cases where the baseline’s two sit 0.0012 apart. (That column is each pair’s own mean difference; the x column’s denominator is still the baseline’s 0.0022 from above, so the two are not the same quantity and the table would mislead if they were read as one.) That is this loss’s documented behaviour - it grows noisier the more of the objective the surface term owns - reproduced on real data, and it is also the denominator the dose claim has to clear. Judged against it the two doses are 2.1x apart, not the twentyfold the baseline’s floor would suggest. And both arms at the higher dose stopped on the epoch cap with their best at the last epoch, so part of their deficit is being undertrained rather than being worse.


Tiling against resizing, where this page’s first section is too strong
Same data, same model, same loss. One arm tiles 2048 into 4 x 4 as the configuration above does; two resize the whole retina to 512 and leave splits unset. All three are scored on the source grid, 2048 x 2048, which for the resized arms means a second scoring pass.

There are two resized arms because sixteen tiles make “the same number of epochs” the wrong comparison: 148 retinas at batch_size: 4 are 37 gradient steps an epoch resized and 592 tiled. The first resized arm is the comparison somebody would actually run - the same 40-epoch cap and the same patience. The second was granted the tiled arm’s 23,680 steps and did not spend them, stopping on patience at 41% of the budget, so that row is converged against converged. The truncation the first arm suffered is worth +0.0038, which is worth knowing before budgeting for the matched arm: a measurement that cannot afford it loses 0.004 and the ability to say so.
The overall column says the two methods are equivalent, and it is hiding the largest effect in the measurement. Resizing is better by 0.027 to 0.029 on the 67 flagged photographs and worse by 0.010 to 0.014 on the 133 clean ones, both many times their own floors - 0.0019 to 0.0025 flagged, 0.0007 to 0.0013 clean. The two are good at different pictures, and a swing of about 0.03 in each direction averages out to 0.0033.
So what survives from “Why a vessel cannot be resized” is the narrow claim: on a clean photograph resizing costs Dice, and splits is what lets an image too large to resize be trained at all. What does not survive is the stronger reading - that resizing a 2048 retina destroys the thin vessels - because on the hard pictures the vessels it was supposed to have destroyed are found more reliably from a whole blurred eye than from a sixteenth of one. A mechanism suggests itself and is recorded as a hypothesis rather than a finding: a 512 tile sees one sixteenth of a retina and has no global context to tell a vessel from an artefact, where a resized image always shows the whole eye. Separating that would need overlapping tiles or a resized arm at 1024, and neither was run.
What tiling costs is also not what the table makes it look like. Per gradient step the three arms are identical to within the noise of six readings, 0.502 to 0.554 s, so tiling is sixteen times the work rather than sixteen times the overhead, and the whole factor shows up in the epoch rather than anywhere surprising.


The rig, which is worth more than the ranking
This is the part to carry away from all three tables, and it is about measuring rather than about retinas.
evaluate_cases() builds its dataset from the model’s own specification, so it scores each model at that model’s own load_shape. Put a tiled model beside a resized one and the first is scored on 2048 while the second is scored on 512, against a truth reduced the same way. Nobody passes a flag for this and nothing warns:

The reported figure is 5.7 times the honest one and the rig alone is 4.7 times the effect. A table built that way would have concluded that resizing beats native-resolution tiling by a wide margin, and every number in it would have been a real Dice of a real prediction against a real mask - just not the mask the other arm was judged against.
And the bias has the opposite sign on clDice: +0.0096 to +0.0156 on Dice against -0.0156 to -0.0230 on clDice. Upsampling a 512 prediction to 2048 smooths it, and a smoothed vessel agrees better with a skeleton and worse with a boundary. So the rigged comparison flatters resizing on Dice and penalises it on clDice, and a comparison reporting only one of the two is wrong in a direction set by which one it picked.
There is an option for this since 0.8.0a32, and there was none when this was measured. The arms above were rescored onto one grid by a function written for that measurement, which lived in the workbench and not in the package - so the honest comparison was available only to somebody who had already noticed the problem, which is what maju116/rplatypus#187 was filed about. evaluate(at="source") is that function now: every prediction goes back onto the grid of the file it came from and is scored against the truth as stored, and the load_shape column reads source so a table says which grid produced it.
The grid is the files’ own rather than one you name, and that is the point rather than a limitation: a named grid resamples the truth, so the thing both models are judged against would itself be an interpolation somebody chose. Here only predictions move.
The rule the numbers above teach is unchanged and is now enforceable rather than advisory: compare two models only where their predictions and the truth are on the same grid, and say which grid that is.


What none of this says
One dataset, one architecture, one loss, at one reduction of one resolution, with 148 retinas rather than 600. The subsets already disagree by about 0.03 in either direction inside this dataset, which is the strongest available warning against reading any overall column as a rule. And the published fives-unet weights’ own score is not comparable to any row above either - different data, a full training set, and a pinned commit.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
Notes
The data’s licence travels. FIVES is CC BY 4.0, which is why the published fives-unet weights are CC BY 4.0 rather than MIT and why their sidecar carries the citation: Jin et al., FIVES: A Fundus Image Dataset for Artificial Intelligence based Vessel Segmentation, Scientific Data 9, 475 (2022).
The cost. 40 epochs over 600 retinas at 2048, cut sixteen ways, is 403 minutes on a GTX 1070; scoring the 200 test images, including reassembling each one for clDice, is about two minutes. Tiling is what makes the first number bearable rather than worse: a tiled run reuses each decoded image for all sixteen of its tiles, which is worth roughly a factor of two against decoding one per tile.
A card that uses the GPU it has. A Pascal-generation card needs the last PyTorch built against CUDA 12; the R package has platypus_use_torch("pascal") for that because it builds its own environment, and here it is an ordinary install of a matching wheel.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
The other articles work on two-dimensional pictures. This one is about volumes, which is where medical imaging mostly lives: a CT or an MRI is a stack of slices, and three things that do not exist in 2D decide whether a result means anything.
Voxels have a physical size, and it differs between scans. Slices belong to a patient, so a split that ignores who they came from measures memory rather than generalisation. And a mask has a position in space, without which it cannot be laid over the scan it describes.
The data here is synthetic, generated by the code below, so every line of this page runs without downloading anything or registering anywhere. That is the reason it is generated inline rather than by a script in examples/: everything else in that directory is a program you point at real data, and a page whose data arrives with it is the one page here that needs nothing.
Where the numbers come from. One run of exactly the code below, on this machine: 24 scans, 12 epochs, and every table transcribed from its output. Nothing is determined - this specification does not ask for deterministic - so a second run moves the per-case scores by about 0.03 of Dice. The shape of every finding survives that; the third decimal does not.
This page mirrors vignette("volumes") in the R package, which is the source for the prose. The walk is the same and the route is not.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
Making something to segment
Twenty-four scans from twelve patients, two each. Each holds one spherical “lesion” in air, and the scans differ in three ways that are ordinary in clinical data: slice thickness, half at 1 mm and half at 2.5 mm, so the same anatomy occupies a different number of voxels; lesion size, 4 to 12 mm in radius; and noise.
The variety is the point. A synthetic dataset where every case is equally easy would make the per-patient section below look like a formality, and it is not one.
import math
from pathlib import Path

import nibabel as nib
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def make_scan(root: Path, patient: int, study: int, slice_mm: float, radius_mm: float, noise: float) -> str:
    shape, spacing = (48, 48, 32), (1.0, 1.0, slice_mm)
    grid = np.stack(np.meshgrid(*[np.arange(s) for s in shape], indexing="ij"), axis=-1)
    # Millimetres from the centre, per voxel - which is what makes the sphere a sphere in
    # the patient rather than in the array.
    offset = (grid - (np.array(shape) - 1) / 2) * np.array(spacing)
    # Move the lesion per patient, so the model cannot learn one position and be done.
    offset[..., 0] -= (patient - 6) * 1.5
    distance = np.sqrt((offset ** 2).sum(axis=-1))

    lesion = (distance <= radius_mm).astype(np.int16)
    # Hounsfield units: air is -1000, soft tissue about 40, plus scanner noise.
    scan = np.where(lesion == 1, 40.0, -1000.0) + rng.normal(0, noise, shape)

    name = f"patient{patient:02d}_study{study}"
    for folder in ("images", "masks"):
        (root / name / folder).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    affine = np.diag([*spacing, 1.0])
    nib.save(nib.Nifti1Image(scan.astype(np.float32), affine), str(root / name / "images" / "ct.nii.gz"))
    nib.save(nib.Nifti1Image(lesion, affine), str(root / name / "masks" / "lesion.nii.gz"))
    return name
Keeping the radius is the part worth copying into a real study where it is possible: the volume of a sphere is known exactly, which makes it possible to ask later whether the model got the size right and not only the overlap. That question is the last third of this page and no overlap metric answers it.
Two scans, the same number of slices, and one covers 32 mm of patient where the other covers 80 mm. volume_spacing() and volume_shape() read that out of the files themselves, through the same reader training uses:
from pyplatypus.data.volumes import volume_shape, volume_spacing

volume_spacing("scans/patient01_study1/images/ct.nii.gz")   # (1.0, 1.0, 2.5)
volume_shape("scans/patient01_study1/images/ct.nii.gz")     # (48, 48, 32)
A voxel in the first is two and a half times the volume of a voxel in the second. Nothing in the arrays says so, which is the whole reason this pair of functions exists.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
section: Splitting by patient, not by scan
text:
Splitting by patient, not by scan
Each of these patients has two studies. Split the twenty-four scans at random and both studies of some patient land on opposite sides: the model meets that patient in training and is then tested on the same anatomy.
How much that costs is a separate question, and it has now been measured rather than asserted. This paragraph used to end “Dice comes out several points too high”, which nothing had ever checked. On MSD Spleen - 41 patients, 1043 slices - a slice-level split put 29 of 29 development patients on both sides, and the model it produced overstated its own score by +0.035 against patients it had never seen. A patient-level split on the same data overstated itself by +0.039. So the inflation is real and it is not the leak: any validation set differs from any test set by a few points because patients differ, and on this data the leak added nothing on top of that.
That is one dataset, one architecture and twelve epochs, which is not evidence that the mistake is harmless where a model has room to memorise. The reason to keep patients whole is that the mechanism is certain and invisible in the result, not that the size is known.
split_dataset() takes a pattern saying which part of a name is the patient, and keeps every patient whole:
import pyplatypus as pp

split = pp.split_dataset(
    "scans", "splits",
    group_by=r"^(patient\d+)_",
    fractions=(0.5, 0.25, 0.25),
    seed=1,
)
Twelve scans to train on, six to validate, six to test - six patients, three and three, with no patient on two sides. A pattern that matches nothing is an error rather than a fallback, which is the point: a silent fallback to one group per scan would reintroduce exactly the bug the argument exists to prevent.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
The specification
Three volume-specific fields carry the weight. labels says the mask is a label map rather than a picture - which is how every volume format stores masks, and the reason colormap is not the only way to name classes. window maps Hounsfield units to 0-1 through a fixed window, so the same tissue is the same brightness in every scan. And target_spacing resamples everything to a common voxel size before cropping to the model’s shape.
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: splits/train.csv
  validation_path: splits/validation.csv
  mode: config_file
  labels: [0, 1]
  window: soft_tissue
  target_spacing: [1, 1, 1]
models:
  - name: lesion
    architecture: u_net
    # Three entries, and that is the only thing making this a 3D run.
    input_shape: [32, 32, 32]
    channels: 1
    blocks: 3
    filters: 16
    epochs: 12
    batch_size: 2
    loss:
      name: dice
    metrics:
      - name: dice
        include_background: false
    augmentation:
      - name: HorizontalFlip
        params:
          p: 0.5
      - name: CubicSymmetry
        params:
          p: 0.5
seed: 1
Nothing else in the specification is different from a 2D run - the same losses, the same metrics, the same tiling if you want it.
window: soft_tissue is worth a sentence of its own. Scaling each scan by its own extremes is the obvious alternative and it throws away the thing Hounsfield units are for: air is -1000 on every scanner ever built, so a fixed window maps the same tissue to the same number in every scan, and one bright voxel - an implant, a marker - cannot rescale everything else.
Not every augmentation works on a volume. albumentations supports them unevenly, so ask rather than guess:
len(pp.available_transforms())           # 118 here
len(pp.available_transforms(rank=3))     # 91 here
Those two counts are a property of the installed albumentations rather than of this package, which is why the difference is not quoted as a fact about pyplatypus. A transform from the difference is refused by name when the run starts, rather than raising something from inside the library an hour in.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
Training
spec = pp.from_yaml("volumes.yaml")
engine = pp.build_engine(spec)
history = engine.fit()["lesion"]
1,401,282 parameters at blocks: 3 and filters: 16, twelve epochs. A 3D U-Net grows quickly: the same blocks and filters in 2D is a fraction of that, because every convolution kernel gains a dimension.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
Looking at a slice
A volume has no single picture, so plot_masks() asks which slice to draw and refuses a volume without one rather than picking the middle:
masks = engine.predict("lesion", split="validation", space="source")
figure = pp.plot_masks(images, prediction=np.stack(masks), truth=truth, slice=16)
The refusal is the useful part. A middle slice is a reasonable default for a sphere in the centre of a scan and a terrible one for anything real - a lesion in the apex of a lung is not at depth // 2, and a page of pictures that quietly all missed it looks exactly like a page of pictures where the model found nothing.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
Millilitres, not voxels
The size of a finding is reported in millilitres. A voxel count means nothing outside the scanner that produced it - the same lesion is 4,000 voxels on one machine and 12,000 on another - and resampling is what makes the conversion trivial: at target_spacing: [1, 1, 1] a voxel is exactly one cubic millimetre.
from pyplatypus import mask_volume

# On the model's grid, where target_spacing has made a voxel one cubic millimetre - and
# `spacing` is passed rather than assumed, because the division is only right while it is
# true and nothing about a voxel count says whether it still is.
prediction = engine.predict("lesion", split="validation", space="model")
millilitres = [
    mask_volume(case.argmax(axis=-1), spacing=(1, 1, 1), class_index=1) for case in prediction
]

Dice 0.914 to 0.948, and volumes 9% to 24% too large. That is not a contradiction. Dice is dominated by the interior of an object and forgiving about its boundary, and for a small lesion the boundary is most of it: a model that draws every lesion one voxel too wide scores well and reports a volume that is wrong by a quarter. If the question is is there a lesion, the Dice is the relevant number. If it is has it grown since March, this table is, and neither follows from the other.
Which grid the counting happens on is not a detail, and getting it wrong is easy. The line above counts on the model’s grid, where target_spacing has made every voxel one cubic millimetre. Count the same lesions on the source grid and half these scans have voxels of 1 x 1 x 2.5 mm, so the identical count means two and a half times the volume. Writing this page, counting source-grid voxels as though they were cubic millimetres reported patient11 as 53% too small where the honest figure is 12% too large - a number that contradicted its own Dice, and the only reason it was caught is that Dice 0.91 and a volume off by half cannot both be true. That is the section’s own lesson arriving uninvited.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
section: Writing a mask back onto its scan
text:
Writing a mask back onto its scan
save_volumes() writes a prediction as NIfTI carrying the affine of the scan it came from. Without that affine a mask cannot be laid over its scan by any viewer or registration tool - it either lands in the wrong place or is refused, and nothing about the file looks wrong.
Carrying the affine means the mask has to be on the same grid as the scan, and after resampling it is not: these scans are 48 x 48 x 32 voxels while the model works at 32 x 32 x 32. space="source" maps each prediction back out of the model’s grid onto the scan’s, undoing the resampling and the crop:
masks = engine.predict("lesion", split="validation", space="source")
len(masks)        # 6
masks[0].shape    # (48, 48, 32, 2)
A list rather than an array, because scans differ in size and a stack needs one shape. That is the API being explicit rather than resizing them to match, which is how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.
Every scan here is called ct.nii.gz inside its own directory, so names taken from the references would collide and every mask would be written to one path - an error rather than five silently lost files. The case keys are what to pass instead:
written = pp.save_volumes(masks, "predictions", reference=images, cases=keys)
[path.name for path in written]
# ['patient06_study1.nii.gz', 'patient06_study2.nii.gz', ...]
and the written masks carry the scans’ geometry, which is what makes them open on top of them - volume_spacing() says (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) and volume_shape() says (48, 48, 32) for patient06_study1, which is that scan’s own grid rather than the model’s.
Two things are lost on the way back and it is worth knowing which. Interpolation softens a boundary, so the mask is slightly smoother than the model drew it. And where reading cropped anatomy away, the mask returns padded with background - which means not examined, not nothing there. If that distinction matters, give the model an input_shape that covers the anatomy.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
section: DICOM, which is how the data usually arrives
text:
DICOM, which is how the data usually arrives
The scans above are NIfTI because that is what research datasets ship. Data out of a hospital arrives as a directory of DICOM files per series, and this package reads those as volumes too - sorting them by their position in the patient rather than by filename, which is the difference between a scan and a shuffled deck.
Point the specification at directories of slices and nothing else changes. Before training, run the export past describe_series():
from pyplatypus.data.dicom_series import describe_series

for directory in sorted(Path("dicom_export").iterdir()):
    report = describe_series(directory)
It reads no pixels - every check runs on the headers - so it stays usable on a hundred gigabytes of data, and it is the first thing worth running on a new export. An archive of a hundred cases will contain a few with a missing slice, duplicated files, or two series sitting in one folder. A missing slice does not shorten a volume: it moves everything past the gap, and no metric would show it.
read_dicom_series() is the reader itself, looks_like_dicom_series() the test that a directory is one, and series_spacing() the slice spacing the headers imply. Unlike NIfTI, which is reliably named, DICOM is detected by content, because exports so often carry no useful extension.

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
What this leaves out
Resampling is offered, not imposed: drop target_spacing and the scans are cropped or padded to input_shape at their own voxel sizes, which is the right choice when they already agree.
What it costs to impose it, and the trap in doing so, were measured on MSD Spleen - 41 abdominal CTs whose slice thickness runs 1.5 mm to 8 mm and whose voxels differ in volume by 5.9 times, which is the variation target_spacing exists for. Three arms, one input_shape of 64 cubed, every one scored against the truth as stored:



what the model reads
dice

of a spleen averaging 234 ml.
The middle row is the trap and it is total. Resampling does not only change the scale: it changes what input_shape means. Without it, the shape is the whole scan squashed to fit. With it, the shape is a box of so many millimetres taken from the middle - 64 voxels at 1.5 mm is a 96 mm cube - and a spleen sits up to 165 mm off the centre of the scan and is up to 143 mm across. The organ is outside the box in every case, so the model finds nothing at all, three runs out of three.
Choose the field of view in millimetres first, then the spacing and the shape that cover it. Here that is a 480 mm box, and it is worth +0.11 of Dice over resizing and a third of the volume error - 14% of the organ against 30%.
The difference in reliability is larger than the difference in the mean: across three runs the resampled arm’s worst case stayed between 0.72 and 0.77, while the resized arm’s was 0.00, 0.58 and 0.01. It does not score a little lower; it loses a whole scan, a different one each time. Which scan is not explained by its geometry - the two volumes covering the most patient came through fine - and that is an open question rather than a tidy ending.
A coarse 7.5 mm is a poor way to see a boundary, so the arm this did not run is a finer spacing with splits, which is how a large field of view is covered without a large input. #201.
Several volumes per sample - one per modality, as BraTS ships - works through channels_from, where the order is stated rather than inferred. That is a design claim, so it was measured. One model was trained on MSD BrainTumour (CC BY-SA 4.0) with the four sequences named in the order dataset.json states, then read back through a specification naming the same four patterns with FLAIR and T1 swapped - the same weights, the same scans, one difference:



what channel one holds
dice




FLAIR, as trained
0.467


T1, after one swap in the list
0.110




The case drawn is the median of the validation split rather than the best or the worst, and it scores 0.540 and 0.160 the two ways round. Nothing failed. No error and no empty mask: the model returns a region of plausible size and plausible shape in the wrong place, which is what a reader would accept from a tool they trust.
The number is the weaker half of this, in two ways. A Dice of 0.467 is not a good tumour model - 60 epochs on 120 cases, still improving at the cap - and this measurement does not need it to be, because both rows are that same model. And it is a number about one permutation of twenty-four and one training budget: the same comparison at a third of the training reported 0.023 against 0.233, which is 10% of the right arm where these two are 23%. The ratio moves with how good the model is; what does not move is that the wrong answer looks like an answer.
So take the order from the dataset’s own record and check it once, because nothing downstream will. Sorting the filenames gives flair, t1, t1gd, t2 - reproducible, and anatomically meaningless. #202.
And one thing above is smaller than it looks: a validation set of six scans from three patients is enough to show a distribution and nowhere near enough to measure one. The spread in the table above is a demonstration of a mechanism, not an estimate of anything.

title: The configuration file
text:
A configuration is one YAML file describing a whole run: where the data is, and one or more models to train on it. It is the same file in both packages - R reads it with platypus_spec(yaml = ...) and Python with from_yaml(), and both hand it to the same pydantic models, which is where every description on this page comes from.
Validation happens before anything is read from disk and before torch is imported, so a mistake here costs a second rather than an epoch. Every refusal names the field.

title: The configuration file
text:
Schema for your editor
The same definitions are published as JSON Schema, so an editor can complete and check a configuration as you type it. In VS Code with the YAML extension, or any editor using yaml-language-server, put this on the first line:
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://maju116.github.io/pyplatypus/schema/spec.schema.json

title: The configuration file
text:
task, which decides the rest
task is required, and it is the only field that is: it chooses which shape the rest of the file has. Give it wrong and the refusal names the tag rather than reporting every field of the other task as unexpected.



task
what it describes

title: The configuration file
text:
task: semantic_segmentation
The SegmentationSpec shape. Its top level:

task

text — semantic_segmentation
Fixed for this specification: semantic_segmentation.

seed

a whole number — unset
Makes a run repeatable as far as the arithmetic is deterministic, which goes further on some hardware than others - so it is worth knowing where it stops.
Repeatable: the split (split_dataset gives the same partition on any machine), a detector’s fitted anchors, the order the data arrives in and its augmentation - including inside the loader’s worker processes - and, on the processor, every number to twelve decimal places.
Not repeatable: a run on a CUDA device. Measured on a GTX 1070: two runs at one seed agreed to twelve decimals on the processor and differed in the fourth after a single epoch on the card, because cuDNN chooses algorithms this does not constrain. Nor across versions of this package - anything that changes the order data is drawn in changes what one seed draws, and 0.8.0a3 did exactly that.
So it is the field for comparing two of your own runs, and not for publishing a number somebody else can land on.

deterministic

true or false — false
Ask torch for deterministic algorithms as well, which is the only thing that makes a run on a card repeatable - seed alone does not, and the field above says so.
It is an opt-in because the cost is real and arrives late. Some convolutions become much slower, and an operation that has no deterministic implementation raises when it is reached - so a run can stop ten minutes in rather than when the specification was checked. Every other refusal here happens before anything is read; this one cannot, because whether an operation has a deterministic algorithm is a fact about the installed torch and the device, not about the configuration.
Needs seed: constraining the algorithms while the draw still varies produces a run that is no more repeatable and only slower, so asking for it without a seed is refused rather than quietly accepted.

output_dir

text — platypus_output
Where a run record is written, and where fit() puts anything it is asked to save. Nothing is written unless something asks to write: naming this does not by itself create a directory.

data

a SegmentationData block — required
Where the images and their masks are, and how to read them.

models

a list of SegmentationModel blocks — required
One or more models, trained in turn against the same data. Names must be unique: a run is recorded under its model’s name, so two models called the same thing would overwrite one record and report it as two. Several entries of the same architecture with different settings is the ordinary case - that is how a comparison is written.



data: for semantic segmentation

train_path

text — required
Where the training data is. For nested_dirs, a directory of sample directories; for config_file, a CSV naming the files. With a split, this is the only path given and the divisions are cut from it.

validation_path

text — unset
Optional only in the sense that split is the other way to get one, and validation: false the third. Exactly one of them, because two sources for the validation set are two places to change it.

test_path

text — unset
A third set, scored only when asked. Whether it can be scored at all depends on whether it carries labels: a folder of images alone is accepted and predict works on it, while evaluate refuses it by name rather than failing two layers down on the first missing mask.

validation

true or false — true
Whether this run validates at all. false is the third and last way of answering the question validation_path and split answer, and it has to be written down.
A final fit on every case you have, once the hyperparameters are settled, is a legitimate thing to want - and until now it meant inventing a split and ignoring the number it produced. What is not legitimate is arriving here by omission: a specification with neither a path nor a split is still an error, because ‘I have no validation set’ and ‘I forgot’ look identical and only one of them is a decision.
With false, giving validation_path or split as well is refused: they say where the validation set comes from and this says there is not one.

split

a SplitSpec block — unset
Divide train_path instead of naming a second folder. Nothing is written: the samples that were already discovered are partitioned, so a specification stays a description and leaves no files behind. split_dataset() is the tool when the CSVs are the point - to keep, to hand to a colleague, or to cite.

mode

nested_dirs or config_file — nested_dirs
How the files are arranged: nested_dirs for one directory per sample, config_file for a CSV whose columns name the files. The CSV form is what to use when the data cannot be moved or copied into a layout.

subdirs

a list — ["images", "masks"]
For nested_dirs, the two subdirectories of each sample directory: the images and their masks. A sample may hold several mask files - one per object, as Data Science Bowl does - and they are united into one mask when read.

column_sep

text — ;
For config_file, what separates several paths inside one cell - a sample with one mask file per object, as Data Science Bowl has, or one file per channel.

shuffle

true or false — true
Shuffle the training data between epochs. Only the training data: validation is read in order so that two epochs measure the same thing in the same way.

window

text or a list — auto
How values in real units are mapped to 0-1: a named window such as ‘lung’ or ‘soft_tissue’, an explicit (centre, width) pair, ‘auto’ for the window the file recorded - DICOM only, since NIfTI stores none - or ‘full’ for the whole range present. A fixed window is what makes two scans comparable: scaling each one by its own extremes lets a single bright voxel rescale everything else. Ignored for ordinary pictures, which are already 0-255. Accepted as dicom_window too, the name it had while DICOM was the only format that needed it.

colormap

a list of lists — unset
One colour per class; index in this list is the class index.

labels

a list of whole numbers — unset
For masks stored as label maps rather than pictures: the voxel value of each class, in class order. This is how volumes label anything - NIfTI holds integers, not colours - and how a single-channel PNG mask can be read too. Exactly one of colormap and labels is given. Include 0 unless the masks really do fill every voxel: a value matching no entry falls back to the first class, so a list without 0 trains the background as whatever that first class is, and fit refuses the combination rather than let it look plausible.

regions

a list of Region blocks — unset
Overlapping classes, named as unions of a label map’s values - the third way of saying what a mask’s classes are, and the only one that lets a voxel belong to more than one. Each entry gives a name and the values it is made of. With regions the model’s channels are independent binary questions: a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them, and no background entry, for the same reason detection’s classes has none. Exactly one of colormap, labels and regions is given. Two regions are the minimum - one region is ordinary binary segmentation, which labels: [0, 1] already says.

classes_from

a list of text values — unset
For masks kept as one binary file per class - the fourth way of saying what a mask’s classes are, and the only one that can express classes which overlap independently: a vessel crossing an organ, or two annotators’ masks of the same structure. One pattern per class, in class order, each a regular expression matched against a sample’s mask file names, and every pattern must match exactly one file - the rules channels_from uses, through the same matcher.
Stated rather than inferred for the reason channels_from gives, with worse consequences: sorting the names is reproducible and anatomically meaningless, and a model trained with ‘tumour’ in channel 1 and used where channel 1 is ‘oedema’ answers plausibly, in range, and nothing downstream can tell.
Like regions this makes every channel an independent binary question - a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them - and has no background entry. The difference between the two is the file on disk and nothing else: regions derives overlap from one label map’s values, which is what BraTS and the liver-and-tumour family need, and this reads overlap that was drawn separately in the first place. Exactly one of colormap, labels, regions and classes_from is given.

channels_from

a list of text values — unset
For datasets that keep one channel per file - BraTS ships T1, T1ce, T2 and FLAIR per patient; 38-Cloud keeps its bands apart - one pattern per channel, in channel order, each a regular expression matched against the file names. Every pattern must match exactly one of a sample’s files. Stated rather than inferred because sorting gives flair, t1, t1ce, t2: reproducible, and anatomically meaningless. A model trained with FLAIR in channel one and used on data where channel one is T1 returns a plausible answer and no error.

target_spacing

a list — unset
Resample every volume to this many millimetres per voxel before training, then centre-crop or pad to the model’s input_shape. Without it a volume is simply resized to input_shape, which gives two scans of the same anatomy different physical scale when they were acquired at different slice thicknesses - and the network has no way to know. Volumes only; ignored for 2D.



split: inside semantic segmentation data:

fractions

a list of numbers — required
Two or three: train, validation, and optionally test. The length rule is enforced by the splitting module rather than restated here - one rule, one place. A third fraction is scoreable, because it comes from annotated data.

group_by

text — required
Required, and may be null. A regular expression read against the sample key; everything sharing a group lands in exactly one split. Usually a patient, sometimes a study, a scanner or a site - whatever must not straddle the division.
Required rather than optional because the mistake it prevents is invisible. Slices of one patient in training and validation at once make validation measure memory instead of generalisation, and Dice comes out several points too high with nothing in the output to say so. An omitted field would be that choice made silently; null is the same choice made on purpose, which is all this asks for.

seed

a whole number — 0
The split is deterministic given the samples, the fractions, the pattern and this. A split that moves between runs makes two results incomparable and the reason for a difference impossible to find.




regions: inside semantic segmentation data:

name

text — required
What this region is called. It names a channel of the output, so it is what a per-class score is reported under and what save_class_masks puts in a filename. Distinct from every other region’s name.

of

a list of whole numbers — required
The label-map values belonging to this region, in any order. A voxel is in the region when its value is one of these, so regions may overlap - that is the point - and a single value is normal: BraTS’s enhancing tumour is of: [4]. Disjoint regions are allowed and mean something useful, grouping several labels into one class and dropping the background channel; they are not a mistake and are not refused.





models: for semantic segmentation

name

text — required
Unique within a spec; names the outputs.

input_shape

a list of whole numbers — required
Spatial size: (height, width) in 2D, (depth, height, width) in 3D.

channels

a whole number — 3
How many channels the network takes: 3 for colour, 1 for greyscale, and one per sequence for multi-modal data such as the four MRI sequences in BraTS. Derived rather than declared when channels_from names the files, because then the data decides. Not adopted from a weights file - the data pipeline needs it before a network exists, and a specification has to be checkable offline.

optimizer

one of adadelta, adagrad, adam, adamax, adamw, nadam, rmsprop, sgd — optional
How the weights are updated. name selects which one and decides which other keys this block accepts.

callbacks

a list, each one of cosine_annealing, csv_logger, early_stopping, ema, linear_annealing, model_checkpoint, reduce_lr_on_plateau, step_decay, stop_after, swa, terminate_on_collapse, terminate_on_nan — optional
Things that happen between epochs: stopping early, writing checkpoints, moving the learning rate, averaging the weights. A callback watching a number no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built rather than waited on forever, and so is one watching val_* in a run with no validation set.

augmentation

a list of AugmentationStep blocks — unset
albumentations transforms, applied to the training data only - never to validation, where the point is to measure the same thing every epoch. Each step is probed at the model’s own input size while the pipeline is built, because support for volumes is uneven and a transform that cannot take one raises from inside the library.

epochs

a whole number — 10
How many passes over the training data. The default is deliberately small: it is enough to see that a run works and not enough to mistake for a result. With cosine_annealing this is also the length the schedule is spread over.

a whole number — 8
How many samples go through the network at once. Limited by memory rather than by the problem, and it is the first thing to lower when a 3D run will not fit. It interacts with batch_normalization: statistics taken over very few samples are noisy.

weights

text — unset
Registry name (e.g. ‘dsbowl-unet’) or a path to a local checkpoint.

fit

true or false — true
Set false to load weights and skip training.

architecture

u_net or u_net_plus_plus or res_u_net or linknet — u_net

a whole number — 4

a whole number — 16

a whole number — 2

true or false — false
Depthwise-separable convolutions: far fewer parameters for the same shape, and a little slower to converge.

true or false — true

true or false — false

true or false — false

a list of whole numbers — unset

text — unset

pretrained

true or false — false
Load the encoder’s ImageNet weights. Separate from encoder on purpose: naming a backbone builds that architecture, and this is the flag that reaches the network, which matters where there is no network.

a number — unset

task: instance_segmentation

text — instance_segmentation

deterministic

true or false — false

train_path

text — unset

a whole number — 0

Spatial size: (height, width) in 2D, (depth, height, width) in 3D.

channels

a whole number — 3
How many channels the network takes: 3 for colour, 1 for greyscale, and one per sequence for multi-modal data such as the four MRI sequences in BraTS. Derived rather than declared when channels_from names the files, because then the data decides. Not adopted from a weights file - the data pipeline needs it before a network exists, and a specification has to be checkable offline.

optimizer

one of adadelta, adagrad, adam, adamax, adamw, nadam, rmsprop, sgd — optional
How the weights are updated. name selects which one and decides which other keys this block accepts.

callbacks

a list, each one of cosine_annealing, csv_logger, early_stopping, ema, linear_annealing, model_checkpoint, reduce_lr_on_plateau, step_decay, stop_after, swa, terminate_on_collapse, terminate_on_nan — optional
Things that happen between epochs: stopping early, writing checkpoints, moving the learning rate, averaging the weights. A callback watching a number no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built rather than waited on forever, and so is one watching val_* in a run with no validation set.

augmentation

a list of AugmentationStep blocks — unset
albumentations transforms, applied to the training data only - never to validation, where the point is to measure the same thing every epoch. Each step is probed at the model’s own input size while the pipeline is built, because support for volumes is uneven and a transform that cannot take one raises from inside the library.

epochs

a whole number — 10
How many passes over the training data. The default is deliberately small: it is enough to see that a run works and not enough to mistake for a result. With cosine_annealing this is also the length the schedule is spread over.

batch_size

a whole number — 8
How many samples go through the network at once. Limited by memory rather than by the problem, and it is the first thing to lower when a 3D run will not fit. It interacts with batch_normalization: statistics taken over very few samples are noisy.

weights

text — unset
Registry name (e.g. ‘dsbowl-unet’) or a path to a local checkpoint.

fit

true or false — true
Set false to load weights and skip training.

architecture

yolo3 — yolo3
Which detector. YOLOv3 is the only one, and it is 2D: boxes in a volume are a different problem with different annotations, so a detection specification at rank 3 is refused while the specification is read rather than failing later. Adopted from the weights file when weights names one, together with the anchors - weights mean nothing without the anchors they were trained with, so a specification naming both is refused.

anchors

a list of a list of lists — unset
The box shapes the model predicts offsets from, as fractions of the input size, one group per grid from coarsest to finest. Unset fits them to the training annotations with k-means under an IoU distance, which is what you want: measured on BCCD’s 2,805 training boxes, COCO’s anchors cover them at a mean IoU of 0.65 against 0.88 for anchors fitted to them. Fitted anchors are recorded with the run, since a detector cannot be reloaded without them.

anchors_per_grid

a whole number — 3
How many anchors to fit per grid, when anchors is not given. It also sets the head’s width, which is anchors_per_grid * (n_class + 5).

ignore_threshold

a number — 0.5
A cell that is not responsible for an object but whose box overlaps one this much is left unsupervised rather than trained towards ‘no object’. Without it a nearly-correct guess beside the responsible cell is punished, which is the one thing a detector should not learn.

box_loss

offsets or giou — offsets
How the box coordinates are scored. offsets is YOLOv3’s own: cross-entropy on the two cell offsets and squared error on the two log sizes, each weighted by 2 - w*h so a small object is not worth less than a large one. giou scores the decoded box against the true box directly, as 1 - GIoU.
The reason to prefer giou is that it can reach zero. Cross-entropy against a soft target bottoms out at that target’s entropy, so the offsets term is still 4.21 on a prediction that is exactly right - measured on three boxes - and a converged run cannot be told from a stalled one by reading it. The same prediction scores 0.000000 under giou.
It is not the better objective here, and that is measured. BCCD, three seeds each, 150 epochs, its own test split:
            mAP@0.5          mAP@COCO         matched IoU
giou        0.8666 +-0.0147  0.5078 +-0.0083  0.7929 +-0.0069
offsets     0.8583 +-0.0167  0.5172 +-0.0195  0.8038 +-0.0001
Average precision cannot separate them in either direction - both gaps are inside the noise. How well the matched boxes fit can, and giou is worse by 0.0109, which is 2.7 standard errors of the difference. It is also far less repeatable on exactly the quantity it targets: offsets gave 0.803853, 0.803656 and 0.803861 across its seeds, sixty times tighter than giou.
The reason is in the same run’s own numbers. GIoU exists because IoU is a flat zero for boxes that do not touch, so it has no gradient where a detector is most wrong - but anchors fitted by k-means already cover BCCD’s truths at a mean IoU of 0.877, so predictions never start disjoint and the advantage never arrives while the cost does. Where fitted anchors cover poorly it should be a different story, which is untested here and therefore not claimed.
So choose giou to make the objective readable, not to raise the score: at 150 epochs its coordinate term sits at 0.05 on the training split against 0.47 on validation, which is a localisation gap you can see, while offsets reads 5.92 and 6.85 against a floor of 5.891 and tells you nothing. On BCCD that legibility costs about 0.011 of matched IoU.

score_threshold

a number — 0.01
Discard a predicted box below this confidence. Low on purpose: average precision is computed over the whole ranking, so a cut here is a ceiling on recall that no threshold chosen later can lift.

nms_threshold

a number — 0.45
Two boxes of the same class overlapping this much are one object, and the lower-scoring one is dropped. Per class, so a platelet sitting on a red cell survives.

operating_point

a number — 0.5
The confidence at which precision and recall are reported. Separate from score_threshold because they answer different questions: that one decides what is computed at all, this one decides where on the curve to stand.

min_visibility

a number — 0.25
How much of a box must survive an augmentation that removes part of the frame, as a fraction of its original area, for the box to be kept. A convention rather than a measurement; what is defensible is the direction. A box keeping two pixels of a cell teaches the model that a two-pixel fragment is a whole cell, which produces false positives everywhere, while dropping a heavily truncated object only fails to teach it about that object. Pascal VOC marks such objects truncated for the same reason. Irrelevant unless a transform can lose part of the frame: flips and rotations never do.



augmentation: inside object detection models:

name

text — required
An albumentations transform, by its own class name - HorizontalFlip, RandomBrightnessContrast. Checked against what the installed albumentations offers, and available_transforms() lists them; at rank 3 the list is shorter, because support for volumes is uneven.

params

a mapping — optional
Arguments passed to that transform, exactly as albumentations names them - so p is the probability of applying it, defaulting to the transform’s own. Not validated here: they are albumentations’ to accept, and each step is probed at the model’s input size when the pipeline is built, so a bad argument is named there rather than guessed at here.

title: The configuration file
text:
Components
Each of these is named by its name: and carries its own fields.

Losses

boundary
A region loss plus a term that knows how far a wrong voxel is from the truth.

name

text — boundary
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

region

one of cce, cce_dice, combo, dice, focal, focal_tversky, generalized_dice, iou, lovasz, tversky — optional
The overlap term this is added to. Dice unless you say otherwise.

alpha

a number — 0.9
How much of the objective is the region term, 1 - alpha the surface term.
0.9 because 0.5 was measured and is unusable. Three seeds on lesions with ambiguous edges, 60 epochs:
                 Dice             volume bias       volume |error|
dice alone       0.9525 ±0.0027   -5.18% ±3.11%     16.90% ±0.90%
boundary a=0.5   0.9164 ±0.0240  +32.22% ±28.28%    42.95% ±19.12%
boundary a=0.9   0.9411 ±0.0093   -0.06% ±4.15%     22.17% ±2.88%
At 0.5 the surface term has half the objective while the prediction is still random, which is where it is known to be unstable - the seed spread is six times the baseline’s and every number is worse. Kervadec schedules this downwards from near 1 rather than fixing it; 0.9 is the closest a single number comes, and the spec deliberately has no schedule to hide behind.
Excludes both ends: at 1 the surface term is absent and the name is a lie, and at 0 nothing measures how much of the object was found.




cce
Per-pixel classification, with no notion of the object.

name

text — cce
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

label_smoothing

a number — 0.0
Train towards 1 - this value instead of towards 1, so the model is not pushed to be certain. Worth having where the labels themselves are uncertain, which on a hand-drawn boundary they are.




cce_dice
The blend to start a segmentation run with.

name

text — cce_dice
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

cce_weight

a number — 0.5
How much of the objective is cross-entropy; the rest is Dice. Cross-entropy cares about every pixel and Dice about the overlap, so raising this helps a class that covers very little of the image and lowering it favours the shape.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.




combo
A lopsided cross-entropy blended with Dice.

name

text — combo
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

alpha

a number — 0.5
How much of the objective is the weighted cross-entropy term; the rest is Dice.

ce_ratio

a number — 0.5
Within the cross-entropy term, how much weight goes on the positive class. This is the key that makes combo worth choosing over cce_dice: it lets the two halves of the objective disagree about which class matters.




dice
Overlap, and nothing about where the error sits.

name

text — dice
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.




focal
Cross-entropy that loses interest in the voxels it already gets right.

name

text — focal
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

gamma

a number — 2.0
How hard to discount the pixels already classified well, so the gradient comes from the ones that are not. 0 is plain cross-entropy; 2 is the usual value.

alpha

a number — unset
Weight on the positive class, between 0 and 1. Unset means no weighting, which is not the same as 0.5: at 0.5 both classes are halved and the gradients are smaller, which looks like a learning-rate change.




focal_tversky
Tversky, with the same loss of interest in what is already right.

name

text — focal_tversky
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

alpha

a number — 0.5
Weight on false negatives, as in tversky, with false positives taking 1 - alpha.

gamma

a number — 1.0
Exponent on the Tversky index, which is where this differs from tversky: above 1 it concentrates the gradient on the cases scoring badly. Note 1 is the default and means plain Tversky, not ‘off’.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.




generalized_dice
Dice with every class weighted by the inverse square of how much of the picture it occupies, so a rare class counts for more than an equal share rather than for less.

name

text — generalized_dice
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.




iou
Dice’s harsher twin: the same ordering, a lower number.

name

text — iou
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.




l1
Absolute error on a continuous target.

where

foreground or everywhere — foreground
Where the target means anything, and so where the error is averaged.
A continuous instance target is defined on the objects and undefined off them - there is no direction towards the centre for a pixel in no object - so the builder writes zero on the background. Measured on the 536 Data Science Bowl cases: the foreground is 13.97% of the pixels at 256x256 (13.48% at native size, 0.03% to 59.2% per case, 167 cases under 5%), so everywhere spends 86% of the objective on a value a single output bias satisfies exactly.
foreground divides by the mask’s own total, which makes the number mean average error per object voxel. everywhere is the other defensible answer and is what CellPose and HoVer-Net’s plain regression terms do - their background zero is a real value rather than a missing one. Both are offered and neither is guessed; foreground is the default because it is the reading whose number means something.
foreground asks the loader for the mask, which is the same mechanism boundary uses for its distance map. It is never read off the target: a flow field is exactly zero at every object’s centre, so a mask taken from the non-zero voxels would drop precisely the seeds - and the seeds are what limits this approach (pyplatypus#211).

name

text — l1
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.




lovasz
Optimise the overlap you are going to report, rather than a proxy for it.

name

text — lovasz
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

per_image

true or false — false
Compute the loss for each image and average, rather than over the whole batch at once. Per image is the honest thing when images differ in how much of them is foreground, because otherwise a large object in one image dominates the batch; it is also noisier.




mse
Squared error on a continuous target.

where

foreground or everywhere — foreground
Where the target means anything, and so where the error is averaged.
A continuous instance target is defined on the objects and undefined off them - there is no direction towards the centre for a pixel in no object - so the builder writes zero on the background. Measured on the 536 Data Science Bowl cases: the foreground is 13.97% of the pixels at 256x256 (13.48% at native size, 0.03% to 59.2% per case, 167 cases under 5%), so everywhere spends 86% of the objective on a value a single output bias satisfies exactly.
foreground divides by the mask’s own total, which makes the number mean average error per object voxel. everywhere is the other defensible answer and is what CellPose and HoVer-Net’s plain regression terms do - their background zero is a real value rather than a missing one. Both are offered and neither is guessed; foreground is the default because it is the reading whose number means something.

It is never read off the target: a flow field is exactly zero at every object’s centre, so a mask taken from the non-zero voxels would drop precisely the seeds - and the seeds are what limits this approach (pyplatypus#211).

name

text — mse
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.




smooth_l1
mse close to the truth and l1 far from it, switching at beta.

where

foreground or everywhere — foreground
Where the target means anything, and so where the error is averaged.
A continuous instance target is defined on the objects and undefined off them - there is no direction towards the centre for a pixel in no object - so the builder writes zero on the background. Measured on the 536 Data Science Bowl cases: the foreground is 13.97% of the pixels at 256x256 (13.48% at native size, 0.03% to 59.2% per case, 167 cases under 5%), so everywhere spends 86% of the objective on a value a single output bias satisfies exactly.
foreground divides by the mask’s own total, which makes the number mean average error per object voxel. everywhere is the other defensible answer and is what CellPose and HoVer-Net’s plain regression terms do - their background zero is a real value rather than a missing one. Both are offered and neither is guessed; foreground is the default because it is the reading whose number means something.
foreground asks the loader for the mask, which is the same mechanism boundary uses for its distance map. It is never read off the target: a flow field is exactly zero at every object’s centre, so a mask taken from the non-zero voxels would drop precisely the seeds - and the seeds are what limits this approach (pyplatypus#211).

name

text — smooth_l1
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

beta

a number — 1.0
Where the quadratic part ends and the linear one begins, in the target’s own units. For a flow field scaled to roughly [-1, 1] the default makes the whole range quadratic, so lower it to get any of the robustness this loss is for.




tversky
Dice with a thumb on the scale: miss less, or over-segment less.

name

text — tversky
Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: tversky takes alpha, focal takes gamma, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

alpha

a number — 0.5
Weight on false negatives; raising it buys recall at the cost of precision, which is the trade a screening task usually wants. The weight on false positives is 1 - alpha and is not a separate key, so the two cannot disagree. At alpha 0.5 this is Dice exactly, but only when smooth is 0.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.





Metrics

cldice
Whether the structure is connected, rather than whether the voxels coincide.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.

include_background

true or false — false
False here where the other metrics default to True, and not for the usual reason. The background’s skeleton lies inside the background by construction, so that class scores 1.0 whatever the model did: measured on a 3-pixel vessel, averaging it in moved 0.7865 to 0.8933. It is not a flattering average, it is a number with no meaning in it.

name

text — cldice
Centreline Dice, which measures whether a structure is connected rather than whether its pixels coincide. A skeleton is a property of a whole mask, so on a tiled run (splits) it is reported per case by evaluate_cases, which reassembles a case’s tiles before measuring it. It is absent from the epoch and from the history there, because a per-batch average of a per-tile skeleton would be a number about nothing - which also means a callback cannot watch val_cldice on a tiled run, and the specification says so when it is read.

iterations

a whole number — 5
How many times the skeleton is peeled. It has to reach the half-width of the thickest structure or its core is never reduced to a centreline, and five covers a ten-pixel object. A retinal vessel is about nine pixels wide in the data - measured on FIVES as mask area over skeleton length, not the one to five often quoted, which is what a naive resize leaves behind - so five is enough for vessels and not much more than enough. Raise it for something thicker, at a cost linear in the number; too few is reported rather than scored, because an empty skeleton otherwise reads as a perfect 1.0.




dice
The number to report unless there is a reason not to.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.

include_background

true or false — true
Average over every class, background included. In medical images the background is often 95% of the pixels, so leaving it in flatters the score; papers usually report foreground only. Set false for that.

name

text — dice
Which metric. These are computed on the mask rather than on the objective, so they stay comparable between models trained on different losses.




iou
The same ordering as Dice, on the scale papers outside medicine use.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.

include_background

true or false — true
Average over every class, background included. In medical images the background is often 95% of the pixels, so leaving it in flatters the score; papers usually report foreground only. Set false for that.

name

text — iou
Which metric. These are computed on the mask rather than on the objective, so they stay comparable between models trained on different losses.




surface_dice
How much of each boundary lies within a tolerance of the other, rather than how much of the volume coincides.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.

include_background

true or false — false
False here where dice and iou default to True, and for a measured reason rather than the usual one. The background’s boundary is the foreground’s boundary plus the edge of the picture, and that edge agrees trivially between any two masks - so the background class reads high whatever the model did. Measured on four random pairs at tau 2: background 0.6110 to 0.7030 against foreground 0.5583 to 0.6266, higher every time, by 0.05 to 0.12. That is agreement on the field of view rather than on the object.

name

text — surface_dice
Normalised surface Dice: the fraction of each boundary lying within tau of the other. A surface is a property of a whole mask, so on a tiled run (splits) it is reported per case by evaluate_cases, which reassembles a case’s tiles first, and it is absent from the epoch history - a per-batch average of per-tile boundaries would be a number about nothing.

tau

a number — required
The tolerance, and it is required because no default is honest: a tolerance belongs to the structure and the dataset, and is conventionally the inter-observer variability for that structure - the distance two people drawing the same boundary differ by. Published values exist per organ and per challenge; take one from the protocol you are comparing against rather than from here. In millimetres when target_spacing puts the data on a common grid, and in voxels when it does not.




tversky
A score that can be asked to care more about what was missed.

smooth

a number — 1.0
Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.

include_background

true or false — true
Average over every class, background included. In medical images the background is often 95% of the pixels, so leaving it in flatters the score; papers usually report foreground only. Set false for that.

name

text — tversky
Which metric. These are computed on the mask rather than on the objective, so they stay comparable between models trained on different losses.

alpha

a number — 0.5
Weight on false negatives, with 1 - alpha on false positives - the same meaning as in the Tversky loss. At 0.5 this is Dice, so it is worth moving or not reporting at all: a Tversky metric at 0.5 beside a Dice metric is one number twice.





Optimisers

adadelta
Adagrad’s idea, bounded by a window instead of a sum.

learning_rate

a number — 0.001
How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.

weight_decay

a number — 0.0
Pull weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents.

name

text — adadelta
Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - sgd takes momentum, the Adam family takes beta_1 and beta_2. learning_rate and weight_decay are accepted by all of them.

rho

a number — 0.9
How long a window of squared gradients to remember. Adadelta exists to avoid Adagrad’s ever-shrinking step, and this is the parameter that does it.

eps

a number — 1e-06
Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. It is a guard, not a knob.




adagrad
Accumulates every squared gradient it has ever seen, and so slows to a stop.

learning_rate

a number — 0.001
How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.

weight_decay

a number — 0.0
Pull weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents.

name

text — adagrad
Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - sgd takes momentum, the Adam family takes beta_1 and beta_2. learning_rate and weight_decay are accepted by all of them.

lr_decay

a number — 0.0
Shrink the rate further as training goes on, on top of the shrinking Adagrad already does by accumulating every squared gradient it has seen. Adagrad’s step only ever gets smaller, which is why long runs with it can stop learning.

eps

a number — 1e-10
Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. It is a guard, not a knob.




adam
The one to use unless there is a reason not to.

learning_rate

a number — 0.001
How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.

weight_decay

a number — 0.0
Pull weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents.

name

text — adam
Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - sgd takes momentum, the Adam family takes beta_1 and beta_2. learning_rate and weight_decay are accepted by all of them.

beta_1

a number — 0.9
Decay for the running average of the gradient. Lower reacts to the last few batches, higher smooths over more of them; 0.9 is the usual value and rarely worth moving.

beta_2

a number — 0.999
Decay for the running average of the squared gradient, which is what scales each parameter’s step. Lowering it below about 0.99 makes training noticeably noisier.

eps

a number — 1e-08
Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. It is a guard, not a knob.

amsgrad

true or false — false
Keep the largest squared-gradient average seen so far rather than the current one, so the step size never grows back. It fixes a convergence case in Adam’s proof and usually changes nothing in practice; worth trying if a run plateaus and then gets worse.




adamax
Adam under the infinity norm, which a few huge batches cannot upset.

learning_rate

a number — 0.001
How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.

weight_decay

a number — 0.0
Pull weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents.

name

text — adamax
Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - sgd takes momentum, the Adam family takes beta_1 and beta_2. learning_rate and weight_decay are accepted by all of them.

beta_1

a number — 0.9
Decay for the running average of the gradient. Lower reacts to the last few batches, higher smooths over more of them; 0.9 is the usual value and rarely worth moving.

beta_2

a number — 0.999
As for Adam, except Adamax tracks the largest gradient seen rather than the average of their squares, which makes it the steadier of the two when a few batches carry very large gradients.

eps

a number — 1e-08
Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. It is a guard, not a knob.




adamw
Adam, with weight decay that actually decays the weights.

learning_rate

a number — 0.001
How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.

weight_decay

a number — 0.01
As for the other optimisers, but applied to the weights directly rather than through the gradient - which is the whole difference between AdamW and Adam, and why the default here is 0.01 rather than 0.

name

text — adamw
Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - sgd takes momentum, the Adam family takes beta_1 and beta_2. learning_rate and weight_decay are accepted by all of them.

beta_2

a number — 0.999
Decay for the running average of the squared gradient, which is what scales each parameter’s step. Lowering it below about 0.99 makes training noticeably noisier.

eps

nadam
Adam with the look-ahead that sgd calls nesterov.

learning_rate

Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.

weight_decay

a number — 0.0
Pull weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents.

alpha

a number — 0.99
Decay for the running average of the squared gradient - RmsProp’s name for what Adam calls beta_2, and it does the same work.

momentum

a number — 0.0
Carry a fraction of the previous step into this one. 0 is plain gradient descent; 0.9 is the usual choice and is what makes SGD competitive with the adaptive methods.

eps

a number — 1e-08

sgd
The plain step, and the one that rewards being tuned.

Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.
