name

text — sgd
Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - sgd takes momentum, the Adam family takes beta_1 and beta_2. learning_rate and weight_decay are accepted by all of them.

momentum

a number — 0.0
Carry a fraction of the previous step into this one. 0 is plain gradient descent; 0.9 is the usual choice and is what makes SGD competitive with the adaptive methods.

nesterov

true or false — false
Look ahead to where momentum is about to carry the weights before measuring the gradient. Needs momentum above 0, and giving it without momentum is refused rather than ignored.





Callbacks

cosine_annealing
Decay the learning rate along a cosine, from its initial value to min_lr.

name

text — cosine_annealing
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

min_lr

a number — 0.0
The rate at the last epoch, which the cosine decays to from the optimiser’s own learning_rate. Each parameter group decays from its own initial rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened at the first epoch - that would have been invisible, since the history records one learning_rate, the first group’s.

epochs

a whole number — unset
How many epochs to spread the decay over. Unset means the model’s epochs, which is what you want: a cosine that ends where the run ends. Setting it shorter parks the rate at min_lr for the remaining epochs, and longer stops the run part way down the curve.




csv_logger
The history, written as it arrives.

name

text — csv_logger
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

path

text — required
Where to append one row per epoch. The same numbers fit() returns, written as they arrive - so a run that is interrupted still leaves its history behind.




early_stopping
Stop when the watched number stops improving, and keep the weights that did.

name

text — early_stopping
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

monitor

text — val_loss
What to watch: val_loss, train_loss, or val_ followed by a metric the model asks for, such as val_dice. Whether the number should rise or fall is worked out from its name - anything ending in loss is minimised. Watching something no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built, and so is watching val_* in a run with validation: false, rather than waiting for a number that never arrives.

patience

a whole number — 10
Epochs to wait, with no improvement, before acting.

min_delta

a number — 0.0
Improvement smaller than this does not count as improvement. Useful where the watched number wanders: without it, noise alone keeps resetting the patience.

restore_best

true or false — true
Put the best weights back when training stops, rather than keeping the last - which are by definition the ones that were not improving. Note that swa replaces nothing if a run stops before averaging began.

start

a number — unset
Do not act before this fraction of the run has passed - 0.1 leaves the first tenth alone. Mutually exclusive with start_epoch: a fraction survives a change to epochs and an epoch count does not. Unset is no warm-up, which is what this callback did before 0.8.0a34.
It delays the stopping and nothing else. An epoch before the warm-up ends can still become the best one and restore_best can still return to it - those weights are the best the run has if it ends for some other reason, and throwing them away to tidy the bookkeeping would lose a real answer.

start_epoch

a whole number — unset
Do not act before this epoch, 1-based. Mutually exclusive with start. This is the one to use when the warm-up is a property of the optimisation rather than of the run’s length - a schedule’s warm-up is fifteen epochs whether the run is 60 or 600.




ema
An exponential moving average of the weights, updated every optimiser step.

name

text — ema
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

decay

a number — 0.999
How much of the average survives each step. 0.999 is the usual value and means a half-life of about 700 steps - roughly three and a half epochs at 200 batches each. Per step, not per epoch, so the published values transfer: a run with few steps wants a smaller number, because an average that forgets more slowly than the run is long never leaves its starting point. The model is replaced by the average when training ends.




linear_annealing
Decay the learning rate in a straight line, from its initial value to min_lr.

name

text — linear_annealing
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

min_lr

a number — 0.0
The rate at the last epoch, which the line descends to from the optimiser’s own learning_rate. Each parameter group descends from its own initial rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened at the first epoch.

epochs

a whole number — unset
How many epochs to spread the decay over. Unset means the model’s epochs, which is what you want: a line that reaches min_lr where the run ends. Setting it shorter parks the rate at min_lr for the remaining epochs.




model_checkpoint
The run’s safety net - one file, overwritten.

name

text — model_checkpoint
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

path

text — required
Where to write the checkpoint. One file, overwritten - this is the run’s safety net, not a history; export_weights() is what produces a file to publish, with a sidecar recording what it is. The extension decides the format: .safetensors is written as safetensors and anything else as a torch archive, which is what .pt has always meant here. Reading does not depend on the name - both formats are recognised by their contents - so a file written by an older version still loads under whatever it was called.

monitor

text — val_loss
What to watch: val_loss, train_loss, or val_ followed by a metric the model asks for, such as val_dice. Whether the number should rise or fall is worked out from its name - anything ending in loss is minimised. Watching something no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built, and so is watching val_* in a run with validation: false, rather than waiting for a number that never arrives.

save_best_only

true or false — true
Write only when the watched number improves. With false every epoch is written, which is what to use when a run may be interrupted rather than when the best epoch is wanted.

when

a mapping — unset
Thresholds that must all hold before anything is written: {val_dice: 0.9, val_loss: 0.2} writes nothing until the model is at least that good. Each key is a quantity this model reports, checked when the specification is built rather than at the first epoch.
The direction is derived, not configured. Anything ending in loss has to be below its threshold and everything else above it, which is the same rule monitor already uses - so there is no above/below to get backwards.
This is an extra gate, not a replacement for save_best_only. With both, a file is written when the watched number improves and every threshold holds.
A threshold is a number about your data. Unlike patience or factor it does not transfer: val_dice: 0.9 copied from somebody else’s configuration means something entirely different on other images. And a run whose conditions never hold writes nothing at all - the callback says so when the run ends, rather than leaving an empty directory to be discovered later.




reduce_lr_on_plateau
Cut the learning rate when the evidence says the run has stalled.

name

text — reduce_lr_on_plateau
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

monitor

text — val_loss
What to watch: val_loss, train_loss, or val_ followed by a metric the model asks for, such as val_dice. Whether the number should rise or fall is worked out from its name - anything ending in loss is minimised. Watching something no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built, and so is watching val_* in a run with validation: false, rather than waiting for a number that never arrives.

factor

a number — 0.1
Multiply the learning rate by this when the watched number stops moving.

patience

a whole number — 5
Epochs to wait, with no improvement, before acting.

min_lr

a number — 0.0
The floor the rate will not go below. Unlike cosine_annealing, this one acts on evidence rather than on a schedule, so it may never fire at all - which is why it is not refused alongside swa and a cosine is.




step_decay
Multiply the learning rate by factor at fixed points in the run.

name

text — step_decay
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

factor

a number — 0.1
What the rate is multiplied by at each drop. 0.1 is the usual recipe’s divide by ten. It must be below 1: a step schedule that raises the rate is a different idea with different arguments, and silently accepting it here would hide a typo.

every

a whole number — unset
Drop every this many epochs. Mutually exclusive with milestones - one of the two, never both. A period survives a change to epochs, where a list of milestones does not, so this is the one to prefer when the schedule is yours rather than somebody else’s.

milestones

a list of whole numbers — unset
The epochs to drop at, 1-based, as a published recipe states them - [30, 60] is divide by ten at thirty and again at sixty. Mutually exclusive with every. Strictly increasing, and an epoch past the end of the run is refused rather than ignored, because a milestone that never fires is almost always a number that was meant to fire.

min_lr

a number — 0.0
The floor the drops stop at, as in reduce_lr_on_plateau.




stop_after
End the run on the clock, whatever the epochs say.

name

text — stop_after
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

hours

a number — required
The budget, in hours. Checked at the end of each epoch, so the real limit is this plus one epoch - said here rather than discovered, because on a long arm that remainder is twenty minutes. The run’s stop_reason names the clock, so a run that ran out of time does not read as a run that converged.




swa
Average the weights over the last part of the run instead of taking the final ones.

name

text — swa
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

start

a number — 0.75
The fraction of the run after which averaging begins - 0.75 folds the last quarter. A fraction rather than an epoch so that it survives a change to epochs, and the final epoch is always folded, so 1.0 averages one set of weights rather than none.

start_epoch

a whole number — unset
Do not act before this epoch, 1-based. Mutually exclusive with start. This is the one to use when the warm-up is a property of the optimisation rather than of the run’s length - a schedule’s warm-up is fifteen epochs whether the run is 60 or 600. For swa that is the epoch averaging begins at, and it is the same concept early_stopping names with these two words.

learning_rate

a number — unset
Hold the rate at this value once averaging begins. Unset leaves whatever the run was doing.
Worth setting, and the reason is the whole mechanism: averaging is only worth something while the weights are still moving. A rate that has decayed towards zero produces a set of nearly identical snapshots, and their average is the last one.




terminate_on_collapse
End the run when the model stops predicting any foreground at all.

name

text — terminate_on_collapse
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.

floor

a number — 0.0001
Below this share of foreground the prediction counts as collapsed. A floor rather than exactly zero, because a model predicting 0.01% foreground on a target that is 14% foreground has collapsed in every sense that matters. The default is deliberately far below any real target: this is a guard against a failure, not a quality threshold, and a floor near a real foreground share would end runs that were merely bad.

patience

a whole number — 3
Epochs in a row below the floor before the run ends. An early epoch legitimately predicts almost nothing, which is why this is not 1.

monitor

text — val_foreground
Which foreground share to watch. train_foreground is the other one, and it answers a different question: a model collapsing on the training data has a different problem from one collapsing only on data it has not seen.




terminate_on_nan
End the run the moment the loss stops being a number.

name

text — terminate_on_nan
Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.





Separations

flows
A unit vector field pointing at each object’s sink, plus the semantic channels.

name

text — flows
Which separation signal, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: rim takes width, flows takes mode, loss and weight. A setting that belongs to the other mechanism is not refused here, it is unwritable - width under name: flows is an unknown key, which is the answer every typo in a specification gets.
That is this block’s reason to be a block, and it was built flat first: separation: rim beside rim_width, flow_mode, flow_loss and flow_weight. The flat form parses, so it needs a validator and a table of which field belongs to which mechanism to refuse half of what it accepts, and it shows every reader four fields of which two can apply to them. This form shows a reader of name: rim one field, and the refusal is gone rather than written - extra="forbid" was already doing that job for every other key in the file.

mode

centroid or diffusion — diffusion
How the vector field is built: towards each object’s centroid in a straight line, or down the gradient of heat diffused inside it.
diffusion is the default because the two were measured on the ground truth before anything was trained: decoded back into objects they reach 0.9924 and 0.9478. The obvious explanation for the gap is not the cause - only 19 of 6000 objects have their centroid outside themselves, 0.32% - and the real one is one level down: a straight line between two pixels of a discrete set can leave the set even when the object looks convex, which splits an object whose own centroid is inside it.
centroid is 23 times cheaper to build (4.9 ms a case against 113.6 ms), which is the reason to reach for it and is small beside an epoch.

loss

one of boundary, cce, cce_dice, combo, dice, focal, focal_tversky, generalized_dice, iou, l1, lovasz, mse, smooth_l1, tversky — unset
The objective on the two vector channels, which is a different question from the model’s own loss - that one scores the mask. A continuous target has nothing in the overlap-and-cross-entropy losses to be trained against, so this is one of mse, l1 or smooth_l1, and anything else is refused by name: loss: dice against a vector field would return a number and a gradient, which is the worst available outcome.
Left unset it is mse with where: foreground, which is what the measured run used. where is the field to read before changing it, because the foreground is 13.97% of a Data Science Bowl image and everywhere spends 86% of the objective on a background zero.

weight

a number — 1.0
How much the vector term counts against the mask term, which are summed. The default is 1.0 and it is measured rather than conventional: on the 60-epoch run the two terms are the same order of magnitude throughout - 0.5937 against 0.6345 after the first epoch and 0.0734 against 0.0659 at the last - so neither half of the objective is drowning the other at this weight.




rim
Background, object interior, object rim - three classes, one extra channel.

name

text — rim
Which separation signal, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: rim takes width, flows takes mode, loss and weight. A setting that belongs to the other mechanism is not refused here, it is unwritable - width under name: flows is an unknown key, which is the answer every typo in a specification gets.
That is this block’s reason to be a block, and it was built flat first: separation: rim beside rim_width, flow_mode, flow_loss and flow_weight. The flat form parses, so it needs a validator and a table of which field belongs to which mechanism to refuse half of what it accepts, and it shows every reader four fields of which two can apply to them. This form shows a reader of name: rim one field, and the refusal is gone rather than written - extra="forbid" was already doing that job for every other key in the file.

width

a whole number — 2
How many pixels wide the rim class is, in pixels of the model’s own input - so it means the same thing whether the image was resized or tiled, because the target is built after the resize and the augmentation rather than before (pyplatypus#210).
There is a measured sweep of this quantity and it is not a sweep of this field, which is worth knowing before quoting either. Four runs differing in nothing else scored 0.5169, 0.5486, 0.5587 and 0.5306 of instance average precision at widths 1 to 4, against a 0.0074 spread between two runs of one configuration - but that pipeline derived the rim at the source resolution and resized the three-class map afterwards. A Data Science Bowl case is around 520 pixels and the model reads 256, so the peak of that sweep is roughly 1.5 pixels of model input, not 3. The default is the nearest width above it. A sweep in these units has not been run.
What that sweep does establish is the shape of the trade, which is the part that transfers: a rim wide enough to learn is wide enough to hollow the object out, so rim Dice climbed 0.48 to 0.76 across those widths while interior Dice fell 0.90 to 0.81, and past the peak the model found more regions and matched fewer of them. Both halves are reported per run, because a single instance number cannot say which of them moved.





Decodings

connected_components
Label the thresholded foreground and ignore the separation signal entirely.

name

text — connected_components
Which decoding, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - follow_flows takes steps and step_size, the others do not. A decoding the chosen separation cannot feed is refused by name with both halves stated, rather than returning a label map of something else.

minimum_area

a whole number — 0
Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. 0 keeps everything, which is the default because the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method - a nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor chosen here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another.
It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.




follow_flows
Follow the field from every foreground pixel and label the basins they arrive in.

name

text — follow_flows
Which decoding, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - follow_flows takes steps and step_size, the others do not. A decoding the chosen separation cannot feed is refused by name with both halves stated, rather than returning a label map of something else.

minimum_area

a whole number — 0
Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. 0 keeps everything, which is the default because the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method - a nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor chosen here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another.
It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.

steps

a whole number — 200
How many Euler steps each pixel takes. Measured as not mattering: one step scores 0.9914 against 0.9923 converged, a span below the 0.0013 two runs differ by. The field is continuous, so one object’s pixels stay together, and it diverges at a seam, so the gap between two objects opens on the first step rather than after many. Left adjustable because that argument is about this data’s object sizes, and lowering it is the cheap thing to try on larger ones.

step_size

a number — 1.0
How far one step moves, in pixels, on a unit-length field. This one is a cliff: 0.9923 at 1.0, 0.4715 at 2.0, 0.0303 at 10.0. A step longer than a pixel jumps over the sink it was converging on and lands in a neighbour’s basin, so this is not a speed knob - raise it and the decoding stops working.




nearest_seed
Grow the predicted interiors outward: every other foreground pixel joins the nearest.

name

text — nearest_seed
Which decoding, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - follow_flows takes steps and step_size, the others do not. A decoding the chosen separation cannot feed is refused by name with both halves stated, rather than returning a label map of something else.

a whole number — 0

It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.




watershed
Flood the foreground from the predicted interiors, over the rim evidence as terrain.

name

text — watershed
Which decoding, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - follow_flows takes steps and step_size, the others do not. A decoding the chosen separation cannot feed is refused by name with both halves stated, rather than returning a label map of something else.

minimum_area

Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. 0 keeps everything, which is the default because the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method - a nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor chosen here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another.

title: DetectionReport
text:
DetectionReport
DetectionReport(model, split, half, coco, at_operating_point)
One model on one split, under the three sets of conventions a table needs.
Held as one object because they come from one pass over the data and because the conventions are part of the result: the same predictions score differently at IoU 0.5 and averaged over 0.50-0.95, and precision and recall mean nothing without a confidence to read them at.

title: ellipse_axes
text:
ellipse_axes(mask, spacing=None)
The semi-axes of the ellipse a region implies, major first.
For a uniform filled ellipse the covariance of the member coordinates has eigenvalues a^2 / 4 and b^2 / 4, so the axes come out of an eigendecomposition of a 2x2 matrix and nothing is fitted iteratively.
It measures the region it is given and repairs nothing, which matters for a prediction: pass it through largest_filled_object first, or use ellipse_circumference, which does.

title: Engine.best_model
text:
Engine.best_model(key='dice', split='validation')
Rank the models on one column.
Refuses to rank on loss when the models were not trained on the same one. Two losses are two different scales: a Focal-Tversky of 0.05 is not better than a CCE-Dice of 0.14, it is not even the same question. Metrics are comparable because they measure the mask, not the objective.

'dice'

    root,
    out_dir,
    *,
    mode=DataMode.NESTED_DIRS,

    seed=0,

    relative=True,
    label_column='masks',
)
Split one folder of data into three CSVs a specification can point at.
The whole point of the function: a researcher has one directory and needs train_path, validation_path and test_path. Returns the paths it wrote plus the counts, so the caller can see what happened without opening the files.
label_column names the second column, and it has to match what the specification will look for - masks for segmentation, annotations for detection. Not derived from subdirs, although that would read well: someone whose directories are called img and lbl has always got a masks column out of this, and deriving it would quietly write a file their existing configuration could no longer read.
The other way to divide one folder is the specification’s own split block, which partitions the samples in memory and writes nothing. Use this one when the CSVs are the point - to keep, to hand to a colleague, or to cite in a paper.

One row per model: the comparison table the whole multi-model idea is for.











Name
Type
Description
Default




split
str
Which data to score on.
'validation'


at
str
Which grid to score on. "model" is each model’s own load_shape and the default, because changing it would silently restate every number anybody has already written down. "source" puts every prediction back on the grid of the file it came from and scores it against the truth as stored, so the rows answer one question.
'model'














Name
Type
Description





list[dict[str, Any]]
One row per model: what it is, how long it trained, its loss and its metrics.



list[dict[str, Any]]
The loss column is comparable only between models trained on the same



list[dict[str, Any]]
objective, which is why loss_function sits beside it - and the metrics are



list[dict[str, Any]]
comparable only between models scored on the same grid, which is why



list[dict[str, Any]]
load_shape sits beside them.



load_shape is the second of those and the one nothing used to say. At at="model" each model is scored through its own loader, so a model at input_shape: [512, 512] is measured against a truth reduced to 512 while a model that tiles 2048 is measured against the truth as stored. Both numbers are a real Dice of a real prediction against a real mask; they are not answers to the same question. Measured on retinal vessels (maju116/rplatypus#187), that difference reported a resized model at +0.0187 where the honest figure was +0.0033, with the bias reversed on clDice because upsampling smooths a prediction - better against a skeleton, worse against a boundary. So when the rows do not share a grid this says so, once, rather than leaving a table that looks like a comparison.
at="source" is what that warning now points at. The truth is never resampled - only predictions move - which is why the grid is the files’ own rather than one the caller names: a named grid interpolates the very thing every model is being judged against. The column then reads source, because what it has always meant is the grid this row’s numbers were computed on.
Two things that are the price of it, neither recoverable: interpolating probabilities softens a boundary, and where the forward crop cut anatomy away the inverse pads it with background, which means not examined rather than nothing there. For a comparison the second is correct rather than unfair - a model whose field of view did not contain the organ did not segment it - but a 0.000 arriving that way is a result and not a bug.
The loss is not reported at at="source". A loss is defined by the objective a model was trained with, on the grid it was trained on; re-deriving one from a resampled prediction would be a number with no training meaning and a column somebody would compare.
The pooling is the same in both: the mean over cases. That has been the claim here since at was added and became true in 0.8.0a40 - until then this branch passed no case names and reported the mean over batches, so the sentence described a pooling the code did not do and the comment in the at="source" branch rested on it. maju116/rplatypus#196.
A case’s own score is a ratio of sums - its tiles’ counts added, the formula applied once - and the split’s is the mean of those. evaluate_cases pools a group the same way, by adding the counts of the images in it, which is a different number again and the better statistic for a patient: summarise_cases is where to read it. So at changes the grid and nothing else, and the gap between its two values is the rig it exists to measure rather than that gap plus a change of definition.

Type
Description

If the split carries no masks - and the message says predict works on it, because that is the question asked next.

)

The comparison table answers “which model”; this answers “on whom does it fail”, which is the question a clinician asks first and the one a single mean cannot answer. Engine.predict(model_name=None, split='test', *, space='model')
Class probabilities, channels-last, one array per source image.
Tiles are reassembled, so an image that went in at 2048x1536 comes back at 2048x1536 rather than as 24 unrelated pieces.
space decides which grid the answer is on, and the two are different enough that the return type differs with it:

"model" - one stacked array, every prediction on the model’s grid. What training saw, and the only form that can be a single array, since a stack requires one shape.
"source" - a list, one array per sample, each on the grid of the file it came from. What a person asked for when they asked to segment their scan: it can be laid over that scan, written beside it, or measured in millilitres of its voxels. Sources differ in size, so this cannot be stacked, and pretending otherwise by silently resizing is how a mask ends up describing the wrong anatomy.

predict returns a stacked array, so the whole split has to fit in memory. For a tiled split that is the whole thing at full resolution - 200 FIVES retinas at 2048 is 6.7 GB for the result alone - and tiling exists precisely for images too large to resize, so the stacked form is least usable exactly where splits is most needed. This yields one image, lets the caller keep what it wants, and drops it.
The case name comes with the prediction rather than being left to the caller to line up against samples: predictions arrive in the dataset’s order, and anything that pairs two sequences by position is one drop_last away from scoring the wrong image. group_of turns a case into a group the same way evaluate_cases does.

The loss is not reported at at="source". A loss is defined by the objective a model was trained with, on the grid it was trained on; re-deriving one from a resampled prediction would be a number with no training meaning and a column somebody would compare.
The pooling is the same in both: the mean over cases. That has been the claim here since at was added and became true in 0.8.0a40 - until then this branch passed no case names and reported the mean over batches, so the sentence described a pooling the code did not do and the comment in the at="source" branch rested on it. maju116/rplatypus#196.
A case’s own score is a ratio of sums - its tiles’ counts added, the formula applied once - and the split’s is the mean of those. evaluate_cases pools a group the same way, by adding the counts of the images in it, which is a different number again and the better statistic for a patient: summarise_cases is where to read it. So at changes the grid and nothing else, and the gap between its two values is the rig it exists to measure rather than that gap plus a change of definition.

available_losses(task=Task.SEMANTIC_SEGMENTATION)
The losses you can name under loss, which is not the same list at every task.
Eleven at semantic_segmentation and fourteen at instance_segmentation, and the three in the difference are the regression family - mse, l1, smooth_l1. They score a continuous target, and the only continuous target this package has is a flow field, so at the semantic task there is nothing to name them on: a model’s own loss scores the classes, and SegmentationModel.the_mask_needs_a_loss_over_classes refuses them there by name (pyplatypus#223). At the instance task they are listed because a separation: flows block has its own loss for the vector channels - but not for the model’s own loss, which is the mask at either separation and refuses them too.

title: Separation
text:
Separation()
The signal that makes one mask into many objects.
One per model, because this is what the network is trained to predict: it sets the width of the head and which losses mean anything against it.
This enum is the vocabulary rather than the field. A specification names a signal inside a block - separation: {name: rim, width: 3} - so that the mechanism’s own settings sit in the mechanism they belong to, and _Separation.signal is what ties a block to its member here. The enum is what the numeric layer takes, because instance_target and decode_instances have to know the signal and must know nothing about the spec; it is also what a weights fingerprint records, since the settings change what the channels were trained towards and not what they are.
hv is deliberately not a member, and that absence is a measurement rather than a gap in the implementation. HoVer-Net’s two distance maps were swept both ways they can be turned into markers, on the ground truth, which is the test pyplatypus#213 set itself: the maps’ own zeros reach an instance average precision of 0.9382 and the published gradient route 0.7995, where a one-pixel erosion of the same truth reaches 0.9807 and plain connected components 0.7583. The better of the two recipes loses to the cheapest marker there is by 0.0425 on perfect inputs, so a trained one cannot win; #213 is closed measured-and-no. Naming the value would promise a mechanism this package measured as absent.





Name
Description




semantic_from
The first channel of the class block, which is where the mask is read from.









Name
Description




head_channels
How wide the output has to be for this signal, given what the data names.





Separation.head_channels(n_class)
How wide the output has to be for this signal, given what the data names.
Derived, never stated, and that is the whole of this method’s reason to exist. n_class already comes from the data - a model restating it could only disagree with its own masks, which is a mistake this package made once and fixed - and the two new targets add channels of their own: rim adds the third class and flows adds two continuous ones in front of the semantic block. A field saying channels: 4 would be a setting that can lie about the target it was built for, and the shape error it causes surfaces deep inside torch rather than here.
It is also the one line that forced examples/train_instance_flows.py to assemble its model outside Engine and call build_model(spec, n_class=4) by hand.



Separation.RIM.head_channels(2), Separation.FLOWS.head_channels(2) (3, 4)

title: Engine.predict_stream
text:
Engine.predict_stream(model_name=None, split='test', *, space='model')
(case, prediction) one source image at a time, instead of all of them at once.
predict returns a stacked array, so the whole split has to fit in memory. For a tiled split that is the whole thing at full resolution - 200 FIVES retinas at 2048 is 6.7 GB for the result alone - and tiling exists precisely for images too large to resize, so the stacked form is least usable exactly where splits is most needed. This yields one image, lets the caller keep what it wants, and drops it.
The case name comes with the prediction rather than being left to the caller to line up against samples: predictions arrive in the dataset’s order, and anything that pairs two sequences by position is one drop_last away from scoring the wrong image. group_of turns a case into a group the same way evaluate_cases does.

The shared base of SegmentationSpec and DetectionSpec.
Not built directly - data and models live on the subclasses, because their types are what task selects. from_dict and from_yaml return whichever one the task asks for, and both are instances of this, so anything that only needs a name, a seed or a rank can take a PlatypusSpec and not care.

Constraining the algorithms while the draw still varies buys nothing.

All models in a spec share one data pipeline, so they share one rank. Mixing

PlatypusSpec.deterministic_needs_a_seed()
Constraining the algorithms while the draw still varies buys nothing.

Without seed the initialisation, the shuffle and the augmentation all still differ, so the run is exactly as unrepeatable as before and only slower - and slower by an amount nobody can see the reason for. Refused here rather than warned about, because this is one of the two halves of the promise and a half promise is what platypus#122 was filed about.

All models in a spec share one data pipeline, so they share one rank. Mixing 2D and 3D in a single run is a mistake, not a feature.

Say what is wrong directly. Without this, PlatypusSpec(data=..., models=...) fails as two ‘extra inputs are not permitted’ errors, which describes the symptom and not the cause.

title: save_spec
text:
save_spec(spec, path, *, defaults=False)
Write a specification back out as YAML - what was set, not what it holds.
from_yaml reads a configuration and PlatypusSpec builds one in code; this is the way back, so the two interfaces are one pipeline rather than one and a half. A worked example can write the YAML of the run it has just done beside the results, and a specification assembled in R or Python can become the file somebody else runs.
It writes the fields that were set. Not the fields the object holds, which on a two-field model is 29 of them - and the difference is not verbosity. A model given weights and no architecture adopts the architecture from the weights sidecar, and that adoption fires on architecture not being in model_fields_set. Dump the defaults into the file and the reloaded specification has all 29 set, so the adoption can never fire again: the file would look like the original and quietly stop doing what it did. R paid for this once already in the other direction (JOURNAL.md §4aa) and dropped its own defaults for the same reason.
defaults=True is the opposite want, which is legitimate and is a second mode rather than the default: freeze this run exactly as it resolved, so it reproduces in five years. The cost is the one above - the file stops adopting anything, by design.
Every discriminator is always written, whatever was set. task is the obvious one - it is what from_yaml dispatches on, and a configuration that does not say what it is asking for means whatever the version reading it decides. The same is true one level down and is easier to miss: DiceLoss(smooth=0.5) sets smooth and not name, because name is a Literal with a default, so a dump of what was set alone writes loss: {smooth: 0.5} - a block with no tag, which comes back as Unable to extract tag using discriminator ‘name’. A field annotated Literal is a tag here, and tags survive.











Name
Type
Description
Default




spec
PlatypusSpec
The specification to write. Either task.
required


path
str | Path
Where to write it. The parent directory must exist.
required


defaults
bool
Write every field at its resolved value, including the ones nobody set.
False














Name
Type
Description





Path
The path written, so a caller can log or return it.






import tempfile, pathlib from pyplatypus.spec import SegmentationSpec, SegmentationData, SegmentationModel spec = SegmentationSpec( … data=SegmentationData( … train_path=“train/”, validation_path=“valid/”, … colormap=[[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]], … ), … models=[SegmentationModel(name=“m”, input_shape=(32, 32))], … ) path = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / “spec.yaml” _ = save_spec(spec, path) sorted(yaml.safe_load(path.read_text())[“models”][0]) [‘input_shape’, ‘name’] frozen = save_spec(spec, path.with_name(“frozen.yaml”), defaults=True) len(yaml.safe_load(frozen.read_text())[“models”][0]) 29

title: InstanceEngine.evaluate
text:
InstanceEngine.evaluate(split='validation')
One row per model and decoding: the comparison this task is for.
A decoding costs a hundredth of an epoch, so the table gains an axis for nearly nothing.
This paragraph used to say connected_components is in every model’s rows whether it was asked for or not, and it is not. It is in the pair decode derives to when a model stayed silent, which is the signal’s own decoding plus the yardstick; a model that writes a decode list gets the list it wrote and nothing added. That is the right behaviour - the engine does not put a row in somebody’s table that they did not ask for - and the claim was wrong rather than the code: the only test on it covered the derived case, and examples/compare_instance_separations.py keeps the yardstick in its own --decode handling precisely because nothing below does it. test_a_written_decode_list_is_what_you_get is the half that was missing.
The reason the yardstick belongs in a comparison is unchanged and is why the derivation includes it: it ignores the separation signal, so it is the row the signal’s row has to be read against.

title: InstanceSpec
text:
InstanceSpec()
Objects rather than classes: which object every pixel belongs to, scored as instances.
The same images and the same U-shaped networks as semantic_segmentation, with the masks read one file per object instead of united into one. Two fields are new on a model - separation, what the network predicts, and decode, a list of ways to turn those channels into objects - and pyplatypus.spec.instances is where both are documented, measurements included.
What this task is honestly worth, said here because the tag’s name promises more. A reader who writes task: instance_segmentation gets a semantic model with a separation target, decoded into objects and scored by the Data Science Bowl’s own average precision. On that dataset the separation signal is worth +0.068 at best while a perfect mask is worth +0.2398, so the limit is the mask rather than the separation - and connected_components, which ignores the signal entirely, is always available as the row every other row is read against. The capability is real, the ceiling is measured, and both are in the documentation rather than in a footnote.

title: overlay_instances
text:
overlay_instances(
    image,
    labels,
    alpha=OVERLAY_ALPHA,
    outline=False,
    colours=None,
)
An instance label map over its image, coloured so no two touching objects match.
The rule is adjacency rather than identity, and it is stated here rather than left to luck: a colour repeats across the picture and never between neighbours. See the comment above _adjacent_pairs for the measurement that made the exact colouring the cheap option rather than the expensive one.
A picture that needs more colours than the palette has gets a UserWarning, naming how many it needs and how many objects lost the guarantee. The slot wraps onto a colour a neighbour already holds - provably, since a slot is only past the end of the palette once every colour before it was taken by a neighbour - so two touching objects are drawn as one and this figure answers its own question wrongly. That is the one failure it is for, so it is said rather than hidden. Unreachable on anything measured here: the hardest of 670 Data Science Bowl cases needs 3 of the 8 colours in the default palette.

Type
Description
Default

np.ndarray
one image, as overlay_mask takes it.
required


labels
np.ndarray
an instance label map, one integer per object and 0 for background.
required


alpha
float
how much of the tint shows. Ignored when outline is true, where a stroke is drawn at full strength - a translucent outline is a smudge.
OVERLAY_ALPHA


outline
bool
draw one stroke per object instead of filling it, which is what a pathologist is used to and what leaves the tissue entirely visible.
False


colours
list[str] | None
the palette to take slots from. Defaults to the engine’s CLASS_COLOURS, which the R package reads too.
None

available_weights()
Registry names and what they are, for listing to a user.
Named to match available_weights() in the R package and available_transforms() here: everything a user can be offered a list of answers to the same verb.
Read the descriptions rather than only the names. What a model cannot do decides whether it answers your question: the nuclei weights are semantic, so touching nuclei come back as one region and a count taken from them would be wrong.

Type
Description

listing = available_weights() sorted(listing) [‘bccd-yolo3’, ‘dsbowl-instances’, ‘dsbowl-unet’, ‘fives-unet’, ‘hc18-unet’] “BBBC038v1” in listing[“dsbowl-unet”] True listing[“dsbowl-unet”].startswith(“U-Net, 256x256”) True

title: save_class_masks
text:
save_class_masks(
    prediction,
    directory,
    *,
    classes,
    cases=None,
    threshold=0.5,
    suffix='',
)
One binary picture per class, which is how an overlapping prediction reaches disk.
onehot_to_colours refuses a prediction where a voxel is in two classes at once, and its refusal says overlapping classes are written one file per class. This is that file per class. regions gives a channel per named region and a sigmoid per channel, so the channels neither compete nor sum to one, and the only lossless thing a picture can hold is one channel.
Each file is <case><suffix>_<region>.png, mode L, 0 or 255 - a mask anything opens and anything thresholds back, rather than a colour that has to be looked up. The class name goes through class_filename, so whole tumour is whole_tumour on disk.
The argument is classes rather than names because the R package’s save_masks and save_volumes already use names for the files they write, and a sibling writer where the same word means the classes instead is the quiet kind of mistake: a call copied from one to the other would pass filenames as class names, the counts would match whenever they happened to, and nothing would refuse it.
What this does not do is decide for you. A channel where nothing reaches threshold is written as an empty picture rather than skipped: a missing file reads as “this run did not produce that class”, and an empty one reads as “it did and the answer was nothing”, which are different findings and only one of them is true.











Name
Type
Description
Default




prediction
np.ndarray
Channels-last probabilities or a one-hot array, either (h, w, c) for one image or (n, h, w, c) for a stack. A volume cannot come here: a PNG carries no voxel spacing and no orientation, so a volume mask written as pictures cannot be laid back over the scan it was computed from. Only rank 5 is refused, because a single volume (d, h, w, c) and a stack of images have the same rank and nothing in the array can tell them apart.
required


directory
str | Path
Where to write. Created, with parents, if it does not exist.
required


classes
Sequence[str]
One name per channel, in channel order - [region.name for region in spec.data.regions]. Channel order is the order the regions were written in, which is also the order every per-class score is reported in.
required


cases
Sequence[str] | None
One name per image, usually the source filenames’ stems. Defaults to mask_0001 and so on.
None


threshold
float
A channel is hot where it reaches this. 0.5 is what every metric in the package thresholds a multilabel channel at, so a different number here writes a picture that disagrees with the score printed beside it.
0.5


suffix
str
Added before the class, so two models can write into one directory.
''

The paths written, image by image and within an image channel by channel.

title: Task
text:
Task
Task()
What the models in a spec are being asked to do.
One task per spec, not one per model: every model in a spec shares a data pipeline, and masks and bounding boxes are not the same pipeline. It decides the type of data and of every entry in models, which is why it is a discriminator rather than a setting - a detection spec holding a colormap is not a spec with an odd field in it, it is two different intentions in one file.

title: split_samples
text:
split_samples(samples, *, fractions=(0.7, 0.15, 0.15), group_by=None, seed=0)
Divide samples between the splits, keeping every group whole.
Deterministic: the same samples, fractions, pattern and seed give the same split on any machine. That is not a nicety - a split that moves between runs makes two results incomparable, and the reason for a difference becomes impossible to find.
Groups are shuffled, then handed out one at a time to whichever split is furthest below its target share in samples. Assigning by group count instead would drift badly whenever groups differ in size, which for patients they always do.











Name
Type
Description
Default




samples
Sequence[Sample]
What was discovered. Nothing is read from disk here - this partitions a list, so a specification with a split block gains no side effect on disk.
required


fractions
Sequence[float] | Mapping[str, float]
Two or three, summing to one: train, validation, and optionally test. A mapping names them instead, for a split that is not in that order.
(0.7, 0.15, 0.15)


group_by
str | None
A regular expression read against each sample’s key; everything sharing a group lands in exactly one split. None means every sample is its own group, which is right only when the samples are genuinely independent - slices of one patient are not.
None


seed
int
Which shuffle. The split is otherwise deterministic.
0














Name
Type
Description





Split
A Split, with train, validation and test tuples and the group each sample



Split
was assigned to.














Name
Type
Description





SplitError
If the fractions are not two or three, if group_by matches no sample key - a pattern that matches nothing is a mistake, not an empty result - or if there are fewer groups than splits to fill.






from pyplatypus.data.paths import Sample import pathlib samples = [ … Sample(key=f”patient{p:02d}_slice{s}“, images=(pathlib.Path(”x.png”),)) … for p in range(1, 5) … for s in range(3) … ] len(samples) 12 split = split_samples(samples, fractions=(0.5, 0.5), group_by=r”^(patient)_“) len(split.train) + len(split.validation) 12



A patient is never on both sides, which is the whole point:



def patients(part): … return {key.split(“_“)[0] for key in (sample.key for sample in part)} patients(split.train) & patients(split.validation) set()



Without group_by, every slice is its own group and the same patient lands in both - which makes validation measure memory rather than generalisation:



loose = split_samples(samples, fractions=(0.5, 0.5)) bool(patients(loose.train) & patients(loose.validation)) True

The reader every other part of this package uses, which is the reason it is public: a picture drawn from a differently resized copy is a picture of something the model never saw, and the disagreements it shows may be the resizing rather than the model. Boxes come back from predict in the source image’s own pixels, so drawing them needs the image at size=None.
Scaled to 0-1 for anything read in real units (DICOM, NIfTI) and left at 0-255 for ordinary pictures, which to_float divides later. Both are drawable: the plotting functions decide by the range rather than by the dtype.
DICOM is detected by content rather than by extension, because exports out of an archive frequently carry no extension or one the archive invented. A directory of slices is read as one volume, so a CSV may name a series directory in the column that names a file.

title: Engine.predict
text:
Engine.predict(model_name=None, split='test', *, space='model')
Class probabilities, channels-last, one array per source image.
Tiles are reassembled, so an image that went in at 2048x1536 comes back at 2048x1536 rather than as 24 unrelated pieces.
space decides which grid the answer is on, and the two are different enough that the return type differs with it:

"model" - one stacked array, every prediction on the model’s grid. What training saw, and the only form that can be a single array, since a stack requires one shape.
"source" - a list, one array per sample, each on the grid of the file it came from. What a person asked for when they asked to segment their scan: it can be laid over that scan, written beside it, or measured in millilitres of its voxels. Sources differ in size, so this cannot be stacked, and pretending otherwise by silently resizing is how a mask ends up describing the wrong anatomy.

Type
Description
Default




split
str
Which data to predict on.
'test'


model_name
str | None
Which model, by name. Defaults to the first.
None


space
str
"model" returns one stacked array on the network’s own grid. "source" maps each prediction back onto the grid of the scan it came from, undoing the resampling and the crop, and returns a list - scans differ in size, a stacked array needs one shape, and quietly resizing them to match is how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.
'model'

Type
Description






An array for space="model", a list for space="source".



Two losses in source space: interpolation softens a boundary, and where the forward crop cut anatomy away the inverse pads with background - which means not examined rather than nothing there.

title: Contributor Code of Conduct
text:
Contributor Code of Conduct
As contributors and maintainers of this project, we pledge to respect all people who contribute through reporting issues, posting feature requests, updating documentation, submitting pull requests or patches, and other activities.
We are committed to making participation in this project a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of level of experience, gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, disability, personal appearance, body size, race, ethnicity, age, or religion.
Examples of unacceptable behavior by participants include the use of sexual language or imagery, derogatory comments or personal attacks, trolling, public or private harassment, insults, or other unprofessional conduct.
Project maintainers have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct. Project maintainers who do not follow the Code of Conduct may be removed from the project team.
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported by opening an issue or contacting one or more of the project maintainers.
This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 1.0.0, available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/1/0/0/code-of-conduct.html
